title: Chinese: Pinyin and Tones
description: Hear, say, read and type Mandarin Chinese sounds from scratch: every initial and final, the four tones and the neutral tone, where the tone mark goes, the tone changes of 一, 不 and two third tones, erhua, ü and the apostrophe, and the whole syllable table, drilled by ear with your device's Chinese voice. Then your first characters, traced stroke by stroke with the basic rules of stroke order, and your first 25 words and greetings, learned through typed review cards (type pinyin with tone numbers). Written in simplified characters, with a switch to traditional. This course comes before Chinese HSK 1.
author: Erudior

modules.title: Honors: Pinyin and characters in depth

lessons.title: How Mandarin is written and said
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Mandarin Chinese looks hard from the outside: thousands of characters, and tones that change
the meaning of a word. Both are learnable, and this course takes them one step at a time. By the
end of it you'll be able to hear, say, read and type every Mandarin syllable with its tone, write
your first characters stroke by stroke, and use your first 25 words and greetings. Then you're
ready for Chinese HSK 1.

This first lesson is the map. It explains how Chinese is written, what pinyin is and what it is
for, how every syllable is built, and why the four tones matter. It ends with a short tour of
the tools this app gives you for Chinese. Say every example out loud: you'll learn the sounds with
your ears and your mouth, not only with your eyes.

## Characters: one syllable, one meaning

Chinese is written with characters, not letters. Each character is said as one **[[syllable]]**, and
almost every character also carries a meaning:

| Character | Said | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 人 | rén | person |
| 大 | dà | big |
| 中 | zhōng | middle |
| 国 | guó | country |

A word is one character or several. {人|rén} is a word on its own; {中国|Zhōng guó}, "the middle
country", is China. Most everyday words have two characters, some have three or four:

- {中国|Zhōng guó} — China (2 characters, 2 syllables)
- {学生|xué sheng} — student (2)
- {图书馆|tú shū guǎn} — library (3)
- {电子邮件|diàn zǐ yóu jiàn} — email (4)

The number of characters tells you the number of syllables (the one exception, an *-r* added to
a syllable, comes in lesson 12). That makes Chinese rhythm
easy to count: {图书馆|tú shū guǎn} has three characters, so you say three syllables.

Chinese is written without spaces between words, and a character's shape usually doesn't tell
you how to say it. A reader simply knows that 人 is *rén*. A learner needs a way to write the
sounds down, and that is what pinyin does.

## Pinyin: the sounds in Latin letters

**[[Hanyu Pinyin]]** ({拼音|pīn yīn} for short, "spelled sounds") is the official way to write
Mandarin in the Latin alphabet. It was adopted in mainland China in 1958 and is also the
international standard. You'll meet it in three places:

- Learning and dictionaries. Children's books, textbooks and dictionaries print pinyin to show
  how characters are said, the way this course does.
- Typing. Most people in mainland China type Chinese by typing pinyin on an ordinary keyboard
  and picking the character they want from a list.
- Names and signs. Street signs, maps and passports use pinyin for names: Beijing, Xi'an,
  Wang Fang.

What pinyin is *not* is a second way of writing Chinese. Nobody reads newspapers or messages in
pinyin; Chinese readers read characters. In this course pinyin is your guide to the sounds, and
it stays switched on until you no longer need it.

In the lessons you'll see pinyin in two ways. Over Chinese words it sits above each character:
{中国|Zhōng guó}. On its own, when we talk about a sound, it is written in *italics*: *zhōng*,
*guó*.

## A syllable: initial, final and tone

Every Mandarin syllable has the same three parts:

- the **[[initial]]**: the consonant at the start (*m*, *zh*, *x*…). Some syllables have none.
- the **[[final]]**: everything after it, the vowel part, which may end in *-n* or *-ng*
  (*a*, *ong*, *ue*…).
- the **[[tone]]**: the pitch pattern of the whole syllable, shown by the mark over a vowel.

| Character | Pinyin | Initial | Final | Tone |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 妈 (mother) | mā | m | a | 1st |
| 中 (middle) | zhōng | zh | ong | 1st |
| 学 (to study) | xué | x | üe (written *ue*) | 2nd |
| 我 (I, me) | wǒ | — | uo (written *wo*) | 3rd |
| 爱 (to love) | ài | — | ai | 4th |

Mandarin has 21 initials and about 35 finals, and they combine in only about 400 ways. With the
tones added, that makes around 1,300 different syllables, far fewer than English. This course
teaches the initials in groups over lessons 03 to 06 and the finals in lessons 03, 07 and 08.
The reference sheet "Initials, finals and tones" has them all on one page.

## Four tones

Say *ma* in English as a statement, then as a surprised question: "Ma." "Ma?" The pitch of your
voice changes, but the word stays the same. In Mandarin the pitch pattern is part of the word.
Change the tone and you have a different syllable with a different meaning:

| Tone | Mark | Pitch | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1st | ā | high and level, held steady | {妈|mā} | mother |
| 2nd | á | rising, like a question "huh?" | {麻|má} | hemp |
| 3rd | ǎ | low, dipping (it rises again only at the end of a phrase) | {马|mǎ} | horse |
| 4th | à | falling sharply from high, like a firm "No!" | {骂|mà} | to scold |

There is also a light, short **[[neutral tone]]** with no mark at all, like the *ma* at the end of
{妈妈|mā ma} (mum) and the question word {吗|ma}. Lesson 02 is all about the tones and the neutral
tone.

Tones aren't decoration. A tone mistake is a different word, just as *bit* and *bet* are different
words in English:

- {买|mǎi} to buy, {卖|mài} to sell
- {问|wèn} to ask, {吻|wěn} to kiss
- {妈|mā} mother, {马|mǎ} horse

Learners often fear that they "have no ear for tones". Everyone already hears pitch: it is how
you tell a question from a statement in English. What's new is listening for it in every
syllable. Listening and repeating, a little every day, is how it becomes automatic.

```speak
{妈|mā}
= mā, 1st tone: mother
{麻|má}
= má, 2nd tone: hemp
{马|mǎ}
= mǎ, 3rd tone: horse
{骂|mà}
= mà, 4th tone: to scold
{妈妈|mā ma}
= māma: mum (1st tone, then a light neutral tone)
```

## Pinyin letters aren't English letters

Pinyin uses the Latin alphabet, but it gives some letters values that English never does. Read
them the English way and you'll say the wrong sound. The first ones to watch:

| Letter | In pinyin it sounds roughly like… | Example |
|---|---|---|
| q | *ch* in *cheese* | {七|qī} seven |
| x | *sh* in *she* | {西|xī} west |
| c | *ts* in *cats* | {菜|cài} dish, vegetable |
| zh | *j* in *jam*, tongue tip curled back | {中|zhōng} middle |
| e | the *u* in *duh*, not the *e* in *bed* | {喝|hē} to drink |
| i after zh, sh, s… | a buzzing sound, not *ee* | {是|shì} to be |

Every English comparison in this course is only an approximation: Mandarin sounds are their own
sounds, and the voice in the app is the model to copy. Lessons 03 to 08 go through every letter.

## A first sentence, taken apart

> {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}。 — I'm a student.

| Characters | Pinyin | Meaning | Tones |
|---|---|---|---|
| {我|wǒ} | wǒ | I, me | 3rd |
| {是|shì} | shì | to be (am, is, are) | 4th |
| {学生|xué sheng} | xuésheng | student | 2nd, then neutral |

Three things to notice. There's no word for "a"; Chinese doesn't need one here. {是|shì} is the
same for "I am", "you are" and "she is": Chinese verbs don't change their form. And the full stop
is a small circle, 。 Chinese punctuation takes the space of a whole character.

One more thing you'll meet in lesson 15 with your first greeting, {你好|nǐ hǎo} (hello). It is
written *nǐ hǎo*, with two third tones, but said *ní hǎo*: when two third tones meet, the first one
rises. Pinyin keeps writing the tones a dictionary gives each character, and lesson 11 explains
the changes that happen in speech.

## How this app helps with Chinese

Pinyin switch. Lessons, questions and word lists have a Pinyin on/off switch. Keep it on
for now. Later, turn it off to check that you can read the characters without help, and back on
when you need it.

Tone colours. A second switch, Tone colours, colours each character and its pinyin by tone:
1st red, 2nd green, 3rd blue, 4th purple, neutral grey. Some learners find that colour helps them
remember tones; others prefer the marks alone. Try it and see.

Listening. Every Chinese line in a "Speaking practice" box has Listen and Slower buttons, and
Record yourself lets you compare your voice with the model. Listening questions and tone
questions play a syllable or word for you to identify. The app uses your device's Chinese
(Mandarin) voice, and it always reads the characters, never the pinyin.

Many devices don't have a Chinese voice until you add one. Look in the speech settings (names
vary a little between versions):

- Windows 11: Settings › Time & language › Speech › Manage voices › Add voices, then choose a
  Chinese (Simplified, China) voice. You may need to add Chinese as a language first.
- macOS: System Settings › Accessibility › Read & Speak (Spoken Content in older versions),
  then the information button next to System voice, and download a Chinese (China mainland) voice.
- iPhone and iPad: Settings › Accessibility › Spoken Content (or Read & Speak) › Voices ›
  Chinese, then download a voice.
- Android: Settings › Accessibility › Text-to-speech output, then the settings of the speech
  engine › Install voice data › Chinese (Mandarin, China).

Restart the app or the browser after adding a voice. Without a Chinese voice nothing breaks: tone
questions show the characters and the pinyin without tone marks, and you pick the tones from memory.

Typing pinyin. When a question asks you to type pinyin, type each syllable followed by its tone
number, and the app writes the mark: `ma3` becomes *mǎ*, `xue2sheng5` becomes *xuésheng* (5 or 0
is the neutral tone). Type `v` for ü: `nv3` becomes *nǚ*. Spaces and capital letters don't matter,
but tones do.

Simplified and traditional. This course is written in simplified characters, the standard
in mainland China. The Simplified/Traditional switch shows the same text in traditional characters,
as used in Taiwan and Hong Kong (the words stay the same; only the character forms change). The honors lesson "Simplified and traditional characters" explains the
difference.

## Common mistakes

- Reading pinyin as English: *xī* is not "zee" or "ksee", *qī* is not "kee", *cài* is not "kai".
- Treating tones as optional. {买|mǎi} and {卖|mài} are opposites; the tone is the only difference.
- Thinking pinyin is how Chinese is "really" written. It's a tool for sounds and typing; texts are
  in characters.
- Counting syllables in pinyin letters instead of characters: {图书馆|tú shū guǎn} is three
  syllables because it has three characters.

## Key points

- Each character is one syllable and usually one meaning; words have one to four characters, most
  often two.
- Hanyu Pinyin writes Mandarin sounds in Latin letters: for learning, dictionaries, typing,
  names and signs, not for reading ordinary texts.
- A syllable = initial + final + tone: *mā* = m + a + 1st tone.
- Four tones plus the neutral tone: *mā* (high level), *má* (rising), *mǎ* (low, dipping), *mà*
  (falling), *ma* (light). A different tone is a different word.
- Pinyin letters have their own values: q, x, c, zh, e and i are the first to learn.
- In the app: the Pinyin and Tone colours switches, Listen and Record yourself, typing with tone
  numbers (`ma3`, `nv3`), and a Chinese voice on your device.

This lesson has no words to learn yet. Your first vocabulary comes in lessons 13 to 15; until then,
the example words are there to practise sounds.

lessons.title: The four tones and the neutral tone
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 01 introduced the four tones with *mā, má, mǎ, mà*. This lesson takes them one at a time:
exactly what each one does with your voice, how the 3rd tone changes when another syllable
follows it, and how the light neutral tone works. The examples use four syllables, *ma*, *ba*,
*yi* and *wu*, in all four tones, so that the only thing changing is the tone.

Tones are the part of Mandarin that most needs your ears. Read this lesson with the Listen
buttons, and repeat every example out loud, more than once.

## The pitch scale

Linguists describe tones on a five-level scale of pitch: 1 is the bottom of your normal speaking
voice, 5 the top. A tone is written as the levels it starts and ends on. The scale is your own
voice: a deep voice and a high voice use the same numbers, each in its own range.

| Tone | Mark | Pitch | In words |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1st | ā | 55 | starts high, stays high |
| 2nd | á | 35 | starts in the middle, rises to the top |
| 3rd | ǎ | 214, usually 21 | starts low, dips to the bottom (and rises again only before a pause) |
| 4th | à | 51 | starts at the top, falls to the bottom |

A tone is a shape, not a single note. Think of the tone marks as small drawings of the shape: ˉ
level, ˊ rising, ˇ down and up, ˋ falling.

## The 1st tone: high and level (55)

Pitch your voice high, near the top of your comfortable range, and hold it steady, as if you were
singing one long note. It mustn't sag at the end.

{八|bā} (eight) · {妈|mā} (mother) · {医|yī} (medicine, as in {医生|yī shēng}, doctor) ·
{屋|wū} (room, as in {屋子|wū zi})

English speakers usually start the 1st tone too low, at a normal talking pitch, and then let it
drop the way an English statement drops. Start higher than feels natural.

## The 2nd tone: rising (35)

Start in the middle of your range and rise smoothly to the top, the way your voice rises on a
surprised "Huh?" or "What?" in English.

{拔|bá} (to pull out) · {麻|má} (hemp) · {姨|yí} (aunt, as in {阿姨|ā yí}) · {吴|wú} (Wu, a
family name)

The rise should be clear but not slow: the whole syllable takes no longer than any other.

## The 3rd tone: low (214, usually 21)

Said on its own, or at the end of a phrase before a pause, the 3rd tone starts low, sinks to the
very bottom of your voice and comes back up a little: 2, 1, 4.

{靶|bǎ} (target) · {马|mǎ} (horse) · {椅|yǐ} (chair, as in {椅子|yǐ zi}) · {五|wǔ} (five)

### The half-third tone

In real speech the full dip is rare. Before a 1st, 2nd or 4th tone, and before most neutral
tones, a 3rd tone keeps only its low part, 21, and doesn't rise at all. This is the
**[[half-third tone]]**: low and level or slightly falling, often a little creaky at the bottom.

| Word | Tones | What you hear |
|---|---|---|
| {北京|Běi jīng} (Beijing) | 3 + 1 | low *bei*, then high *jing* |
| {法国|Fǎ guó} (France) | 3 + 2 | low *fa*, then rising *guo* |
| {米饭|mǐ fàn} (cooked rice) | 3 + 4 | low *mi*, then falling *fan* |
| {老师|lǎo shī} (teacher) | 3 + 1 | low *lao*, then high *shi* |

So most of the 3rd tones you'll hear are simply low. The rise only comes when nothing follows.
(When a 3rd tone is followed by another 3rd tone, the first one changes to a rising tone:
{你好|nǐ hǎo} is said *ní hǎo*. Lesson 11 covers that change.)

**The key habit for English speakers: the 3rd tone is low.** If you think "low" rather than
"dip", you'll get it right most of the time. Learners who draw a big, slow V on every 3rd tone
sound odd and slow, and they confuse it with the 2nd tone, which also rises.

## The 4th tone: falling (51)

Start at the top and drop quickly all the way down, firm and short, the way you'd say a sharp
"No!" or "Stop!" in English.

{爸|bà} (dad) · {骂|mà} (to scold) · {亿|yì} (a hundred million) · {雾|wù} (fog)

Don't start it in the middle: a 4th tone that starts at normal pitch sounds half-hearted and can be
heard as a 3rd tone.

## The neutral tone

The **[[neutral tone]]** is a fifth possibility: a syllable said short and light, with no tone shape
of its own. Pinyin gives it no mark at all. It's common in the second syllable of family words,
in grammar words and in many two-syllable words:

| Word | Pinyin | Meaning | First syllable |
|---|---|---|---|
| {妈妈|mā ma} | māma | mum | 1st |
| {爷爷|yé ye} | yéye | grandpa (father's father) | 2nd |
| {姐姐|jiě jie} | jiějie | older sister | 3rd |
| {爸爸|bà ba} | bàba | dad | 4th |

A neutral syllable has no pitch of its own: it takes its pitch from the syllable before it. After
a 1st, 2nd or 4th tone it is low; after a 3rd tone it is a little higher, because the half-third
tone before it is at the bottom and the voice comes up into the light syllable. Listen to
{姐姐|jiě jie}: low *jiě*, then a higher, quick *jie*. In {爸爸|bà ba} the second syllable is low,
at the bottom of the fall.

The key to the neutral tone is length: it's short. Say the first syllable fully and let the
second one go almost without effort.

## Tone marks and tone numbers

| Tone | Mark | Number (for typing) | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1st | ˉ | 1 | *mā* = ma1 |
| 2nd | ˊ | 2 | *má* = ma2 |
| 3rd | ˇ | 3 | *mǎ* = ma3 |
| 4th | ˋ | 4 | *mà* = ma4 |
| neutral | no mark | 5 or 0 | *ma* = ma5 |

The mark always sits on a vowel. When a syllable has more than one vowel, it goes on a or e if
there is one (*hǎo*, *xiě*), on the o of ou (*gǒu*), and otherwise on the last vowel (*liù*,
*guì*); lesson 09 practises the rule. On *i* the mark replaces the dot: *yī*, *nǐ*.

In the app you type the number after the syllable: `ba3` gives *bǎ*, `jie3jie5` gives *jiějie*.

## Four syllables in four tones

| | 1st | 2nd | 3rd | 4th |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ma | {妈|mā} mother | {麻|má} hemp | {马|mǎ} horse | {骂|mà} to scold |
| ba | {八|bā} eight | {拔|bá} to pull out | {靶|bǎ} target | {爸|bà} dad |
| yi | {医|yī} medicine | {姨|yí} aunt | {椅|yǐ} chair | {亿|yì} 100 million |
| wu | {屋|wū} room | {吴|wú} Wu (name) | {五|wǔ} five | {雾|wù} fog |

Each row is four different words. Read across, then down, then at random. Then play the
syllables in the box below and name each tone before you look at the pinyin.

```speak
{八|bā}
= bā, 1st tone: eight
{拔|bá}
= bá, 2nd tone: to pull out
{靶|bǎ}
= bǎ, 3rd tone: target
{爸|bà}
= bà, 4th tone: dad
{医|yī}
= yī, 1st tone: medicine
{姨|yí}
= yí, 2nd tone: aunt
{椅|yǐ}
= yǐ, 3rd tone: chair
{亿|yì}
= yì, 4th tone: a hundred million
{屋|wū}
= wū, 1st tone: room
{吴|wú}
= wú, 2nd tone: Wu (a family name)
{五|wǔ}
= wǔ, 3rd tone: five
{雾|wù}
= wù, 4th tone: fog
```

```speak
{北京|Běi jīng}
= Běijīng: half-third (low), then high
{米饭|mǐ fàn}
= mǐfàn: half-third (low), then falling
{姐姐|jiě jie}
= jiějie: low, then a light, higher syllable
{爸爸|bà ba}
= bàba: falling, then a light, low syllable
```

## Hearing the difference

Two pairs cause most of the trouble:

- **2nd and 3rd.** Both can rise. The 2nd starts in the middle and rises at once; the 3rd starts
  low and stays low (it rises, if at all, only at the end). If the syllable is mostly low, it's
  the 3rd.
- **1st and 4th.** Both start high. The 1st stays there; the 4th drops at once.

A trick for practising: hum the tone with your mouth closed, then say the syllable on the same
hum. A hand helps too: draw the tone in the air as you say it, level, up, low, down.

## Common mistakes

- A 1st tone that starts at normal pitch and sags at the end, like an English statement. Keep it
  high and flat.
- A full, slow dip on every 3rd tone. Before another syllable it's just low (21).
- A 4th tone that starts in the middle of the voice. Start at the top.
- Stressing a neutral syllable: {妈妈|mā ma} with two full 1st tones sounds stiff. Make the second
  one short and light.
- Reading the tone marks the wrong way round: ˊ (rising) and ˋ (falling) look like slopes going up
  and down from left to right, just as the voice goes.

## Key points

- Pitch scale 1 (low) to 5 (high): 1st tone 55, 2nd 35, 3rd 214, 4th 51.
- 1st high and level; 2nd rising; 3rd low; 4th falling from the top.
- The **[[half-third tone]]** (21): before other tones, a 3rd tone is just low. Think "tone 3 is low".
- The neutral tone is short and light, with no mark; its pitch is low after tones 1, 2 and 4 and
  a little higher after tone 3.
- Marks ˉ ˊ ˇ ˋ, numbers 1 to 4, and 5 or 0 for neutral when typing.

This lesson has no words to learn: the example words are there to practise the tones. Your first
vocabulary comes in lessons 13 to 15.

lessons.title: Simple finals and the lip sounds: b p m f
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can now hear and say the four tones and the neutral tone. From here on, every lesson adds
sounds: first the six vowels that make the simplest finals, then the initials in groups by where
they're made in the mouth. This lesson starts with the lips, *b p m f*, and with the idea that
matters most for Mandarin consonants: **[[aspiration]]**, the puff of air that tells *b* from *p*.

## Six simple finals: a o e i u ü

The simplest finals are single vowels. Mandarin vowels are "pure": hold your tongue and lips
still while you say them, without the glide English adds to *go* (*go-w*) or *day* (*da-y*).

| Final | Mouth | Roughly like… | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| a | wide open, tongue low | *a* in *father* | {八|bā} eight |
| o | lips rounded, mouth half open | *aw* in *saw*, with rounded lips | {波|bō} wave |
| e | lips spread, tongue pulled back | *u* in *duh*, said further back in the mouth | {饿|è} hungry |
| i | lips spread, tongue high and forward | *ee* in *see* | {笔|bǐ} pen |
| u | lips tightly rounded, tongue high and back | *oo* in *food* | {五|wǔ} five |
| ü | lips rounded as for u, tongue as for i | no English sound: say *ee*, then round your lips | {鱼|yú} fish |

### e is not the English e

Pinyin *e* on its own is a vowel English doesn't really have. Start from the *o* position, then
spread your lips into a slight smile without moving your tongue: what comes out is a back,
unrounded *uh*, close to the vowel in *duh* or *the*. {饿|è} (hungry) is not "eh" and not "ee".
Listen to {鹅|é} (goose), {饿|è} (hungry), {喝|hē} (to drink) and {德国|Dé guó} (Germany).

(When *e* comes after *i* or *ü*, in *ie* and *üe*, it changes to the *e* of *yes*: lesson 07.)

### o after b, p, m, f

The final *o* on its own is found almost only after *b p m f*, and there it's said with a short
*w*-like glide: *bō* sounds close to "bwo", *pó* to "pwo". Everywhere else the same sound is
spelled *uo* (*duō*, *guó*). Treat *bo po mo fo* as a little family: {波|bō} (wave), {婆|pó} (as in
{婆婆|pó po}, a husband's mother), {墨|mò} (ink), {佛|fó} (Buddha).

### ü: round your lips, keep your tongue

Say a long *ee*. Without moving your tongue, round your lips tightly as if to whistle. That's
*ü*. If your tongue slides back you'll say *u* instead, a different sound. The dots matter in
writing only after *n* and *l* (lesson 04); after *j q x y* pinyin drops them (lesson 05), which is
why {鱼|yú} (fish) has no dots even though it is *ü*.

One more final: *er*, as in {二|èr} (two), is an *uh* with the tongue tip curled back. It never
takes an initial.

## The lip initials: b p m f

| Initial | How | Roughly like… |
|---|---|---|
| b | lips together, then open, no puff | *p* in *spin* |
| p | lips together, then open with a strong puff | *p* in *pin* |
| m | lips together, through the nose | *m* in *man* |
| f | top teeth on the lower lip | *f* in *fan* |

*m* and *f* are just like English. *b* and *p* need a new way of thinking.

## Aspiration: puff or no puff

English speakers think of the difference between *b* and *p* as voicing: the vocal cords buzz in
*b* (they really do between vowels, as in *rubber*). In Mandarin neither *b* nor *p* buzzes. The difference is aspiration: *p* is **[[aspirated]]**, a
strong puff of air bursts out as the lips open; *b* is **[[unaspirated]]**, the lips open with no
puff at all.

English speakers already make both sounds without noticing. Hold your hand in front of your mouth and
say *pin*: you feel a puff. Say *spin*: almost no puff. Mandarin *p* is the *p* of *pin*;
Mandarin *b* is the *p* of *spin*.

The paper test: Hold a strip of paper or a tissue a few centimetres in front of your lips.
Say {怕|pà} (to fear): the paper should jump. Say {爸|bà} (dad): it should barely move.

| Unaspirated | Aspirated | |
|---|---|---|
| {爸|bà} dad | {怕|pà} to fear | |
| {鼻|bí} nose (in {鼻子|bí zi}) | {皮|pí} skin, leather | |
| {步|bù} step | {普|pǔ} general (in {普通话|pǔ tōng huà}, Mandarin) | |
| {八|bā} eight | {趴|pā} to lie face down | |

The same contrast runs through all of Mandarin, and you'll meet it again in every lesson:

| Unaspirated | b | d | g | j | zh | z |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Aspirated | p | t | k | q | ch | c |

So when you see *b, d, g*, don't buzz them: say them crisp and quiet, like the
*p, t, k* of *spin, stop, skin*. Speakers of French, Spanish or Italian already have unaspirated
*p, t, k* in their languages; English speakers have to learn to hear them as a separate sound.

A small extra: in quick speech, in a light syllable in the middle of a word, *b* may come out
slightly voiced. That's normal and doesn't change anything.

## Which combinations exist

Not every initial goes with every final. With the lip sounds:

| | a | o | e | i | u | ü |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| b | ba | bo | — | bi | bu | — |
| p | pa | po | — | pi | pu | — |
| m | ma | mo | (me) | mi | mu | — |
| f | fa | fo | — | — | fu | — |

- There's no *fi*: "fee" isn't a Mandarin syllable. (*fei* exists: {飞|fēi}, to fly.)
- *b p m f* never go with *ü*: *bu*, *pu*, *mu*, *fu* are all plain *u*, lips rounded and tongue
  back.
- *me* is found only as a neutral syllable, as in {什么|shén me} (what).

## Practice syllables

| Syllable | Character | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| bā | {八|bā} | eight |
| pá | {爬|pá} | to climb |
| mǎ | {马|mǎ} | horse |
| fó | {佛|fó} | Buddha |
| bù | {步|bù} | step |
| pǔ | {普|pǔ} | general |
| mù | {木|mù} | wood |
| fú | {福|fú} | good fortune |
| bǐ | {笔|bǐ} | pen, writing brush |
| pí | {皮|pí} | skin |
| mǐ | {米|mǐ} | rice (grain) |
| pò | {破|pò} | broken |

```speak
{八|bā}
= bā: eight (no puff on b)
{趴|pā}
= pā: to lie face down (puff on p)
{爸|bà}
= bà: dad
{怕|pà}
= pà: to fear
{鼻|bí}
= bí: nose
{皮|pí}
= pí: skin
{饿|è}
= è: hungry (the back e)
{鹅|é}
= é: goose
{鱼|yú}
= yú: fish (ü, written u after y)
{米饭|mǐ fàn}
= mǐfàn: cooked rice
{皮包|pí bāo}
= píbāo: handbag
{跑步|pǎo bù}
= pǎobù: to go running
```

## Common mistakes

- Buzzing *b*, as English *b* does between vowels (*rubber*). It's quiet and crisp, like the *p* in
  *spin*.
- Too weak a puff on *p*. Exaggerate it at first: the paper test should make the strip jump.
- Saying *e* as "eh" (*bed*) or "ee". It's a back *uh*.
- Letting *ü* slide into *u* or *ee*. Keep the tongue forward and the lips rounded the whole time.
- Saying *fó* as "foe" with an English glide. Keep the *o* pure (with its small *w* after *f*).
- Adding a glide to every vowel: *mǐ* is a steady *ee*, not "mee-y".

## Key points

- Six simple finals: *a o e i u ü*. *e* is a back *uh*; *ü* is *ee* with rounded lips.
- *o* alone comes after *b p m f* and is said with a slight *w*: *bō* ≈ "bwo".
- *b p m f*: *m* and *f* as in English; *b* and *p* differ by aspiration, not voicing.
- Unaspirated *b d g j zh z*: no puff, like *p t k* after *s* in English. Aspirated *p t
  k q ch c*: a strong puff.
- No *fi*, and no *ü* after *b p m f*.

This lesson has no words to learn: the example words are there to practise sounds.

lessons.title: d t n l and g k h
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 03 gave you the six simple finals, the lip sounds *b p m f* and the most important idea
for Mandarin consonants: aspiration. This lesson adds seven more initials in two groups: four
made with the tip of the tongue, *d t n l*, and three made with the back of the tongue, *g k h*.
Two of each group are another unaspirated/aspirated pair, so you'll use the puff test again.
You'll also learn why *nü* and *lü* keep the dots on their ü when no other syllables do.

## Tip of the tongue: d t n l

All four are made with the tip of the tongue touching the ridge just behind your top front teeth,
as for English *t* and *d*.

| Initial | How | Roughly like… | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| d | tongue tip up, then release, no puff | *t* in *stop* | {低|dī} low |
| t | the same, with a strong puff | *t* in *top* | {踢|tī} to kick |
| n | tongue tip up, air through the nose | *n* in *no* | {你|nǐ} you |
| l | tongue tip up, air around the sides | *l* in *leaf* | {李|lǐ} Li (a family name) |

*d* and *t* are the same pair as *b* and *p*: neither is voiced, and only *t* has the puff. Hold
a hand in front of your mouth: {踢|tī} (to kick) should blow on it, {低|dī} (low) should not.

| Unaspirated d | Aspirated t |
|---|---|
| {低|dī} low | {踢|tī} to kick |
| {敌|dí} enemy | {题|tí} topic, question (in {问题|wèn tí}) |
| {赌|dǔ} to bet | {土|tǔ} soil |
| {搭|dā} to put up | {他|tā} he, him |

Mandarin *l* is always the light *l* of *leaf*, never the dark, swallowed *l* of *full*: in
Mandarin, *l* only ever starts a syllable.

### n and l

*n* and *l* are separate sounds in standard Mandarin, and plenty of words differ only by them:

| n | l |
|---|---|
| {你|nǐ} you | {李|lǐ} Li (a family name) |
| {努|nǔ} effort (in {努力|nǔ lì}) | {鲁|lǔ} Lu (a family name) |
| {怒|nù} anger | {路|lù} road |
| {男|nán} male | {蓝|lán} blue |

In some regional varieties of Chinese, for example the Southwestern Mandarin spoken in Sichuan,
*n* and *l* fall together as one sound, so you may hear speakers from those areas say {你|nǐ} with
an *l*, or {路|lù} with an *n*. That's a feature of their regional speech, not carelessness. The
standard keeps them apart, and so should you. Check your *n* by pinching your nose: an *n* stops
when the nose is closed, an *l* doesn't.

## Back of the tongue: g k h

| Initial | How | Roughly like… | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| g | back of the tongue against the soft palate, no puff | *k* in *skin* | {姑|gū} aunt (father's sister) |
| k | the same, with a strong puff | *k* in *kin* | {哭|kū} to cry |
| h | back of the tongue raised close to the soft palate, air rubbing through | a rough *h*, between English *h* and the *ch* of Scottish *loch* | {河|hé} river |

*g* and *k* are the third unaspirated/aspirated pair:

| Unaspirated g | Aspirated k |
|---|---|
| {姑|gū} aunt | {哭|kū} to cry |
| {古|gǔ} ancient | {苦|kǔ} bitter |
| {歌|gē} song | {科|kē} branch of study |

### h is rougher than English h

English *h* is just breath from the throat, with the mouth open. Mandarin *h* is made higher up,
with the back of the tongue raised close to the roof of the mouth, so you hear friction, a soft
rasp, like a gentle version of the *ch* in Scottish *loch* or German *Bach*. Say {河|hé} (river)
and {湖|hú} (lake) with that rasp. It doesn't need to be strong; some speakers make it quite soft.
What matters is that *h* is made at the back of the mouth.

## Which combinations exist

| | a | e | i | u | ü |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| d | da | de | di | du | — |
| t | ta | te | ti | tu | — |
| n | na | ne | ni | nu | nü |
| l | la | le | li | lu | lü |
| g | ga | ge | — | gu | — |
| k | ka | ke | — | ku | — |
| h | ha | he | — | hu | — |

- *g k h* never go with *i* or *ü*: there's no *gi*, *ki* or *hi*. (When you see *ji, qi, xi*
  in lesson 05, those are different initials.)
- *d* and *t* don't go with *ü* either. Of this group, only *n* and *l* do.
- *e* after these initials is the back *uh* from lesson 03: {哥|gē} (brother), {课|kè} (class),
  {河|hé} (river), {特|tè} (special).
- *o* almost never follows them alone: after *d t n l g k h* that sound is spelled *uo* ({多|duō},
  lesson 07).

## nü and lü keep their dots

After *n* and *l* both *u* and *ü* are possible, and they make different syllables. So the dots
must stay, or you couldn't tell them apart:

| u (lips rounded, tongue back) | ü (lips rounded, tongue forward) |
|---|---|
| {炉|lú} stove | {驴|lǘ} donkey |
| {鲁|lǔ} Lu (a family name) | {旅|lǚ} to travel (in {旅游|lǚ yóu}) |
| {路|lù} road | {律|lǜ} law (in {法律|fǎ lǜ}) |
| {努力|nǔ lì} to make an effort | {女儿|nǚ ér} daughter |

Only *n* and *l* need this. In lesson 05 you'll see that after *j q x y* the dots are left off,
because no plain *u* can follow those letters. The syllables *nü* and *lü* (and *lüe*, *nüe*) are
the only ones where you write ü in pinyin.

Typing in the app: `nv3` or `nu:3` gives *nǚ*; `lv4` gives *lǜ*. `nu3` gives *nǔ*, a different
syllable.

## Practice syllables

| Syllable | Character | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| dá | {达|dá} | to reach |
| tā | {他|tā} | he, him |
| nǐ | {你|nǐ} | you |
| lǜ | {律|lǜ} | law |
| gē | {哥|gē} | older brother (in {哥哥|gē ge}) |
| kè | {课|kè} | class, lesson |
| hú | {湖|hú} | lake |
| kě | {渴|kě} | thirsty |
| tǎ | {塔|tǎ} | tower, pagoda |
| lì | {力|lì} | strength |

```speak
{低|dī}
= dī: low (no puff)
{踢|tī}
= tī: to kick (puff)
{姑|gū}
= gū: aunt (no puff)
{哭|kū}
= kū: to cry (puff)
{你|nǐ}
= nǐ: you
{李|lǐ}
= lǐ: Li (a family name)
{路|lù}
= lù: road
{律|lǜ}
= lǜ: law
{河|hé}
= hé: river (the rough h)
{湖|hú}
= hú: lake
{努力|nǔ lì}
= nǔlì: to make an effort
{旅游|lǚ yóu}
= lǚyóu: to travel
{课|kè}
= kè: class, lesson
```

## Common mistakes

- *d* and *g* buzzed, as English *d* and *g* are between vowels (*ladder*, *bigger*). Keep them
  quiet and crisp, like the *t* and *k* in
  *stop* and *skin*.
- Too little puff on *t* and *k*.
- A breathy English *h* in {河|hé} and {湖|hú}: raise the back of the tongue and let the air rub.
- Mixing up *n* and *l*, or *u* and *ü* after them: {路|lù} (road) and {律|lǜ} (law) are different
  words.
- Writing *nu* or *lu* when you mean ü. The dots stay after *n* and *l*.
- Inventing *gi*, *ki* or *hi*: they don't exist.

## Key points

- *d t n l*: tongue tip behind the top teeth. *d* (no puff) and *t* (puff) are a pair.
- *g k h*: back of the tongue. *g* (no puff) and *k* (puff) are a pair; *h* is a rough,
  back-of-the-mouth *h*.
- Standard Mandarin keeps *n* and *l* apart, though some regional speech merges them.
- After *n* and *l*, *u* and *ü* are both possible, so ü keeps its dots: *nǚ*, *lǜ*. Type it with
  `v` (`nv3`).
- No *gi, ki, hi*; no *ü* after *d, t, g, k, h*.

This lesson has no words to learn: the example words are there to practise sounds.

lessons.title: j q x and ü
topics: ü after j q x y
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

So far you have eleven initials: *b p m f*, *d t n l* and *g k h*. This lesson adds three that
English readers misread more than any others, *j q x*. They look like English letters but stand
for sounds made with the tongue flat against the roof of the mouth. It also covers the spelling
rule learners get wrong most often: after *j q x* (and *y*) the vowel *ü* is written without its
dots, so *ju*, *qu*, *xu* and *yu* are all ü, never u.

## The tongue-flat initials: j q x

For all three, the tip of your tongue rests behind your lower front teeth, and the front of the
tongue (just behind the tip) presses up flat against the front of the roof of your mouth. The
lips are spread, as for a smile. That flat, smiling position is what gives these sounds their
bright, "thin" quality.

| Initial | How | Roughly like… | Not like… |
|---|---|---|---|
| j | tongue flat against the roof of the mouth, release, no puff | *j* in *jeep*, but without voicing | — |
| q | the same, with a strong puff | *ch* in *cheese* | English *k* or *kw* (*queen*) |
| x | tongue flat, close to the roof, air rubbing through | *sh* in *she*, lips spread | English *x* (*ks*) or *z* |

- *j* and *q* are another unaspirated/aspirated pair: hold your hand up, and {七|qī} (seven) should
  puff, {鸡|jī} (chicken) should not.
- *x* is the "smiling" *sh*. Say *she* with your lips pulled wide and the tip of your tongue down
  behind your lower teeth: that's very close to {西|xī} (west).
- The letters were chosen for the alphabet, not for English: *q* is not "kw" and *x* is not "ks".
  {七|qī} is "chee" said with the tongue flat, and {西|xī} is a smiling "she".

| | j | q | x |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1st | {鸡|jī} chicken | {七|qī} seven | {西|xī} west |
| 2nd | {急|jí} urgent | {旗|qí} flag | {习|xí} to practise (in {学习|xué xí}, to study) |
| 3rd | {挤|jǐ} crowded | {起|qǐ} to rise | {喜|xǐ} joy (in {喜欢|xǐ huan}, to like) |
| 4th | {记|jì} to remember | {气|qì} air, gas | {戏|xì} play, opera |

## j q x go only with i and ü

*j q x* never come before *a*, *o*, *e* or *u* directly. They only start syllables whose final
begins with *i* or *ü*:

- with *i*: *ji qi xi*, and the compound and nasal finals that start with *i*: {家|jiā} (home),
  {小|xiǎo} (small), {九|jiǔ} (nine), {钱|qián} (money), {鞋|xié} (shoe), {桥|qiáo} (bridge)
- with *ü*: *ju qu xu*, and *jue que xue*, *juan quan xuan*, *jun qun xun*: {学|xué} (to study),
  {去|qù} (to go)

So you'll never see *ja*, *qo*, *xe* or *xu* with a back *u*: those syllables don't exist.

## ju qu xu yu are ü

Here is the rule to learn by heart:

> After *j*, *q*, *x* and *y*, the letter *u* always means ü.

The dots are left off because no plain *u* can follow these letters, so nothing can be confused.

| Written | Said | Example |
|---|---|---|
| ju | jü | {剧|jù} play, drama (in {剧场|jù chǎng}, theatre) |
| qu | qü | {去|qù} to go |
| xu | xü | {许|xǔ} Xu (a family name); {许多|xǔ duō} many |
| yu | ü | {鱼|yú} fish; {玉|yù} jade |
| jue, que, xue, yue | jüe… | {学|xué} to study; {月|yuè} moon, month |

Say {去|qù}: tongue flat for the *q*, then *ü*, tongue forward and lips rounded. If you say "koo"
or "choo" with the back vowel *u*, you've said a syllable that doesn't exist.

Compare this with lesson 04: after *n* and *l* the dots stay (*nǚ*, *lǜ*), because *nu* and *lu*
exist too. Put together:

| Initial | u (back) | ü (front, rounded) | How ü is written |
|---|---|---|---|
| n, l | {路|lù} road | {律|lǜ} law | with dots: lǜ |
| j, q, x | — | {去|qù} to go | without dots: qù |
| y (no initial) | — | {鱼|yú} fish | without dots: yú |
| d, t, g, k, h, z, c, s, zh, ch, sh, r, b, p, m, f | {图|tú}, {哭|kū}, {书|shū}… | — | — |

So whenever you see *u* after *j q x y*, read ü. Everywhere else, *u* is the back vowel *u*.

Typing ü in the app: type `v` for ü wherever you need the dots: `nv3` gives *nǚ*, `lv4` *lǜ*.
After *j q x y* just type `u` as written: `qu4` gives *qù*, `xue2` *xué*, `yu2` *yú*. (The app
also accepts `qv4`, but the standard spelling has no dots.)

## The y in yi and yu

Syllables with no initial that start with *i* or *ü* are written with *y* (lesson 07 has the full
rule). For the two simple finals:

- *i* alone is written *yi*: {医|yī} (medicine), {椅|yǐ} (chair). Said like *ee*; the *y* is
  silent spelling.
- *ü* alone is written *yu*: {鱼|yú} (fish), {羽|yǔ} (feather). Said *ü*, not "you".

## Preview: j q x vs zh ch sh

Lesson 06 brings three initials that sound a little like *j q x* but are made with the tongue
tip curled back: *zh ch sh*. Learners mix them up, so start listening for the difference now:

| Tongue flat, lips spread | Tongue tip curled back |
|---|---|
| {鸡|jī} chicken | {知|zhī} to know |
| {七|qī} seven | {吃|chī} to eat |
| {西|xī} west | {诗|shī} poem |

Two clues: *j q x* are bright and thin, and the vowel after them is a real *ee*. *zh ch sh* are
darker, and the *i* after them isn't *ee* at all, but a buzz. There's a third clue in spelling:
*j q x* only ever come before *i* or *ü*; *zh ch sh* never come before *ü* or before *i* + another
vowel.

```speak
{鸡|jī}
= jī: chicken (no puff)
{七|qī}
= qī: seven (puff)
{西|xī}
= xī: west
{去|qù}
= qù: to go (ü, written u)
{许|xǔ}
= xǔ: Xu (a family name)
{剧|jù}
= jù: play, drama
{鱼|yú}
= yú: fish
{学习|xué xí}
= xuéxí: to study
{需要|xū yào}
= xūyào: to need
{继续|jì xù}
= jìxù: to continue
{鸡|jī}
= jī: chicken (tongue flat)
{知|zhī}
= zhī: to know (tongue curled back)
```

## Common mistakes

- Reading *x* as English "ks" or "z": {西|xī} is a smiling *sh*.
- Reading *q* as "k" or "kw": {七|qī} is a *ch* with a puff.
- Saying *ju qu xu yu* with the back vowel *u* ("joo", "choo", "shoo", "you"). They are all ü.
- Writing the dots after *j q x y* (*qǜ*, *yǘ*). Correct pinyin leaves them off.
- Leaving the dots off after *n* and *l* (*nu* for *nǚ*). There they must stay.
- Curling the tongue for *j q x*. Keep the tip down behind the lower teeth.

## Key points

- *j q x*: tongue tip down, front of the tongue flat against the roof of the mouth, lips spread.
  *j* (no puff) and *q* (puff) are a pair; *x* is a smiling *sh*.
- *j q x* only come before *i* or *ü* (and finals starting with them).
- After *j q x y*, *u* means ü and the dots are dropped: *jù, qù, xū, yú, xué, yuè*.
- After *n* and *l* the dots stay: *nǚ, lǜ*. Type them with `v`.
- *yi* = i, *yu* = ü when there's no initial.
- Don't confuse *j q x* (flat, bright, real *ee*) with *zh ch sh* (curled, darker): lesson 06.

This lesson has no words to learn: the example words are there to practise sounds.

lessons.title: zh ch sh r and z c s
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This lesson completes the 21 initials with the last seven: *zh ch sh r*, made with the tongue tip
curled back, and *z c s*, made with the tongue tip at the teeth. It's the hardest lesson of the
module, for two reasons. These sounds are close to each other and to *j q x* from lesson 05, so
your ear needs time; and after all seven the letter *i* stands for a vowel that isn't *ee* at
all. Take it slowly, use the Listen and Slower buttons a lot, and come back to the listening
questions more than once.

## Tongue curled back: zh ch sh r

For these four, raise the tip of your tongue and curl it slightly back, so that it points at the
hard roof of your mouth just behind the ridge where *t* and *d* are made. These are called
**[[retroflex]]** initials ("bent back"). Don't curl it all the way: a gentle lift is enough, and
the sides of the tongue stay against the upper side teeth.

| Initial | How | Roughly like… | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| zh | tongue tip curled up, release, no puff | *j* in *jug* said with the tongue tip back, not voiced | {知|zhī} to know |
| ch | the same, with a strong puff | *ch* in *church*, tongue tip back | {吃|chī} to eat |
| sh | tongue tip curled up, air rubbing through | *sh* in *shrub* | {书|shū} book |
| r | tongue tip curled up, voiced, little friction | between the *r* of *run* and the *s* of *measure* | {热|rè} hot |

- *zh* and *ch* are the fifth unaspirated/aspirated pair. {吃|chī} (to eat) puffs, {知|zhī} (to know)
  doesn't.
- *sh* is close to English *sh*, but darker, because the tongue tip is up and back. English *sh*
  in *shrub* (before an *r*) is nearer than *sh* in *she*.
- *r* isn't the English *r* with rounded lips, and it isn't rolled. Hold the tongue in the *sh*
  position and add your voice: you get something between *r* and the *zh* sound in *measure*.
  Some speakers make it softer, more like an *r*; both are heard.

In much of southern China and in Taiwan, many speakers pronounce *zh ch sh* close to *z c s*. That
is a common regional feature. The standard keeps the two sets apart. Learn to make and hear both
sets: it helps you speak clearly and understand speakers from everywhere.

## Tongue at the teeth: z c s

For these three, the tongue tip touches or comes close to the back of your upper front teeth, and
the lips are relaxed.

| Initial | How | Roughly like… | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| z | tongue tip at the teeth, release, no puff | *ds* in *beds* (not English *z*) | {字|zì} character, word |
| c | the same, with a strong puff | *ts* in *cats*, with a puff | {菜|cài} dish, vegetable |
| s | air hissing past the tongue tip | *s* in *sun* | {四|sì} four |

- *z* is not the buzzing *z* of *zoo*: it's a short "ds", as at the end of *beds*.
- *c* is always "ts" with a puff of air. It is the letter English readers misread most often:
  {菜|cài} is "tsai", never "kai" or "sai". *z* and *c* are the sixth unaspirated/aspirated pair.

## The special i after these seven initials

After *zh ch sh r* and *z c s*, the final written *i* is not the *ee* of *see*. It stands for a
buzzing vowel that simply carries on the consonant with your voice, the tongue staying where the
consonant put it.

- After *zh ch sh r*: keep the tongue tip curled up and let the voice run through. It sounds a
  little like the *ir* of American English *sir*, said with the tongue tip high and without
  rounding the lips. {是|shì} (to be) is roughly "shrr", not "shee".
- After *z c s*: keep the tongue at the teeth, teeth almost closed, lips relaxed. It sounds like a
  short buzz after the consonant, a voiced *zzz*. {四|sì} (four) is roughly "sz", not "see".

| Syllable | Character | Meaning | Not said… |
|---|---|---|---|
| zhī | {知|zhī} | to know | "jee" |
| chī | {吃|chī} | to eat | "chee" |
| shì | {是|shì} | to be | "shee" |
| rì | {日|rì} | sun, day | "ree" |
| zì | {字|zì} | character, word | "zee" |
| cì | {次|cì} | time (occurrence) | "tsee" |
| sì | {四|sì} | four | "see" |

The real *ee* after these seven initials doesn't exist. So when you see *zhi* or *si*, you know it
has the buzzed vowel; when you see *ji* or *xi*, you know it has *ee*. Syllables with this *i* are
some of the most common in Chinese: {是|shì}, {十|shí}, {四|sì}, {日|rì}, {字|zì}, {吃|chī}.

## Three rows that sound alike

Here are the three sets side by side. The difference is where the tongue tip is: down behind the
lower teeth (*j q x*), curled up (*zh ch sh*), or at the upper teeth (*z c s*).

| | Tongue flat: j q x | Tongue curled: zh ch sh | Tongue at teeth: z c s |
|---|---|---|---|
| unaspirated, 1st tone | {鸡|jī} chicken | {知|zhī} to know | {资|zī} funds |
| aspirated, 2nd tone | {旗|qí} flag | {迟|chí} late | {词|cí} word |
| hiss, 1st tone | {西|xī} west | {诗|shī} poem | {丝|sī} silk |
| unaspirated, 4th tone | {记|jì} to remember | {志|zhì} will, aim | {字|zì} character |
| aspirated, 4th tone | {气|qì} air | {赤|chì} red | {次|cì} time (occurrence) |
| hiss, 4th tone | {戏|xì} play | {是|shì} to be | {四|sì} four |
| hiss, 2nd tone | {习|xí} to practise | {十|shí} ten | — |

Listening clues:

- *ji qi xi* have a bright, real *ee*, and the lips are spread.
- *zhi chi shi ri* sound dark and "r-coloured".
- *zi ci si* sound sharp and hissy, with a short buzz.

A well-known tongue twister plays on two of these:

> {四|sì}{是|shì}{四|sì}，{十|shí}{是|shì}{十|shí}。 — Four is four, ten is ten.

Say it slowly: *sì* (teeth), *shì* (curled), *sì*, then *shí* (curled, rising), *shì*, *shí*. Then
faster.

## With other finals

The seven initials combine with most finals that start with *a*, *e*, *o* or *u*, but never with
*ü*, and never with *i* + another vowel:

| | Examples |
|---|---|
| zh ch sh r | {猪|zhū} pig, {茶|chá} tea, {书|shū} book, {热|rè} hot, {肉|ròu} meat, {人|rén} person |
| z c s | {早|zǎo} early, {菜|cài} dish, {三|sān} three, {做|zuò} to do, {错|cuò} wrong, {自己|zì jǐ} oneself |

Words to practise, with the special *i* in context: {日本|Rì běn} (Japan), {生日|shēng rì} (birthday),
{老师|lǎo shī} (teacher), {吃饭|chī fàn} (to eat a meal), {汉字|hàn zì} (Chinese characters),
{公司|gōng sī} (company), {四十|sì shí} (forty), {十四|shí sì} (fourteen).

```speak
{知|zhī}
= zhī: to know (curled, no puff)
{吃|chī}
= chī: to eat (curled, puff)
{诗|shī}
= shī: poem
{日|rì}
= rì: sun, day
{资|zī}
= zī: funds (teeth, no puff)
{词|cí}
= cí: word (teeth, puff)
{丝|sī}
= sī: silk
{四|sì}{是|shì}{四|sì}，{十|shí}{是|shì}{十|shí}。
= Four is four, ten is ten.
{四十|sì shí}
= sìshí: forty
{十四|shí sì}
= shísì: fourteen
{汉字|hàn zì}
= hànzì: Chinese characters
{生日|shēng rì}
= shēngrì: birthday
```

## Common mistakes

- Saying *zhi chi shi ri zi ci si* with *ee*. That's the most frequent beginner error, and it
  turns {是|shì} into something like {戏|xì}.
- Reading *c* as "k" or "s". It's always "ts": {菜|cài}, {次|cì}.
- Reading *z* as the English buzzing *z*. It's a short "ds".
- Rounding the lips for *r* as in English *red*. Keep them relaxed and the tongue tip up.
- Curling the tongue for *j q x*, or not curling it for *zh ch sh*. Check your tongue tip: down,
  up, or at the teeth.
- Too little puff on *ch* and *c*.

## Key points

- Retroflex *zh ch sh r*: tongue tip curled up. *zh* (no puff) / *ch* (puff); *sh* a dark *sh*;
  *r* between *r* and the *s* of *measure*.
- *z c s* at the teeth: *z* = "ds", *c* = "ts" with a puff, *s* = *s*.
- After these seven initials, *i* is a buzzed vowel, never *ee*: *zhī chī shì rì zì cì sì*.
- Three sets that sound alike: tongue flat (*j q x* + real *ee*), curled (*zh ch sh*), at the
  teeth (*z c s*).
- These initials never take *ü* or *i* + another vowel.
- All 21 initials are now done: see the reference sheet.

This lesson has no words to learn: the example words are there to practise sounds.

lessons.title: Compound finals and y/w spelling
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You now know all 21 initials and the six simple finals. Most Mandarin syllables, though, have a
final made of two or three vowels: *ai* in {爱|ài} (to love), *ia* in {家|jiā} (home), *uo* in
{我|wǒ} (I). These are the compound finals, and this lesson covers all of them. It also teaches the
spelling rules that turn *i*, *u* and *ü* into *y* and *w* when a syllable has no initial, and the
two shortened spellings, *iu* and *ui*, that hide a vowel you can still hear. After this lesson,
only the nasal finals (*-n*, *-ng*) are left, and module 2 starts with them.

## How a compound final works

In a compound final one vowel is the main one, said fully and with the tone on it; the others
are quick glides into or out of it. The pinyin tone mark sits on the main vowel (with one
exception, *iu* and *ui*, below). Hold the whole final within one syllable, the length of one
beat.

## Group 1: the main vowel first — ai ei ao ou

| Final | Roughly like… | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| ai | *eye* | {爱|ài} to love, {来|lái} to come |
| ei | *ay* in *day* | {北|běi} north, {黑|hēi} black |
| ao | *ow* in *how* | {高|gāo} tall, high; {小|xiǎo} small (with *i-*, group 2) |
| ou | *oh* in *go*, with rounded lips | {狗|gǒu} dog, {走|zǒu} to walk |

The second vowel is light: *ai* glides toward *i* without reaching a full *ee*, and *ao* glides
toward *u*. Two traps: *ei* is never "ee" (it's {北|běi}, "bay"), and *ou* is never "oo" (it's
{狗|gǒu}, "go"). The spelling *ao* looks odd to English readers, but the sound is just *ow*.

## Group 2: starting with i — ia ie iao iou

The *i* is a quick *y*-glide, and the main vowel follows.

| Final | Roughly like… | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| ia | *ya* in *yacht* | {家|jiā} home, {下|xià} down |
| ie | *ye* in *yes* | {鞋|xié} shoe, {谢|xiè} to thank (in {谢谢|xiè xie}) |
| iao | *yow* in *yowl* | {小|xiǎo} small, {叫|jiào} to be called |
| iou, written iu | *yo* in *yoke* | {九|jiǔ} nine, {牛|niú} cow, ox |

The *e* in *ie* is the *e* of *yes*, not the back *uh* of lesson 03's *e*. The same goes for
*üe* (group 4). So {鞋|xié} is "shyeh", not "shyuh".

## Group 3: starting with u — ua uo uai uei

The *u* is a quick *w*-glide with rounded lips.

| Final | Roughly like… | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| ua | *wa* in *waffle* | {花|huā} flower, {话|huà} speech, words |
| uo | *wo* in *woke*, more open | {多|duō} many, {国|guó} country |
| uai | *why* | {快|kuài} fast, {坏|huài} bad |
| uei, written ui | *way* | {贵|guì} expensive, {水|shuǐ} water, {对|duì} right, correct |

## Group 4: üe

| Final | Roughly like… | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| üe, written ue after j q x and y | *ü* + the *e* of *yes* | {学|xué} to study, {雪|xuě} snow, {月|yuè} moon, month |

After *n* and *l* it keeps its dots: {略|lüè} (brief, outline), {虐|nüè} (cruel). These
are rare; *xue*, *jue*, *que* and *yue* are the common ones.

## Spelling with y and w

When a syllable has no initial, pinyin doesn't let it start with *i*, *u* or *ü*. It uses *y* and
*w* instead. The sound doesn't change; it's a spelling rule that makes syllable boundaries easy to
see.

| Final | With an initial | With no initial | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| i | *li*, *ji* | yi (add y) | {医|yī} medicine |
| ia | *jia* | ya (i → y) | {牙|yá} tooth |
| ie | *xie* | ye | {也|yě} also |
| iao | *xiao* | yao | {药|yào} medicine (drug) |
| iou | *jiu* | you | {有|yǒu} to have |
| u | *bu*, *hu* | wu (add w) | {五|wǔ} five |
| ua | *hua* | wa (u → w) | {瓦|wǎ} tile |
| uo | *guo* | wo | {我|wǒ} I, me |
| uai | *kuai* | wai | {外|wài} outside |
| uei | *gui* | wei | {位|wèi} seat, place |
| ü | *nü*, *ju* | yu (y, dots dropped) | {鱼|yú} fish |
| üe | *xue* | yue | {月|yuè} moon, month |

The pattern in one sentence: a single vowel gets *y* or *w* added (*yi*, *wu*, *yu*); in a longer
final the first letter becomes *y* or *w* (*ya*, *wo*), and *ü* always becomes *yu*.

Notice that *you* and *wei* are written in full: the shortening to *iu* and *ui* (next section)
happens only after an initial.

## iu and ui: the hidden vowel

Two finals are shortened in writing when an initial comes before them:

- *iou* is written *iu*: *l* + *iou* = *liu*, *j* + *iou* = *jiu*
- *uei* is written *ui*: *g* + *uei* = *gui*, *sh* + *uei* = *shui*

The middle vowel is still there in speech. It's clearest in the 3rd and 4th tones: {九|jiǔ} (nine)
sounds close to "jyoh", {六|liù} (six) to "lyoh", {贵|guì} (expensive) to "gway", {水|shuǐ}
(water) to "shway". In the 1st and 2nd tones it's shorter and you may hardly hear it: {牛|niú}
(cow), {丢|diū} (to lose), {灰|huī} (grey), {球|qiú} (ball). Don't say *iu* as "you" or *ui* as
"wee" in any tone.

Where the tone mark goes: in *iu* and *ui* it goes on the second letter, the last vowel written:
*liù*, *jiǔ*, *guì*, *shuǐ*. That's the one exception to "the mark goes on the main vowel", and it
follows from the general rule you met in lesson 02: *a* or *e* first, then the *o* of *ou*,
otherwise the last vowel. Lesson 09 practises it.

## Which initials go with which finals

You've seen most of this already. Together:

| Initials | Finals they take |
|---|---|
| j q x | only finals starting with *i* or *ü* (*jia*, *xiao*, *qiu*, *xue*) |
| zh ch sh r, z c s | never *i* + vowel, never *ü* (*zhua*, *shuo*, *cai*, *zui* yes; *zhia*, *sie* no) |
| g k h | *a*, *e*, *u* and *u*-finals, never *i* or *ü* (*gua*, *kuai*, *hui*) |
| b p m f | no *u* + vowel (*bo*, not *buo*); *ie*, *iao* after b p m (*bie*, *piao*, *miao*) |
| d t n l | almost everything; *ü*-finals only after n and l |

## Practice

```speak
{爱|ài}
= ài: to love
{北|běi}
= běi: north
{高|gāo}
= gāo: tall, high
{狗|gǒu}
= gǒu: dog
{家|jiā}
= jiā: home
{鞋|xié}
= xié: shoe (the e of "yes")
{小|xiǎo}
= xiǎo: small
{九|jiǔ}
= jiǔ: nine (the hidden o)
{花|huā}
= huā: flower
{国|guó}
= guó: country
{快|kuài}
= kuài: fast
{贵|guì}
= guì: expensive (the hidden e)
{学|xué}
= xué: to study
{月|yuè}
= yuè: moon, month
{有|yǒu}
= yǒu: to have
{外|wài}
= wài: outside
```

## Common mistakes

- *ei* said as "ee": {北|běi} is "bay".
- *ou* said as "oo": {狗|gǒu} is "go", not "goo".
- The *e* of *ie* and *üe* said as the back *uh*: {鞋|xié}, {学|xué} have the *e* of *yes*.
- *iu* said "you" and *ui* said "wee": {六|liù} is "lyoh", {贵|guì} is "gway".
- Spelling the long forms after an initial (*liou*, *guei*) or the short forms without one
  (*iu*, *ui* for *you*, *wei*).
- The tone mark on the wrong letter: *gùi*, *líu* are wrong; write *guì*, *liú*.
- Writing a syllable with no initial as *ia*, *uo*, *üe*: they need *y* or *w*: *ya*, *wo*, *yue*.

## Key points

- Compound finals: one main vowel with quick glides. Group 1 *ai ei ao ou*; group 2 *ia ie iao
  iou*; group 3 *ua uo uai uei*; group 4 *üe*.
- The *e* in *ie* and *üe* is the *e* of *yes*.
- With no initial: *i* → *yi*/*y-*, *u* → *wu*/*w-*, *ü* → *yu* (*yi ya ye yao you*, *wu wa wo wai
  wei*, *yu yue*).
- After an initial, *iou* → *iu* and *uei* → *ui*, and the mark goes on the last letter (*liù*,
  *guì*); the hidden *o* or *e* is still heard, most clearly in tones 3 and 4.
- Every initial and every vowel final is now done: the reference sheet "Initials, finals and
  tones" has them all, and module 2 adds the nasal finals.

This lesson has no words to learn: the example words are there to practise sounds. Your first
vocabulary comes in lessons 13 to 15.

lessons.title: Nasal finals: -n and -ng
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 1 gave you every initial and the finals made of vowels: the simple ones (a o e i u ü) and
the compound ones (ai, ao, ie, uo…), with the y and w spelling rules. One family is left: finals
that end in a consonant, either *-n* or *-ng*. These are the **[[nasal finals]]**, and there are 16 of
them. They are everywhere: {中国|Zhōng guó} (China) starts with one, and {今天|jīn tiān} (today),
{电影|diàn yǐng} (film) and {房间|fáng jiān} (room) have two each.

By the end of this lesson you will have met every final in Mandarin, and you'll see them all in
one table. The new skill is one English speakers find surprisingly hard: hearing and saying the
difference between *-n* and *-ng* at the end of a syllable.

## Two endings: -n and -ng

Mandarin syllables can end in only two consonants, *n* and *ng* (plus the *-r* of erhua, which
comes in lesson 12). There is never a *-m*, *-t* or *-k* at the end of a syllable.

- *-n* is made with the tip of the tongue pressed against the ridge just behind your upper
  front teeth, as for English *n* in *ten*. Close it fully and hold it for a moment.
- *-ng* is made with the back of the tongue raised against the soft palate, as for the *ng*
  in English *sing*. The tongue tip stays down behind your lower teeth. There is no *g* sound
  after it: *-ng* is the *ng* of *singer*, never the *ng-g* of *finger*.

A self-test: say *fan* and freeze at the end. If your tongue tip is touching the roof of your
mouth, you said *-n*. Now say *fang* and freeze: the tip should be lying low and your mouth a
little more open.

The ending isn't the only clue. The vowel before it changes too, and native listeners use both.
Before *-n* the vowel is made further forward in the mouth; before *-ng* it's further back. So
*an* has a brighter *a*, a little like the *a* in *fan* said with a more open mouth, while *ang*
has a deep *a* like the one in *father*, followed by *ng*. All English comparisons in this
lesson are approximations: Mandarin vowels are never exactly the English ones.

Some pairs of real words that differ only in the ending:

| ends in -n | ends in -ng |
|---|---|
| {饭|fàn} meal, cooked rice | {放|fàng} to put |
| {班|bān} class (of students) | {帮|bāng} to help |
| {山|shān} mountain | {伤|shāng} wound |
| {盆|pén} basin, bowl | {朋|péng} (in {朋友|péng you}, friend) |
| {新|xīn} new | {星|xīng} star |
| {钱|qián} money | {墙|qiáng} wall |
| {民|mín} people (in many words) | {名|míng} name (in {名字|míng zi}) |

Many speakers in southern China (and in Taiwan) merge some of these pairs, especially *in* and
*ing*, *en* and *eng*. That's a regional feature, not a mistake on their part, but the standard
keeps them apart, and so should you: {新|xīn} and {星|xīng} are different words.

## The five open nasal finals: an, en, ang, eng, ong

| Final | Roughly like | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| an | *ahn*, with a bright, forward *a* | {饭|fàn} meal, {看|kàn} to look, {男|nán} male, {晚上|wǎn shang} evening |
| en | *un* in *taken* (a short, central vowel) | {很|hěn} very, {人|rén} person, {本|běn} (measure word for books), {门|mén} door |
| ang | *ahng*, a deep *a* as in *father* | {忙|máng} busy, {上|shàng} on, above, {房间|fáng jiān} room |
| eng | roughly the *ung* of *lung* | {冷|lěng} cold, {朋友|péng you} friend, {生病|shēng bìng} to fall ill |
| ong | *oong*: the vowel of *book*, then *ng* | {中国|Zhōng guó} China, {工作|gōng zuò} work, {东西|dōng xi} thing |

Notes:

- The *e* in *en* and *eng* is the same central vowel as the *e* of {的|de}: never the *e* of
  English *bed*. *Hen* is not English *hen*; {很|hěn} sounds closer to *hun* with a dip.
- *ong* has no *on* partner: Mandarin has no syllable ending in *-on*. And *ong* always has an
  initial before it ({东|dōng}, {工|gōng}, {中|zhōng}). On its own, the same sound is spelled
  *weng* (below).
- After b, p, m and f you'll find *-eng* ({朋|péng}, {风|fēng} wind, {梦|mèng} dream) but
  never *-ong*: there is no *bong* or *fong*.

## Nasal finals with i: ian, in, iang, ing, iong

When there's no initial, these are spelled with y, following the rule from lesson 07: *ian* → *yan*,
*in* → *yin*, *iang* → *yang*, *ing* → *ying*, *iong* → *yong*. Note that *in* and *ing* simply add
a y: *yin*, *ying*, not ~~*yiin*~~.

| Final | Alone | Roughly like | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| ian | yan | *yen* (not *yahn*) | {天|tiān} day, sky, {钱|qián} money, {电话|diàn huà} phone, {年|nián} year |
| in | yin | *een* (*ee* + *n*, nothing in between) | {今天|jīn tiān} today, {新|xīn} new, {您|nín} you (polite) |
| iang | yang | *ee-ahng* (a deep *a*) | {想|xiǎng} to want to, {两|liǎng} two, {漂亮|piào liang} pretty |
| ing | ying | *eeng*, often with a slight glide: *ee-ung* | {星期|xīng qī} week, {听|tīng} to listen, {请|qǐng} please |
| iong | yong | *yoong* (y + the *ong* above) | {用|yòng} to use, {穷|qióng} poor |

The one to watch is *ian*. Between the *i* and the *n*, the *a* is pulled up almost to an *e*,
so {天|tiān} sounds like *tyen* and {钱|qián} like *chyen*. Learners who read the letters and say
*tee-ahn* sound foreign at once. Compare *iang*, where the *a* stays deep and open: {钱|qián} money
against {墙|qiáng} wall. The raised *a* belongs to *ian* (and to *üan*, below) only.

## Nasal finals with u: uan, uen, uang, ueng

Alone, these are spelled with w: *uan* → *wan*, *uen* → *wen*, *uang* → *wang*, *ueng* → *weng*.

| Final | Alone | With an initial | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| uan | wan | -uan | {玩|wán} to play, {晚|wǎn} late, {穿|chuān} to wear, {关|guān} to close |
| uen | wen | -un | {问|wèn} to ask, {中文|Zhōng wén} Chinese; {春天|chūn tiān} spring |
| uang | wang | -uang | {往|wǎng} towards, {忘|wàng} to forget, {床|chuáng} bed, {双|shuāng} pair |
| ueng | weng | (spelled -ong) | {翁|wēng} old man (rare) |

Two spelling rules hide inside this table:

- *uen* is written *un* after an initial, just as *uei* became *ui* in lesson 07: {春|chūn},
  {村|cūn} village, {孙|sūn} grandchild. The *e* is still there in the sound, faintly: *chwun*,
  not *choon*. Alone it keeps every letter: *wen*.
- *ueng* exists only as *weng*. After a consonant, the nearly identical sound is written *ong*
  ({东|dōng}, {中|zhōng}). *Weng* itself is rare; you'll meet it in a few words and names.

## Nasal finals with ü: üan and ün

| Final | Alone | After j q x | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| üan | yuan | juan, quan, xuan | {元|yuán} yuan (money), {医院|yī yuàn} hospital, {选|xuǎn} to choose, {全|quán} whole |
| ün | yun | jun, qun, xun | {运动|yùn dòng} sport, {裙子|qún zi} skirt, {军|jūn} army |

You know the rule from lesson 05: after j, q, x and y the dots on ü are dropped, because those
initials never come before a plain *u*. So *yuan*, *juan*, *quan* and *xuan* all contain ü. Round
your lips for the start of each one. And like *ian*, *üan* raises its *a*: {元|yuán} sounds close to
*ywen*, not *yoo-ahn*.

*üan* and *ün* never come after n or l, so a nasal final never shows dots.

### The two un's and the two uan's

The same spelling can stand for two finals, and the initial tells you which:

| Spelling | After j, q, x, y it is… | After any other initial it is… |
|---|---|---|
| un | ün: {军|jūn}, {裙子|qún zi}, *xùn*, *yún* | uen: {春|chūn}, {村|cūn}, *dùn*, *lùn* |
| uan | üan: *juǎn*, {全|quán}, {选|xuǎn}, {元|yuán} | uan: {关|guān}, {穿|chuān}, {玩|wán}, *duǎn* |

The rule never fails: j, q, x and y can't be followed by a plain *u*, so whenever you see *u* after
one of them, say ü.

## Every final in one table

You have now met all the finals in the official table of Hanyu Pinyin: 35 in its four columns,
plus *er* (lesson 12), the buzzed *-i* of *zhi chi shi ri zi ci si* (lesson 06) and *ê*, a rare
interjection. Spellings used when there's no initial are in brackets. The new ones from this
lesson are the bottom five rows.

| Open | With i | With u | With ü |
|---|---|---|---|
| | i (yi) | u (wu) | ü (yu) |
| a | ia (ya) | ua (wa) | |
| o | | uo (wo) | |
| e | ie (ye) | | üe (yue) |
| ai | | uai (wai) | |
| ei | | uei (wei), -ui | |
| ao | iao (yao) | | |
| ou | iou (you), -iu | | |
| an | ian (yan) | uan (wan) | üan (yuan) |
| en | in (yin) | uen (wen), -un | ün (yun) |
| ang | iang (yang) | uang (wang) | |
| eng | ing (ying) | ueng (weng) | |
| ong | iong (yong) | | |

The four columns are a good way to remember the system: every final either starts with nothing
special, or with an *i*, *u* or *ü* glide in front of the same core. Read the rows across: *an*,
*ian*, *uan*, *üan* all share the *-an* core (and two of them raise the *a*). The reference sheet
"The syllable table" lists every syllable you can make with these finals.

## Listening

The quiz for this lesson asks you to tell *-n* from *-ng* by ear and to pick the tones of words
with nasal finals. Some tips:

- Listen to the vowel as much as to the end. A deep, back *a* means *-ang*; a bright *a* means *-an*.
- Words help more than single syllables. If you know the word {星期|xīng qī} (week), you'll never
  mishear {星|xīng} as {新|xīn}.
- Record yourself saying the pairs in the table above, then compare with the voice.

## Say it

Listen, then repeat. Freeze on the last sound of each pair to check your tongue.

```speak
{饭|fàn}，{放|fàng}
= meal; to put (-an, -ang)
{新|xīn}，{星|xīng}
= new; star (-in, -ing)
{钱|qián}，{墙|qiáng}
= money; wall (-ian, -iang)
{盆|pén}，{朋|péng}
= basin; friend (-en, -eng)
{今天|jīn tiān}
= today
{房间|fáng jiān}
= room
{电影|diàn yǐng}
= film
{中文|Zhōng wén}
= Chinese (the language)
{医院|yī yuàn}
= hospital
{运动|yùn dòng}
= sport
```

## Common mistakes

- Adding a *g* after *-ng*: {星期|xīng qī} isn't *xing-gi*. The *ng* stops in the nose.
- Saying *ian* as *ee-ahn*. {天|tiān} sounds like *tyen*; {电|diàn} like *dyen*.
- Saying *en* like English *hen*. The Mandarin vowel is the central *uh* sound of {的|de}.
- Reading *jun*, *qun*, *xun*, *yun* with a plain *oo*. They're ü: round your lips.
- Reading *chun*, *dun*, *lun* as *choon*. They're *uen*: a faint *e* is still there.
- Dropping the ending in fast English-style speech. Every *-n* and *-ng* is said, even in
  long words: {中国|Zhōng guó} has its *ng*.

## Key points

- Mandarin syllables end only in a vowel, *-n*, *-ng* (or the *-r* of erhua). The 16 nasal finals
  are an en ang eng ong; ian in iang ing iong; uan uen uang ueng; üan ün.
- *-n*: tongue tip up behind the teeth; *-ng*: back of the tongue up, no *g*. The vowel before it
  helps you hear the difference.
- *ian* and *üan* sound like *yen* and *ywen*: the *a* is raised.
- Spelling: *uen* → *-un* after an initial; *ueng* only as *weng* (*ong* after initials); alone,
  i-finals take y and u-finals take w, ü-finals take *yu*.
- After j, q, x, y, *un* is ün and *uan* is üan.
- You've now met every final: 35 in the official table, plus *er*, the buzzed *-i* and *ê*.

lessons.title: Writing pinyin: tone marks, ü, the apostrophe and words
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can now say every Mandarin syllable. This lesson is about writing them down correctly, which
matters more than it might seem: dictionaries, phone keyboards, textbooks and signs all use the
same rules, and a mark on the wrong letter or a missing dot can turn one syllable into another.
You'll learn four things:

1. which vowel gets the **[[tone mark]]**;
2. when ü keeps its two dots;
3. when to write an **[[apostrophe]]** inside a word;
4. how pinyin is written in words and sentences, and how tone numbers fit in.

The rules come from the official standards: the Scheme for the Chinese Phonetic Alphabet of 1958
and the national standard for writing pinyin, GB/T 16159. The explanations here are this course's
own.

## Where the tone mark goes

Every syllable with a full tone has one mark, and it sits on a vowel. When there's only one vowel,
that's easy: *mā*, *nǐ*, *lù*. When there are two or three, use this order:

1. If there's an *a*, it takes the mark.
2. Otherwise, if there's an *e*, it takes the mark.
3. Otherwise, in *ou*, the *o* takes the mark.
4. Otherwise, the mark goes on the last vowel.

*a* and *e* never appear in the same syllable, so rules 1 and 2 never compete. Rule 4 covers *uo*
(the *o* is last), *iu* and *ui*, the two shortened finals from lesson 07: *liù*, not ~~*lìu*~~;
*guì*, not ~~*gùi*~~.

| Final | Mark on | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| ao, ai, ia, ua, iao, uai, an, ang, ian, uan… | a | {好|hǎo} good, {家|jiā} home, {快|kuài} fast, {小|xiǎo} small, {钱|qián} money |
| ei, ie, üe, en, eng | e | {谢|xiè} (in {谢谢|xiè xie}, thanks), {学|xué} to learn, {很|hěn} very |
| ou, iou | o | {狗|gǒu} dog, {有|yǒu} to have |
| uo | o (the last vowel) | {多|duō} many, {国|guó} country |
| iu | u (the last vowel) | {六|liù} six, {九|jiǔ} nine, {牛|niú} cow |
| ui | i (the last vowel) | {贵|guì} expensive, {水|shuǐ} water, {对|duì} right |
| a single vowel | that vowel | {不|bù} not, {女|nǚ} female, {一|yī} one |

Why these rules? The Scheme says the mark goes on the main vowel of the syllable, the loudest
and longest part. In *hǎo* that's the *a*; the *o* is only a glide at the end. *iu* and *ui* are
shortened from *iou* and *uei*: their main vowel (*o*, *e*) isn't written, so the rule just
picks the last letter.

Two small points:

- On an *i*, the mark replaces the dot: *ī í ǐ ì*. Don't write both.
- Handwriting the marks: draw them short and clearly sloped, and over the right letter. A mark
  drifting between two letters is a common source of confusion in notes.

## ü and its dots

You met the rule in lesson 05. Here it is as a writing rule:

| After | ü is written | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| n, l | ü, with its dots | {女|nǚ} female, {绿|lǜ} green, {女儿|nǚ ér} daughter |
| j, q, x | u, no dots | {去|qù} to go, {学|xué} to learn, {句|jù} (measure word for sentences) |
| no initial | yu | {鱼|yú} fish, {月|yuè} month, moon, {元|yuán} yuan |

After j, q, x and y, a plain *u* can't occur, so the dots tell you nothing and are left off.
After n and l both are possible, and they are different words: {路|lù} is a road, {绿|lǜ} is green;
*nǔ* and *nǚ* differ in the same way. So the dots stay.

With a tone mark, ü carries both: *ǖ ǘ ǚ ǜ*.

## The apostrophe

Pinyin words are written without spaces between their syllables, and that can make a word
readable in two ways. *Xian* could be one syllable, *xiān* ({先|xiān}, first), or two, *Xī* + *ān*:
the city of Xi'an ({西安|Xī ān}). The apostrophe settles it.

The rule: inside a word, write ' before a syllable that starts with *a*, *o* or *e*.

| Word | Written | Without the apostrophe it could also be read… |
|---|---|---|
| {西安|Xī ān} Xi'an | *Xī'ān* | *xiān*, one syllable ({先|xiān}, first) |
| {平安|píng ān} safe and sound | *píng'ān* | *pín* + *gān* |
| {方案|fāng àn} plan | *fāng'àn* | *fān* + *gàn* |

The official rule asks for the apostrophe when the boundary could be confused. In practice
dictionaries and textbooks write it before every *a*, *o* or *e* that begins a syllable inside a
word, even where nothing could be misread: {女儿|nǚ ér} *nǚ'ér* (daughter), {可爱|kě ài} *kě'ài*
(cute), {答案|dá àn} *dá'àn* (answer), {海鸥|hǎi ōu} *hǎi'ōu* (seagull). That is the simplest
habit, so it's the one to learn.

You never need it before *y* or *w*, because those letters already show where a new syllable
begins: *dàyī* (coat), *Zhōngwén* (Chinese). And you never need it at the start of a word.

In this app, the pinyin over the characters is spaced one syllable per character, so the
apostrophe appears only where pinyin is written as whole words, like the italics in these
lessons. When you type an answer, apostrophes don't count: `Xi1an1` and `Xi1'an1` are both fine.

## Writing words, not syllables

Pinyin is written word by word. The syllables of one word are joined, and words are separated by
spaces, as in English:

- {朋友|péng you} friend → *péngyou*, not *péng you*
- {中国|Zhōng guó} China → *Zhōngguó*
- {学生|xué sheng} student → *xuésheng*
- {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}。 → *Wǒ shì xuésheng.*

Capitals work as in English: at the start of a sentence, and for names. Personal names are written
surname first, then the given name, each with a capital and a space between them; a two-syllable
given name is joined: {王芳|Wáng Fāng} *Wáng Fāng*, {李明|Lǐ Míng} *Lǐ Míng*. Place names are
capitalised and joined: {北京|Běi jīng} *Běijīng*, {上海|Shàng hǎi} *Shànghǎi*. In English text the
tone marks are usually dropped: Wang Fang, Beijing, Shanghai.

Which syllables make up a word is sometimes a judgment call (a very long name may be split), and
you'll see published pinyin spaced syllable by syllable too, especially in materials for
learners. The word list in this course always shows you how each word is split.

Over the characters in this app you'll see the pinyin one syllable per character:
{朋友|péng you}. That's a display choice so each syllable sits over its character; when you write
pinyin on its own, join the word.

## Tone numbers

Tone marks are the standard way of writing pinyin, but they're awkward to type. Numbers are the
common substitute: put the tone after each syllable, 1 to 4, and 5 (or 0, or nothing) for the
neutral tone.

| With marks | With numbers |
|---|---|
| *nǐ hǎo* | ni3 hao3 |
| *xièxie* | xie4 xie5 |
| *nǚ'ér* | nv3 er2 (or nu:3 er2) |
| *Xī'ān* | Xi1 an1 |

Some dictionaries, such as the free CC-CEDICT, write pinyin this way, with *u:* for ü. In this app,
whenever you type pinyin, type the number after each syllable and the app puts the mark on the
right vowel for you: `gui4` becomes *guì*, `liu4` becomes *liù*. Type `v` (or `u:`) for ü after n
and l: `nv3` becomes *nǚ*, `lv4` becomes *lǜ*. After j, q, x and y, type a plain `u`: `qu4` gives
*qù*. Spaces and capital letters don't matter when your answer is checked; tones do.

Numbers are a typing aid, not a way of writing: in anything you write by hand or publish, use
the marks.

## Practice: which spelling is right?

Cover the answers and decide for each pair.

1. *guì* or *gùi* (expensive)
2. *xué* or *xüé* (to learn)
3. *liù* or *lìu* (six)
4. *haǒ* or *hǎo* (good)
5. *Xīān* or *Xī'ān* (the city)
6. *nǚ* or *nǔ* (female)
7. *duō* or *dūo* (many)
8. *péngyou* or *péng you* (friend, written as a word)

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. *guì*: in *ui* the last vowel takes the mark.
2. *xué*: no dots after x.
3. *liù*: in *iu* the last vowel takes the mark.
4. *hǎo*: *a* comes first in the order.
5. *Xī'ān*: an apostrophe before a syllable starting with *a*.
6. *nǚ*: after n the dots stay; *nǔ* is a different syllable.
7. *duō*: in *uo* the last vowel takes the mark.
8. *péngyou*: one word, written joined.
</details>

## Say it

These words all appear in this lesson. Say each, then picture how it's spelled.

```speak
{贵|guì}
= expensive
{六|liù}
= six
{学|xué}
= to learn
{女儿|nǚ ér}
= daughter
{西安|Xī ān}
= Xi'an
{先|xiān}
= first
{平安|píng ān}
= safe and sound
{朋友|péng you}
= friend
```

## Common mistakes

- Marking the first vowel of *iu* and *ui*: ~~*lìu*~~, ~~*gùi*~~. The last vowel takes it.
- Marking the *o* of *ao*: ~~*haǒ*~~. *a* always wins.
- Writing dots after j, q, x, y (~~*xüé*~~), or leaving them off after n and l (*nu* is a
  different syllable from *nü*).
- Leaving out the apostrophe: *Xian* for the city, *pingan* for *píng'ān*.
- Splitting words: ~~*péng you*~~ when pinyin is written on its own.
- Writing the dot of *i* under a tone mark: *nǐ* has the mark only.

## Key points

- The tone mark goes on *a*, else *e*, else the *o* of *ou*, else the last vowel: *hǎo*, *xiè*,
  *gǒu*, *duō*, *liù*, *guì*. On *i*, the mark replaces the dot.
- ü keeps its dots after n and l (*nǚ*, *lǜ*); after j, q, x and y it's written u (*qù*, *xué*,
  *yú*).
- Inside a word, an apostrophe goes before a syllable starting with *a*, *o* or *e*: *Xī'ān*,
  *nǚ'ér*, *kě'ài*.
- Pinyin is written in words (*péngyou*, *Zhōngguó*), with capitals for names and sentence starts.
- Tone numbers (ni3 hao3, 5 for neutral, v for ü) are for typing; the app turns them into marks.

lessons.title: Tone pairs and the neutral tone in words
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

So far you've mostly practised tones one syllable at a time. Real Mandarin doesn't come in single
syllables: most words have two, and in a sentence the tones run into each other. A tone that's
easy alone can go wrong next to another. A rising tone after a high one, a low tone before a
falling one: these are the combinations to train.

So this lesson works with **[[tone pairs]]**: the tones of two syllables said together. There are
20 patterns: 16 with two full tones (1+1 up to 4+4) and 4 with a neutral second syllable (1+0 to
4+0, writing 0 for the neutral tone). Each has a common word you'll meet again in HSK 1. Learn
the 20 words as models, and you have a template for the tones of almost any two-syllable word.

At the end there's your first dialogue: a greeting between a student and a teacher.

## The 16 pairs of full tones

Read across: the first syllable's tone is the row, the second's the column.

| | + 1st | + 2nd | + 3rd | + 4th |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1st | {今天|jīn tiān} today | {中国|Zhōng guó} China | {中午|zhōng wǔ} noon | {工作|gōng zuò} work, to work |
| 2nd | {明天|míng tiān} tomorrow | {学习|xué xí} to study | {苹果|píng guǒ} apple | {学校|xué xiào} school |
| 3rd | {老师|lǎo shī} teacher | {小时|xiǎo shí} hour | {你好|nǐ hǎo} hello | {米饭|mǐ fàn} cooked rice |
| 4th | {上班|shàng bān} to go to work | {问题|wèn tí} question | {电脑|diàn nǎo} computer | {再见|zài jiàn} goodbye |

Some more, if you want extra models: 1+1 {飞机|fēi jī} plane; 1+3 {开始|kāi shǐ} to begin; 2+3 {牛奶|niú nǎi} milk; 3+2
{女儿|nǚ ér} daughter; 3+3 {水果|shuǐ guǒ} fruit; 4+3 {下午|xià wǔ} afternoon; 4+4 {电话|diàn huà}
phone.

### What happens inside the pairs

- First tone first (1+x): keep the first syllable high and flat right to the end, then make
  the move of the second: {中国|Zhōng guó} stays high, then rises; {工作|gōng zuò} stays high, then
  drops. Don't let the high tone sag before a fall.
- Third tone first (3+1, 3+2, 3+4): this is where the half-third tone from lesson 02 matters.
  Before any tone except another third, a third tone is just low. It doesn't rise again. In
  {老师|lǎo shī}, {小时|xiǎo shí} and {米饭|mǐ fàn}, the first syllable sits at the bottom of your
  voice and the second starts from there. A full dip-and-rise in {老师|lǎo shī} sounds like two
  separate words.
- Third tone second (1+3, 2+3, 4+3): at the end of a word the third tone is low, and may rise a
  little at the end of a phrase. In {苹果|píng guǒ} the voice rises on {苹|píng} and then drops low
  for {果|guǒ}; in {电脑|diàn nǎo} it falls on {电|diàn} and stays low.
- 3+3: two third tones in a row are hard to say, so the first one changes. {你好|nǐ hǎo} is
  said *ní hǎo*, exactly like 2+3. It's still written *nǐ hǎo*. Lesson 11 is about this change.
- 2+3 against 3+2, the two most confused pairs: in 2+3 ({苹果|píng guǒ}) the voice goes up,
  then down low. In 3+2 ({小时|xiǎo shí}) it starts low, then climbs. Hum them: *mm-MM-mm* versus
  *mm-mm-MM*.
- 4+4: two falls in a row, in a zigzag. The first starts at the top and falls only about halfway;
  the second starts a little lower and falls all the way down: {再见|zài jiàn}, {电话|diàn huà}.
  Don't make two identical full falls with a jump in between.
- 2+1 and 1+2: make the rise reach the top. In {明天|míng tiān} the rise of {明|míng} should
  end at the height where {天|tiān} stays.

## The neutral tone in words

The other four patterns end in a neutral tone: a short, light syllable with no tone of its own
and no mark. Its pitch comes from the syllable before. After a 1st, 2nd or 4th tone it's low;
after a 3rd it's higher, because the low third tone leaves the voice room to go up.

| Pattern | Model | More |
|---|---|---|
| 1 + neutral | {妈妈|mā ma} mum | {哥哥|gē ge} older brother, {桌子|zhuō zi} table, {东西|dōng xi} thing |
| 2 + neutral | {朋友|péng you} friend | {学生|xué sheng} student, {名字|míng zi} name, {什么|shén me} what |
| 3 + neutral | {姐姐|jiě jie} older sister | {我们|wǒ men} we, {喜欢|xǐ huan} to like, {饺子|jiǎo zi} dumplings |
| 4 + neutral | {爸爸|bà ba} dad | {谢谢|xiè xie} thanks, {弟弟|dì di} younger brother, {妹妹|mèi mei} younger sister |

Where you'll find neutral tones:
