- Repeated family words ({妈妈|mā ma}, {爸爸|bà ba}, {哥哥|gē ge}, {姐姐|jiě jie}, {弟弟|dì di},
  {妹妹|mèi mei}): the second syllable is always neutral.
- Little suffixes and particles: {子|zi} in {桌子|zhuō zi}, {包子|bāo zi}, {饺子|jiǎo zi};
  {们|men} in {我们|wǒ men}; question particles such as {吗|ma} and {呢|ne}.
- Many common two-syllable words, which you simply learn with their neutral tone:
  {朋友|péng you}, {学生|xué sheng}, {喜欢|xǐ huan}, {谢谢|xiè xie}. The word list always shows it.

The neutral tone isn't decoration: it can tell words apart. {东西|dōng xi} with a neutral second
syllable means "thing, stuff"; said with two first tones, *dōngxī* means "east and west".

Don't give a neutral syllable a full tone (*xiè xiè* with two strong falls sounds stilted), but
don't swallow it either: the vowel is still there, just short and light.

## Stress in two-syllable words

Neutral-tone words have an obvious rhythm: strong, then weak. {妈妈|mā ma} is *MA-ma*,
{谢谢|xiè xie} is *XIE-xie*, much as in English *mother* or *thank you*.

Words with two full tones are less clear-cut, and linguists describe them differently. Some say
the first syllable carries the stress, others the second, and some say Mandarin words have no
fixed stress at all. What matters for you: give both syllables their full tone and their full
length. English speakers tend to shorten one syllable of a word, which makes *gōngzuò* sound like
*g'ZUO*; in Mandarin both syllables keep their vowels and tones. At the end of a phrase the last
syllable is often a little longer, which is one reason the second syllable can sound stronger.

## How to practise tone pairs

- Hum first: before saying a word, hum its pitch shape. {中国|Zhōng guó} is a high hum, then a
  rising one. Then put the syllables on top.
- Use the 16 models: when you learn a new two-syllable word, find its pattern in the table and
  say the model word, then the new one: {明天|míng tiān} → {时间|shí jiān} (time), both 2+1.
- Exaggerate, then relax: make the tones too big at first, then say the word at normal speed.
- Listen in pairs: the quiz for this lesson plays words for you to pick the tone of each
  syllable: a row of buttons for each syllable, or keys 1 to 4 and 5 for neutral.

## Dialogue: Hello, teacher

{王芳|Wáng Fāng} (王芳) is a student; {陈刚|Chén Gāng} (陈刚) is a teacher. They meet for the first
time. Some of these words are taught in lesson 15 and the rest in HSK 1 (all are glossed in the
table below); for now, listen to the tone pairs.

```dialogue
# Hello, teacher
王芳: {你好|nǐ hǎo}！
= Hello!
陈刚: {你好|nǐ hǎo}！{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}{吗|ma}？
= Hello! Are you a student?
王芳: {是|shì}。{你|nǐ}{也|yě}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}{吗|ma}？
= Yes. Are you a student too?
陈刚: {不是|bú shì}，{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī}。
= No, I'm a teacher.
王芳: {老师|lǎo shī}{好|hǎo}！
= Hello, teacher!
陈刚: {你好|nǐ hǎo}。{明天|míng tiān}{见|jiàn}！
= Hello. See you tomorrow!
王芳: {老师|lǎo shī}{再见|zài jiàn}！
= Goodbye, teacher!
```

| Word | Meaning | Tones |
|---|---|---|
| {你好|nǐ hǎo} | hello | 3+3, said 2+3 |
| {你|nǐ} | you | 3 |
| {是|shì} | to be; yes | 4 |
| {学生|xué sheng} | student | 2 + neutral |
| {吗|ma} | (turns a sentence into a yes/no question) | neutral |
| {也|yě} | also, too | 3 |
| {不是|bú shì} | no, isn't | 2+4: {不|bù} changes before a 4th tone (lesson 11) |
| {我|wǒ} | I | 3 |
| {老师|lǎo shī} | teacher | 3+1 |
| {明天|míng tiān}{见|jiàn} | see you tomorrow | 2+1, then 4 |
| {再见|zài jiàn} | goodbye | 4+4 |

Notice {老师|lǎo shī}{好|hǎo}: "teacher + good" is how students greet a teacher in China. And
{老师|lǎo shī}{再见|zài jiàn}, "teacher, goodbye", puts the person first.

## Say it

```speak
{今天|jīn tiān}
= today (1+1)
{中国|Zhōng guó}
= China (1+2)
{苹果|píng guǒ}
= apple (2+3)
{小时|xiǎo shí}
= hour (3+2)
{老师|lǎo shī}
= teacher (3+1)
{米饭|mǐ fàn}
= cooked rice (3+4)
{电脑|diàn nǎo}
= computer (4+3)
{再见|zài jiàn}
= goodbye (4+4)
{妈妈|mā ma}
= mum (1 + neutral)
{朋友|péng you}
= friend (2 + neutral)
{姐姐|jiě jie}
= older sister (3 + neutral)
{谢谢|xiè xie}
= thank you (4 + neutral)
```

## Common mistakes

- A full dip on a third tone before another tone: {老师|lǎo shī} sounds like *lǎo… shī*. Keep it
  low and go straight on.
- Mixing up 2+3 and 3+2: {苹果|píng guǒ} rises first; {小时|xiǎo shí} rises second.
- Letting a 1st tone droop before a 4th: {工作|gōng zuò} needs a high, flat {工|gōng}.
- Giving neutral syllables a full tone: ~~*xiè xiè*~~, ~~*bà bà*~~.
- Swallowing a full-tone syllable English-style: both syllables of {工作|gōng zuò} are full.

## Key points

- Practise tones in pairs: 16 patterns of two full tones and 4 with a neutral second syllable.
- A third tone before a non-third tone is a low half-third with no rise; 3+3 is said 2+3.
- The neutral tone is short and light, low after tones 1, 2 and 4 and higher after tone 3. It
  appears in repeated family words, after {子|zi} and {们|men}, in particles and in many common
  words, and it can tell words apart ({东西|dōng xi}).
- Neutral-tone words go strong-weak; in other words give both syllables their full tone.
- 20 model words: learn them, and every new two-syllable word has a pattern to copy.

lessons.title: Tone changes: two third tones, 一 and 不
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

A few syllables change their tone because of the syllable after them. This is called **tone
sandhi** (*sandhi* is a Sanskrit word for "joining"). Mandarin has three common cases, and you
need all three from your first conversation:

1. a third tone before another third tone, as in {你好|nǐ hǎo};
2. {不|bù} (not) before a fourth tone;
3. {一|yī} (one) before other syllables.

The first is never written; the other two are written changed in this course, but not in most
dictionaries. This lesson explains each change, how pinyin shows it (or doesn't), and how to hear
it.

## Two third tones: 3 + 3 → 2 + 3

When two third tones come together, the first one is said as a second tone:

| Written | Said | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {你好|nǐ hǎo} | *ní hǎo* | hello |
| {水果|shuǐ guǒ} | *shuí guǒ* | fruit |
| {可以|kě yǐ} | *ké yǐ* | can, may |
| {很好|hěn hǎo} | *hén hǎo* | very good |
| {我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng} | *wó xiǎng* | I'd like to |

Why? A third tone is low. Two low syllables in a row, each with a dip, would be slow and heavy, so
the first one rises instead. The changed syllable sounds like a normal second tone, and listeners
generally can't tell the two apart: *ní hǎo* and a real 2+3 pair such as {苹果|píng guǒ} have the same tune.

It works across words, too, whenever two thirds meet inside a phrase: {很|hěn} + {好|hǎo},
{我|wǒ} + {想|xiǎng}, {你|nǐ} + {早|zǎo} (good morning, said *ní zǎo*).

### It's never written

Pinyin always shows each syllable's own tone, the one in the dictionary: *nǐ hǎo*, *shuǐguǒ*,
never ~~*ní hǎo*~~. There are good reasons:

- The change depends on what comes next. {好|hǎo} is *hǎo* alone and in {好吃|hǎo chī}, but its
  neighbour changes in {你好|nǐ hǎo}. Writing the change would make the same word look different
  in every phrase.
- In longer runs, how the change falls depends on how the words group (below), so there isn't
  always one right way to write it.
- It's completely regular. Once you know the rule, you apply it automatically.

So when you read two marks ˇ ˇ side by side, say the first as a rise. In this app's tone
questions, both answers are accepted for a 3+3 word: the tones as written (3+3) and as you hear
them (2+3). For three third tones in a row, the written 3+3+3 counts, and so do both ways of
saying it shown below, 2+2+3 and 3+2+3.

### Runs of three or more

With three or more third tones in a row, split the run into words and apply the rule inside each
group first:

| Words | Written | Usually said |
|---|---|---|
| {展览|zhǎn lǎn} + {馆|guǎn} (exhibition + hall) | *zhǎnlǎnguǎn* | *zhán lán guǎn* (2+2+3) |
| {小|xiǎo} + {老虎|lǎo hǔ} (little + tiger) | *xiǎo lǎohǔ* | *xiǎo láo hǔ* (3+2+3) |
| {我也|wǒ yě} + {很好|hěn hǎo} (I too + very well) | *wǒ yě hěn hǎo* | *wó yě hén hǎo* |

In the second example, {小|xiǎo} isn't followed directly by a third tone once {老|lǎo} has risen,
so it stays low (a half-third). Speakers vary, especially when talking fast: you'll also hear
*xiáo láo hǔ*. Don't worry about long runs. Get the pairs right, and the rest comes with
listening.

### Third tones before other tones

The other half of the rule you know from lessons 02 and 10: before a 1st, 2nd, 4th or neutral
tone, a third tone is a low half-third with no rise ({老师|lǎo shī}, {米饭|mǐ fàn},
{姐姐|jiě jie}). The full dip and rise is heard only alone or at the end of a phrase. So the full dip is
much rarer in speech than the usual drawing of the third tone suggests.

## 不 bù: bú before a fourth tone

{不|bù} (not) is a fourth tone. Before another fourth tone it becomes a second tone, *bú*. Before
anything else it stays *bù*.

| Before | 不 is | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| a 4th tone | *bú* | {不是|bú shì} isn't, {不要|bú yào} don't, {不对|bú duì} not right, {不去|bú qù} not go |
| a 1st, 2nd or 3rd tone | *bù* | {不吃|bù chī} not eat, {不忙|bù máng} not busy, {不来|bù lái} not come, {不好|bù hǎo} not good |
| nothing (said alone) | *bù* | {不|bù}！ No! |

{不客气|bú kè qi} (you're welcome) follows the rule too: {客|kè} is a fourth tone.

In a few places {不|bù} goes light, a neutral *bu*:

- in the middle of a yes-or-no question built as "A not A": {是不是|shì bu shì} (is it or not?),
  {好不好|hǎo bu hǎo} (is that OK?), {忙不忙|máng bu máng} (are you busy?);
- in some set words, such as {对不起|duì bu qǐ} (sorry).

## 一 yī: three tones, depending on the next syllable

{一|yī} (one) is a first tone, and keeps it whenever it's a number on its own:

- alone and in counting: {一|yī}, {二|èr}, {三|sān};
- as the last digit or inside a number: {十一|shí yī} (eleven), {二十一|èr shí yī} (21);
- in ordinals and dates: {第一|dì yī} (first), {一月|yī yuè} (January), {一号|yī hào} (the 1st);
- read digit by digit, as in years: {一九九八|yī jiǔ jiǔ bā} (1998);
- at the end of a word: {统一|tǒng yī} (to unify).

(In phone and room numbers, people often say *yāo* for 1 instead, so it can't be mistaken for
{七|qī}, seven.)

When 一 is "one of something", in front of a measure word, a noun or a verb, it changes like 不,
and has one more case:

| Before | 一 is | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| a 4th tone | *yí* | {一个|yí gè} one (of anything), {一下|yí xià} (for) a moment, {一定|yí dìng} certainly, {一样|yí yàng} the same |
| a 1st, 2nd or 3rd tone | *yì* | {一天|yì tiān} one day, {一年|yì nián} one year, {一起|yì qǐ} together, {一点儿|yì diǎnr} a little |
| between a repeated verb | *yi* (neutral) | {看一看|kàn yi kàn} have a look, {想一想|xiǎng yi xiǎng} think it over |

{一个|yí gè} counts as a fourth-tone case because {个|gè} is a fourth tone, even though {个|gè} is often
said lightly. And 一 before a number word such as {百|bǎi} (hundred) changes too: {一百|yì bǎi}.

## How this app writes 一 and 不

Dictionaries, and most books and websites, write 一 and 不 with their original tones everywhere:
*yīdìng*, *bùshì*. The Chinese national standard for writing pinyin allows the changed tones in
language teaching, and this course uses that: you see *yídìng*, *búshì*, which is what you say.
Expect to see *yī* and *bù* written in other places, and say them changed anyway.

Third-tone sandhi is the exception: it's never written here, and standard pinyin doesn't write it
either (a few textbooks mark it, but dictionaries don't).

## Dialogue: going together

{王芳|Wáng Fāng} (王芳) meets {高文|Gāo Wén} (高文) at the school gate. Listen for 不, 一 and
the third tones.

```dialogue
# Going together
王芳: {你好|nǐ hǎo}！{你|nǐ}{是不是|shì bu shì}{老师|lǎo shī}？
= Hi! Are you a teacher?
高文: {我|wǒ}{不是|bú shì}{老师|lǎo shī}，{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}。{你|nǐ}{呢|ne}？
= I'm not a teacher, I'm a student. And you?
王芳: {我|wǒ}{也|yě}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}。{我们|wǒ men}{一起|yì qǐ}{去|qù}{吧|ba}！
= I'm a student too. Let's go together!
高文: {好|hǎo}！{你|nǐ}{等|děng}{一下|yí xià}。
= OK! Wait a moment.
```

| Phrase | Written | Said |
|---|---|---|
| {你好|nǐ hǎo} | *nǐ hǎo* | *ní hǎo* (3+3) |
| {是不是|shì bu shì} | *shì bu shì* | the 不 is light (A-not-A) |
| {不是|bú shì} | *bú shì* | 不 before a 4th tone |
| {我也|wǒ yě} | *wǒ yě* | *wó yě* (3+3) |
| {一起|yì qǐ} | *yìqǐ* | 一 before a 3rd tone |
| {你等|nǐ děng} | *nǐ děng* | *ní děng* (3+3): {等|děng}, to wait |
| {一下|yí xià} | *yíxià* | 一 before a 4th tone |

Other new words: {呢|ne} (and you?), {我们|wǒ men} (we), {去|qù} (to go), {吧|ba} (makes a
suggestion: let's…).

## Say it

```speak
{你好|nǐ hǎo}
= hello (said ní hǎo)
{水果|shuǐ guǒ}
= fruit (said shuí guǒ)
{很好|hěn hǎo}
= very good (said hén hǎo)
{不是|bú shì}
= isn't
{不吃|bù chī}
= not eat
{一定|yí dìng}
= certainly
{一起|yì qǐ}
= together
{第一|dì yī}
= first
{看一看|kàn yi kàn}
= have a look
```

## Common mistakes

- Saying both syllables of {你好|nǐ hǎo} with a full dip. The first one rises.
- Writing the 3+3 change: ~~*ní hǎo*~~. Pinyin keeps *nǐ hǎo*.
- Saying *bù shì* with two full falls. Before a 4th tone it's *bú*.
- Changing 一 in numbers and dates: {十一|shí yī} and {一月|yī yuè} keep *yī*.
- Treating {一个|yí gè} as a neutral-tone case because {个|gè} often sounds light: it's still *yí*.
- Being thrown by dictionaries: *yīdìng* and *bùshì* in a dictionary are the same words as
  *yídìng* and *búshì* here.

## Key points

- Tone sandhi: some tones change before others.
- 3+3 → 2+3 ({你好|nǐ hǎo} said *ní hǎo*), in words and across words. Never written. Longer runs
  are grouped by words.
- 不 is *bú* before a 4th tone, *bù* elsewhere, and light in A-not-A questions.
- 一 is *yī* as a number (counting, digits, ordinals, dates, word-final), *yí* before a 4th tone,
  *yì* before tones 1, 2 and 3, and light in V-一-V.
- This course writes the 一 and 不 changes; dictionaries usually don't.

lessons.title: Erhua and the syllable table
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This lesson finishes the sound system. First, the last spelling feature you need: **[[erhua]]**, the
*-r* ending typical of Beijing and northern speech, as in {哪儿|nǎr} (where?) and
{一点儿|yì diǎnr} (a little). Then a step back to look at the whole system: the syllable table,
which shows every syllable Mandarin has, why some combinations never occur, and how to use the
table to check a spelling. The lesson ends with a review of the confusions learners meet most
often, as a checklist before module 3 brings in characters.

## Erhua: the -r ending

The character {儿|ér} on its own means "child, son" and is a syllable of its own: {女儿|nǚ ér}
(daughter). But after many words it isn't said as a separate syllable. Instead it melts into the
syllable before it, which ends with an *r* sound, the tongue tip curling up and back. Pinyin
writes this by adding *-r*; in characters, 儿 is still written.

| Characters | Pinyin | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {哪儿|nǎr} | *nǎr* | where? |
| {这儿|zhèr} | *zhèr* | here |
| {那儿|nàr} | *nàr* | there |
| {一点儿|yì diǎnr} | *yìdiǎnr* | a little |
| {有点儿|yǒu diǎnr} | *yǒudiǎnr* | a bit, rather |
| {一会儿|yí huìr} | *yíhuìr* | a moment |
| {好玩儿|hǎo wánr} | *hǎowánr* | fun |
| {面条儿|miàn tiáor} | *miàntiáor* | noodles |

Two characters, one syllable: in {哪儿|nǎr} the pinyin *nǎr* sits over both 哪 and 儿. The tone
mark stays where it was, and the *r* adds no tone of its own.

### How it sounds

The *r* is a curl of the tongue added to the end of the syllable, rather like the end of
American English *car* or *her* (only an approximation). What happens to the syllable depends on
how it ends:

| The syllable ends in… | What happens | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| a, o, e, u (and ao, ou, iao…) | the *r* is simply added | {这儿|zhèr}, {花儿|huār} flower, {面条儿|miàn tiáor} |
| -n or -i | the -n or -i is dropped, then *r* | {一点儿|yì diǎnr} sounds *yìdiǎr*; {玩儿|wánr} *wár*; {一块儿|yí kuàir} (together) *yíkuàr*; {小孩儿|xiǎo háir} (child) *xiǎohár* |
| -ng | the -ng is dropped and the vowel goes nasal, then *r* | {空儿|kòngr} free time |
| i or ü (also in, ün) | the vowel becomes a glide, then an *er* sound | {劲儿|jìnr} energy, sounds *jièr* |
| the buzzed -i of zhi, chi, shi… | replaced by an *er* sound | {事儿|shìr} matter, thing |

Because -n and -i disappear, some erhua words rhyme that look different in writing: *bànr* and
*gàir* end the same way. Spelling keeps the original syllable (*diǎnr*, not ~~*diǎr*~~), so you
can still find the word in a dictionary.

### Where you'll hear it

Erhua is common in Beijing and in much of northern China, where it's part of everyday speech and
can make a word sound small, familiar or casual. In the south many speakers use it much less, and
in Taiwan and Singapore it's very rare: there, {哪里|nǎ lǐ} is the usual "where", {这里|zhè lǐ} and
{那里|nà lǐ} "here" and "there", and {面条|miàn tiáo} plain "noodles". Both forms are standard
Mandarin; this course teaches the common erhua words of the HSK lists and mentions the plain forms
beside them.

Occasionally erhua makes a different word: {头|tóu} is a head, but {头儿|tóur} is a boss or
leader. You'll learn those as separate words.

Typing erhua in this app: put the tone number before or after the *r*. `na3r` and `nar3` both
give *nǎr*; `yi4dian3r` gives *yìdiǎnr*.

## The syllable table

Put every initial together with every final, and keep the combinations that exist: that's the
syllable table, in the reference sheet "The syllable table". It has about 400 syllables without
tones. With tones, about 1,300 are in use, because not every syllable has words in all four tones.

That's a small number. English has thousands of different syllables; Mandarin makes do with a few
hundred, and thousands of characters share them. {是|shì}, {事|shì} (matter), {试|shì} (to try)
and {室|shì} (room) are all *shì*. This is one reason most Mandarin words have two syllables, and
why tones matter: each tone multiplies the stock of distinct syllables.

### Why some combinations don't exist

The gaps in the table aren't random. Five rules cover nearly all of them:

1. j, q and x go only with i and ü (written u): *jī*, *qù*, *xuǎn*. No *ja*, *jo* or *jong*.
2. g, k, h and the seven tongue-curled and tongue-front initials (zh ch sh r, z c s) never go with
   i or ü. So there's no *gi* or *shü*; the *i* in *zhi* and *si* is the buzzed vowel, not *ee*.
3. ü goes only after n, l, j, q, x and y. There's no *bü*, *dü* or *gü*.
4. b, p, m and f don't take *u* + another vowel (no *bua*, *muo*) or *ong*; f takes very few
   finals at all.
5. *ong* always has an initial; *er* never does.

So when you meet a spelling, you can often tell straight away whether it's possible. *Jü* can't
be right (after j the dots go); *zhiang* can't exist (zh doesn't go with i-finals); *fong* doesn't
exist (it's *feng*).

### Using the table

- To check a spelling: find the initial's row and look for the syllable.
- To learn a sound you find hard: practise its whole row or column (*ji qi xi*, *zhi chi shi ri*,
  *zi ci si*) with the tone questions in each lesson's quiz.
- To learn words: when two words share a syllable, the tone and the other syllable of the word
  tell them apart. Learn words, not single syllables.

The reference sheet also marks the syllables for which no character in HSK 1–3 has only that
reading. A computer voice can't be trusted to say those syllables alone with a given tone,
so this course practises them inside words.

## Review: the confusions to watch

| Easily confused | The difference | Pair to practise |
|---|---|---|
| n and l | n through the nose, l with air round the tongue | {女|nǚ} female, {绿|lǜ} green |
| -n and -ng | tongue tip up, or back of the tongue up | {新|xīn} new, {星|xīng} star |
| b, d, g and p, t, k | without and with a puff of air | {爸|bà} dad, {怕|pà} to be afraid |
| zh ch sh and z c s | tongue tip curled back, or flat behind the teeth | {是|shì} to be, {四|sì} four |
| j q x and zh ch sh | tongue flat and forward, or curled back | {鸡|jī} chicken, {知|zhī} to know; {七|qī} seven, {吃|chī} to eat; {西|xī} west, {师|shī} (in {老师|lǎo shī}) |
| u and ü after n, l | lips rounded on *oo*, or on *ee* | {路|lù} road, {绿|lǜ} green |
| ju qu xu yu | always ü, though written u | {去|qù} to go, {鱼|yú} fish |
| -ui, -iu | said *uei*, *iou* | {贵|guì} expensive, {六|liù} six |
| ian | *yen*, not *yahn* | {天|tiān} sky, {钱|qián} money |
| the e of *hē* | a back vowel, never English *e* | {饿|è} hungry, {喝|hē} to drink |
| 2nd and 3rd tones | rising from the middle, or staying low | {麻|má} hemp, {马|mǎ} horse |
| 3+3 | said 2+3, never written | {你好|nǐ hǎo} said *ní hǎo* |

## Say it

```speak
{哪儿|nǎr}
= where?
{这儿|zhèr}
= here
{一点儿|yì diǎnr}
= a little
{好玩儿|hǎo wánr}
= fun
{一会儿|yí huìr}
= a moment
{空儿|kòngr}
= free time
{女|nǚ}，{绿|lǜ}
= female; green (n, l)
{是|shì}，{四|sì}
= to be; four (sh, s)
{七|qī}，{吃|chī}
= seven; to eat (q, ch)
```

## Common mistakes

- Saying 儿 as a separate syllable in erhua words: {哪儿|nǎr} is one syllable, not *nǎ ér*.
- Keeping the -n in {一点儿|yì diǎnr}: it's said *yìdiǎr*, though written *diǎnr*.
- Writing the sound instead of the spelling: write *diǎnr*, *wánr*, not *diǎr*, *wár*.
- Thinking the plain forms are wrong: {哪里|nǎ lǐ} and {这里|zhè lǐ} are just as standard as
  {哪儿|nǎr} and {这儿|zhèr}.
- Inventing syllables: *jü*, *gi*, *fong*, *zhiang* don't exist. Check the table.

## Key points

- Erhua adds an *r* sound to the end of a syllable: pinyin *-r*, characters 儿. One syllable for two
  characters: {哪儿|nǎr}.
- A final -n or -i is dropped before the *r*, and -ng leaves a nasal vowel; the spelling stays
  *diǎnr*.
- Erhua is typical of Beijing and the north, rare in Taiwan and Singapore; the plain forms
  ({哪里|nǎ lǐ}, {这里|zhè lǐ}) are standard too.
- Mandarin has about 400 syllables (about 1,300 with tones). The gaps follow a few rules: j q x
  only with i and ü; ü only after n l j q x y; no i or ü after g k h, zh ch sh r, z c s.
- Review the common confusions until each pair sounds different to you.

lessons.title: Strokes and stroke order: 一 二 三 十 人 大
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

For twelve lessons you've worked on sound: initials, finals, tones, spelling rules and the
syllable table. You've seen characters all along, always with pinyin over them. Now you start
writing them. This module teaches 21 characters and 25 first words: numbers, greetings and the
words for "I", "you" and "China". By the end of lesson 15 you can greet someone, thank them,
apologise, say goodbye and count to ninety-nine, and write every character you use.

This lesson is about how characters are built and written. You'll learn what a character is made
of, the basic strokes and their Chinese names, the rules for which stroke comes first, and six
characters that are also six words: {一|yī} (one), {二|èr} (two), {三|sān} (three), {十|shí} (ten),
{人|rén} (person) and {大|dà} (big). They are some of the simplest characters there are, and good
ones to learn the rules on.

## What a character is

A **[[character]]** ({汉字|hàn zì}, "Han character", hanzi) is the unit of Chinese writing. As lesson
01 showed, each character is one syllable, and most have a meaning of their own; words are one
character or more. Three facts about characters matter for writing them:

- *Every character fills the same square.* {一|yī} has one line and {我|wǒ} (I) has seven, but in
  print and in neat handwriting both take up the same space. A simple character is written
  bigger and bolder, a busy one smaller and tighter. Text is a row of equal squares.
- *A character is made of strokes.* A **[[stroke]]** is one movement of the pen, from the moment it
  touches the paper until it lifts. A stroke can be straight, can curve, and can even turn a
  corner, but it's never two pen movements. Strokes are what you count: {十|shí} has two strokes,
  {大|dà} three.
- *Strokes form parts, and parts form characters.* Many characters are built from smaller
  pieces, and those pieces are often characters themselves. A part of a character is called a
  **[[component]]**. {你|nǐ} (you, lesson 15) has two: 亻 on the left, a narrow form of {人|rén}
  (person), and {={尔|ěr}=} on the right. One component of each character is its **[[radical]]**, the part a
  dictionary files the character under; 亻 is the radical of {你|nǐ}. You'll meet radicals
  properly in Chinese HSK 1. For now it's enough to know that the same pieces come back again
  and again, so every character you learn makes the next ones easier.

Where do characters come from? A few began as pictures: {人|rén} was drawn as a person, {日|rì} as
the sun and {月|yuè} as the moon (you'll write those two in lesson 14). A few are signs: {一|yī},
{二|èr}, {三|sān} are one, two and three lines. Most characters, though, combine a part that hints at
the meaning with a part that hints at the sound. So characters aren't a picture language: think of
them as a writing system with a huge but well-organised set of building blocks.

### Simplified and traditional

In the 1950s and 1960s mainland China adopted **[[simplified characters]]**, with fewer strokes for many
common characters. Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau kept the older **[[traditional characters]]**. This
course is written in simplified characters, the standard in mainland China, and the
Traditional switch shows every text in traditional characters instead: {={中国|Zhōng guó}=} (China)
becomes {+{中国|Zhōng guó}+}. Many characters are the same in both. All 21 characters of this module are, so you
write them the same way whichever script you read. The honors lesson "Simplified and traditional
characters" tells the story.

## The basic strokes

Every character is built from a small set of strokes. Chinese schools give each one a name, and
the names are worth learning: teachers, dictionaries and stroke-order videos use them all the time.

| Stroke | Name | How it goes | You see it in |
|---|---|---|---|
| horizontal | {横|héng} | left to right, level or rising very slightly | {一|yī}, {二|èr}, {三|sān}, {十|shí} |
| vertical | {竖|shù} | top to bottom, straight down | {十|shí}, {中|zhōng} |
| left-falling | {撇|piě} | from the top right, sweeping down to the left, thinning out | {人|rén}, {大|dà}, {八|bā} |
| right-falling | {捺|nà} | from the top left, down to the right, thickening and ending in a flat tip | {人|rén}, {大|dà}, {八|bā} |
| dot | {点|diǎn} | short, usually pressed down to the right | {六|liù}, {小|xiǎo} |
| rising | {提|tí} | short and quick, from the bottom left up to the right | {我|wǒ}, {好|hǎo} |
| turning | {折|zhé} | changes direction at a corner without lifting the pen | {口|kǒu}, {日|rì}, {五|wǔ} |
| hook | {钩|gōu} | a small flick at the end of another stroke | {小|xiǎo}, {你|nǐ}, {我|wǒ} |

Strokes combine, and their names combine too. {口|kǒu} (mouth, lesson 15) has a {横折|héng zhé},
"horizontal-turning": across the top and down the right side in one movement. {小|xiǎo} starts
with a {竖钩|shù gōu}, a vertical with a hook at the bottom. However many corners and hooks it has,
a combined stroke is *one* stroke when you count.

The official school standard in mainland China sorts strokes into five basic kinds, {横|héng},
{竖|shù}, {撇|piě}, {点|diǎn} and {折|zhé}, counting the rising stroke as a kind of horizontal and
the right-falling stroke as a kind of dot, with hooks as endings of other strokes. You'll see both
the five and the eight in books. The eight in the table are easier to tell apart when you're
starting.

### Which way each stroke goes

Direction matters as much as shape. Horizontals go left to right, verticals top to bottom, a
left-falling stroke from the top right down to the left, a right-falling one from the top left
down to the right, a rising stroke from the bottom left upwards. No stroke is ever written
backwards: there are no right-to-left horizontals and no bottom-to-top verticals. The tracing
pads check direction, and a backwards stroke is erased with a hint.

## Stroke order

Characters are written in a fixed order of strokes, the **[[stroke order]]**. It isn't a school
superstition. Writing in the standard order makes characters come out balanced, makes fast
handwriting readable to others, helps you remember the shapes, and makes handwriting input on a
phone work (it recognises characters better when they're written the usual way). A handful of
rules decide the order for nearly every character:

1. *Top before bottom.* {三|sān}: the top horizontal, then the middle, then the bottom.
2. *Left before right.* {八|bā} (eight): the left stroke, then the right. {你|nǐ}: the whole of 亻,
   then the right side.
3. *Horizontal before vertical when they cross.* {十|shí}: the horizontal first, then the vertical
   down through it.
4. *Left-falling before right-falling.* {人|rén}: {撇|piě}, then {捺|nà}. The same in {八|bā} and
   at the bottom of {大|dà}.
5. *Outside before inside.* {月|yuè} (moon): the outer frame, then the two short strokes inside.
6. *Close the box last.* In a box such as {日|rì} (sun) or {四|sì} (four), write the left side, the
   top and right side, then what's inside, and only then the bottom stroke that closes it. {口|kǒu}
   has nothing inside: left side, top and right, bottom.
7. *Centre before the sides* when a character is symmetric. {小|xiǎo} (small): the middle hook
   first, then the short left-falling stroke on the left, then the dot on the right.
8. *A stroke that cuts through everything comes last.* In {中|zhōng} (middle) you write the box
   first and the long vertical through it at the very end.

There are exceptions, and they're worth knowing early so they don't surprise you:

- {火|huǒ} (fire) is symmetric too, but here the two short side strokes come first, then the long
  {撇|piě} and the {捺|nà}.
- A dot at the top right is often the last stroke: {我|wǒ} (lesson 15) ends with it.
- The "walking" component 辶 sits below and to the left, like a frame, but it's written last:
  {={这|zhè}=} (this, Chinese HSK 1) is 文 first, then 辶.
- Look-alikes can have opposite orders: {九|jiǔ} (nine, lesson 14) begins with its {撇|piě}, while
  {力|lì} (strength), which looks similar, begins with the turning stroke and ends with the {撇|piě}.

The pads in this course follow the mainland order. When in doubt, press "Show me" on the pad
and watch the stroke.

## The practice grid

Chinese children practise in squares divided by a dashed cross, the {田字格|tián zì gé}, "the grid
shaped like {田|tián}" ({田|tián} is a field). A second kind, the {米字格|mǐ zì gé}, adds the two diagonals, like
the character {米|mǐ} (rice). The dashed lines aren't part of the character: they help you place it. Keep
the character in the middle of its square and use the cross to check balance. The vertical of
{十|shí} should run close to the dashed vertical, the bottom horizontal of {三|sān} should be the
widest thing in the square, and {人|rén} should stand with both feet near the bottom edge.

The tracing pads look the same: a square with a dashed cross. Squared paper, or any paper with
squares of about 2 cm drawn on it, works for writing from memory.

## Characters

{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Strokes | Order |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 一 ✎ | one | yī | 1 | one {横|héng} |
| 二 ✎ | two | èr | 2 | short {横|héng}, then a longer one |
| 三 ✎ | three | sān | 3 | three {横|héng}, top to bottom; the middle one is shortest, the bottom one longest |
| 十 ✎ | ten | shí | 2 | {横|héng}, then {竖|shù} |
| 人 ✎ | person | rén | 2 | {撇|piě}, then {捺|nà} |
| 大 ✎ | big | dà | 3 | {横|héng}, {撇|piě}, {捺|nà} |

All six are the same in traditional characters, and all six are on the list of characters to know
by hand (✎).

- 一, 二, 三 were tally lines: one, two and three strokes for one, two and three. Lengths matter: in
  二 the bottom line is clearly longer; in 三 the middle one is the shortest and the bottom one
  the longest, so the character sits on a wide base.
- 十 is a horizontal crossed by a vertical. Where they cross is a little above the middle.
- 人 is a person, drawn in ancient times standing and seen from the side. The {撇|piě} is the long left leg,
  from the top down to the left. The {捺|nà} starts a little way down the {撇|piě}, not at its top,
  and falls to the right.
- 大 began as a picture of a person standing with arms stretched out wide: "this big". The
  {横|héng} is the arms. The {撇|piě} starts above the arms and sweeps through them; the {捺|nà}
  starts where they cross. So 大 is 人 with a {横|héng} through it, but the {横|héng} is written
  first.

Look-alikes: 人 (person) has two strokes that meet at the top, with the longer one on the left; in
八 ({八|bā}, eight, lesson 14) the two strokes don't touch; in 入 ({入|rù}, to enter) the longer one
is on the right. 大 has a horizontal through 人; 太 ({太|tài}, too, very) is 大 with a dot at the bottom.

```trace
一二三十人大
```

Write it: all six are characters to know by hand. After tracing, write each one three times on
paper or on the pad, from memory, then check the order against the pad with "Show me".
=}

## The six characters as words

Each of these characters is also a word on its own:

| Word | Meaning | Tone | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| {一|yī} | one | 1st | {一|yī}、{二|èr}、{三|sān} one, two, three |
| {二|èr} | two | 4th | {十二|shí èr} twelve (lesson 14) |
| {三|sān} | three | 1st | {三十|sān shí} thirty |
| {十|shí} | ten | 2nd | {十三|shí sān} thirteen |
| {人|rén} | person, people | 2nd | {中国|Zhōng guó}{人|rén} a Chinese person (lesson 15) |
| {大|dà} | big | 4th | {大人|dà ren} an adult, a grown-up |

When you count, {一|yī} keeps its first tone: *yī, èr, sān*. In lesson 11 you saw that {一|yī}
changes its tone in front of other words; in counting and in the numbers up to 99 it doesn't, so
lesson 14 writes it *yī* throughout.

{大人|dà ren}, literally "big person", is how Chinese says "adult": words built from characters
often explain themselves like this. In this word {人|rén} loses its tone and is said short and light
(the neutral tone of lesson 02): *dà ren*. One sentence to finish, with words you'll learn in lesson 15:

{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{大人|dà ren}。 — I'm an adult.

### Pronunciation

- {一|yī}: just the vowel *i* as in *machine*, high and level. The *y* is only spelling (lesson 07).
- {二|èr}: a vowel with the tongue curled back, the one syllable *er*. Start like the *u* of
  English *duh* and curl the tongue tip up as you fall. It's a full syllable, not an erhua *-r*
  added to something else.
- {三|sān}: *s* plus *an*. Keep the *a* open, as in *father*, and the *n* short; not English *sun*.
- {十|shí}: *sh* with the tongue curled back, and the buzzing *-i* of *zhi chi shi ri* (lesson 06),
  not *she*. It rises: the second tone.
- {人|rén}: Mandarin *r* (lesson 06), then *en* with the *e* of *duh*. Rising.
- {大|dà}: unaspirated *d* (no puff of air), open *a*, falling sharply.
- {十|shí} and {四|sì} (four, lesson 14) are a famous pair: *shí* is retroflex and rising, *sì* has
  the tongue at the teeth and falls.

## Say it

```speak
{一|yī}、{二|èr}、{三|sān}
= one, two, three
{十|shí}
= ten
{人|rén}
= person
{大|dà}
= big
{大人|dà ren}
= adult
{十三|shí sān}
= thirteen
```

## Common mistakes

- Writing {十|shí} vertical first. Horizontal first, then the vertical down through it.
- Writing 人 or 八 right stroke first. The left-falling stroke always comes before the
  right-falling one.
- Starting the {捺|nà} of 人 at the very top, so the character looks like an upside-down V. It
  starts partway down the {撇|piě}.
- Writing 大 as 人 plus a horizontal. The horizontal is the first stroke.
- Making the three lines of 三 the same length. Short, shorter, longest.
- Writing a stroke backwards, for example a horizontal from right to left. It looks the same on
  paper, but it isn't the same stroke, and fast handwriting gives it away.
- Counting a turning stroke as two. {口|kǒu} is three strokes, not four: the top and the right side
  are one {横折|héng zhé}.

## Key points

- A character fills one square and is made of strokes; strokes form components, and one
  component of each character is its radical.
- Eight basic strokes: {横|héng}, {竖|shù}, {撇|piě}, {捺|nà}, {点|diǎn}, {提|tí}, {折|zhé},
  {钩|gōu}. Each has one direction, and no stroke goes backwards.
- Stroke order: top before bottom, left before right, horizontal before vertical, left-falling
  before right-falling, outside before inside, close the box last, centre before the sides, and a
  stroke through everything last. Exceptions: 火, a top-right dot, 辶.
- 一 二 三 十 人 大: 1, 2, 3, 2, 2 and 3 strokes, the same in traditional characters.
- Counting: {一|yī}, {二|èr}, {三|sān} … {十|shí}, with {一|yī} always in the first tone.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Numbers from one to ninety-nine: 四 五 六 七 八 九, 日 and 月
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 13 gave you {一|yī}, {二|èr}, {三|sān} and {十|shí}. This lesson fills in the rest of the
digits, {四|sì} to {九|jiǔ}, and shows how Chinese builds every number up to ninety-nine from them
with no new words at all. You'll also learn the hand signs Chinese speakers use for numbers, and two
characters that began as pictures: {日|rì}, the sun, and {月|yuè}, the moon. They'll give you the
days and months of the calendar in Chinese HSK 1.

## One to ten

| | Character | Pinyin | Tone |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | {一|yī} | yī | 1st |
| 2 | {二|èr} | èr | 4th |
| 3 | {三|sān} | sān | 1st |
| 4 | {四|sì} | sì | 4th |
| 5 | {五|wǔ} | wǔ | 3rd |
| 6 | {六|liù} | liù | 4th |
| 7 | {七|qī} | qī | 1st |
| 8 | {八|bā} | bā | 1st |
| 9 | {九|jiǔ} | jiǔ | 3rd |
| 10 | {十|shí} | shí | 2nd |

Count them aloud until the tones come by themselves: *yī, èr, sān, sì, wǔ, liù, qī, bā, jiǔ, shí*.
The tone pattern is 1-4-1-4-3-4-1-1-3-2. Every tone is there, and the numbers are the best tone
drill you'll ever carry with you: phone numbers, prices and dates will exercise them every day.

Some sounds from module 1 to watch:

- {四|sì}: *s* with the tongue at the teeth and the buzzing *-i* of *zi ci si*, falling. Not *see*.
- {五|wǔ}: just *u*, low; the *w* is only spelling (lesson 07).
- {六|liù}: *liu* is short for *liou*, so a light *o* is heard before the *u*: something like *lyoh*,
  falling.
- {七|qī}: *q* is like the *ch* of *cheese*, with a puff of air, and the tongue flat behind the lower
  teeth. High and level.
- {九|jiǔ}: *j* is unaspirated, like a soft *j* of *jeep*; *iu* is *iou* again, and the tone is low.

{四|sì} and {十|shí} are the pair to practise: four is a flat-tongue *s* and falls; ten is a
curled-tongue *sh* and rises. A folk tongue twister starts with exactly this contrast:

{四|sì}{是|shì}{四|sì}，{十|shí}{是|shì}{十|shí}。 — Four is four, ten is ten.

## Eleven to ninety-nine

Chinese numbers say what they mean, tens first:

| Number | Chinese | Literally |
|---|---|---|
| 11 | {十一|shí yī} | ten-one |
| 12 | {十二|shí èr} | ten-two |
| 15 | {十五|shí wǔ} | ten-five |
| 19 | {十九|shí jiǔ} | ten-nine |
| 20 | {二十|èr shí} | two-ten |
| 21 | {二十一|èr shí yī} | two-ten-one |
| 30 | {三十|sān shí} | three-ten |
| 48 | {四十八|sì shí bā} | four-ten-eight |
| 50 | {五十|wǔ shí} | five-ten |
| 67 | {六十七|liù shí qī} | six-ten-seven |
| 99 | {九十九|jiǔ shí jiǔ} | nine-ten-nine |

Three rules cover everything up to 99:

1. *The teens are 十 + a digit.* 11 is {十一|shí yī}, 17 is {十七|shí qī}. Ten on its own and at
   the start of the teens is just {十|shí}, never "one ten".
2. *The tens are a digit + 十.* 20 is {二十|èr shí}, 70 is {七十|qī shí}. A digit before 十
   multiplies; a digit after it adds. That's why {十四|shí sì} is 14 and {四十|sì shí} is 40.
3. *Everything else is tens + ones.* 35 is {三十五|sān shí wǔ}, 82 is {八十二|bā shí èr}.

In the middle of a number, as in {二十三|èr shí sān}, the {十|shí} is often said quickly and lightly,
but it's always written shí.

### 一 in numbers

Lesson 11 showed that {一|yī} changes its tone before other syllables. In the numbers of this lesson it doesn't: it
stays *yī* in {十一|shí yī}, {二十一|èr shí yī} and {九十一|jiǔ shí yī}, and in dates such as {一月|yī yuè}
(January). This app writes it *yī* there, as you hear it.

### 二 and 两

Chinese has two words for "two". {二|èr} is the number: for counting, in {十二|shí èr} and {二十|èr shí},
and for the digit. When you count *things*, you use {两|liǎng} with a measure word:
{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{人|rén}, two people. You'll learn {两|liǎng} and measure words in Chinese HSK 1; for
now, know that "two people" isn't ~~{二|èr}{个|gè}{人|rén}~~.

### Writing numbers

Chinese text often uses the digits 0–9, especially for prices, times and phone numbers: 21, 99.
Characters are usual in words and in writing out a number in full. Both are read the same way:
21 is read {二十一|èr shí yī}. In pinyin a whole number is written as one word, *èrshíyī*,
*jiǔshíjiǔ*.

## Counting on one hand

Chinese speakers can show every number from one to ten on one hand. One to five are much as in
English, but six to ten have their own signs, and you'll see them when people bargain, order or
say their age across a noisy room. The signs most common in mainland China, especially in the
north:

| Number | Sign |
|---|---|
| 1–5 | index finger; index and middle; three fingers; four fingers, thumb folded in; the open hand |
| 6 | thumb and little finger out, the other fingers folded (like the "hang loose" sign) |
| 7 | the tips of the thumb, index and middle fingers pinched together |
| 8 | thumb and index finger out, in an L |
| 9 | the index finger hooked |
| 10 | a fist, or the middle finger crossed over the index finger, like 十 |

Signs vary by region: in parts of the south, 7 and 8 are made differently, and Taiwan has its own
sign for 9. If a sign confuses you, say the number aloud and check.

## Characters

{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Strokes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 四 ✎ | four | sì | 5 |
| 五 ✎ | five | wǔ | 4 |
| 六 ✎ | six | liù | 4 |
| 七 ✎ | seven | qī | 2 |
| 八 ✎ | eight | bā | 2 |
| 九 ✎ | nine | jiǔ | 2 |
| 日 ✎ | sun; day | rì | 4 |
| 月 ✎ | moon; month | yuè | 4 |

All eight are the same in traditional characters, and all eight are characters to know by hand.

### Stroke order

- 四: a box with something inside, so "close the box last": the left vertical; the top and right
  side in one turning stroke; inside, a short left-falling stroke, then a vertical that bends to
  the right; and last the bottom horizontal. Five strokes.
- 五: the top horizontal; a vertical going down a little to the left; a horizontal that turns down
  (one stroke, like the top and right of a box); and the long bottom horizontal. Four strokes.
- 六: a dot on top, then the horizontal, then a short left-falling stroke and a dot below it, left
  before right.
- 七: the horizontal first, rising slightly; then one stroke that goes down through it, bends right
  along the bottom and ends in a hook upwards. Two strokes.
- 八: the left-falling stroke, then the right-falling one. They don't touch.
- 九: the left-falling stroke first, then one long stroke for the rest: across, down and out to the
  right with a hook. Two strokes. (In {力|lì}, strength, the turning stroke comes first: compare
  lesson 13.)
- 日: like 口 with a stroke inside: the left vertical, the top and right side, the middle
  horizontal, then the bottom horizontal that closes the box.
- 月: outside before inside: first a vertical that sweeps to the left at the bottom, then the top
  and right side ending in a hook, then the two short horizontals inside. The bottom stays open.

### Where they come from

{日|rì} and {月|yuè} are among the oldest characters, and both began as pictures. The sun was drawn as
a circle with a dot or a line in it, which over the centuries became the squared 日.
The moon was a crescent, still visible in the curved left stroke of 月. As words, {日|rì} means
"day" and {月|yuè} "month" (and "moon" in a few words): {一月|yī yuè} is January, the first month.
You'll learn the calendar in Chinese HSK 1.

The digits are not pictures. {四|sì} was once written as four lines, like 一 二 三 with one more;
the shape used now was borrowed from another word. Learn the others as shapes: they're small, and
you'll write them thousands of times.

Look-alikes: 日 is taller than wide and has a stroke across the middle; 口 is square and empty. 月
is open at the bottom, with two short strokes inside; 日 is closed. 八 has two strokes that don't
touch; 人 has two that meet at the top.

```trace
四五六七八九
```

```trace
日月
```

Write it: all eight are characters to know by hand. Write each one three times from memory, then
write the numbers 11, 25, 48 and 99 in characters.
=}

## Dialogue: how many are we?

A class is getting on a bus. The teacher, {王老师|Wáng lǎo shī} (王老师, Teacher Wang: Chinese
addresses teachers by surname + {老师|lǎo shī}), counts the students; {李明|Lǐ Míng} (李明) is one
of them. New words: {个|gè} (a measure word for people), {也|yě} (also), {对|duì} (right).

```dialogue
# How many are we?
王老师: {二十六|èr shí liù}、{二十七|èr shí qī}、{二十八|èr shí bā}。{二十八|èr shí bā}{个|gè}{人|rén}。
= Twenty-six, twenty-seven, twenty-eight. Twenty-eight people.
李明: {王老师|Wáng lǎo shī}，{不|bú}{是|shì}{二十八|èr shí bā}，{是|shì}{二十九|èr shí jiǔ}。
= Teacher Wang, it isn't twenty-eight, it's twenty-nine.
王老师: {二十九|èr shí jiǔ}？
= Twenty-nine?
李明: {我|wǒ}{也|yě}{是|shì}{人|rén}！
= I'm a person too!
王老师: {对|duì}，{对|duì}！{二十九|èr shí jiǔ}{个|gè}{人|rén}。
= Right, right! Twenty-nine people.
```

Listen for {二十九|èr shí jiǔ} each time: the light middle *shi*, then the low *jiǔ*. And notice
{不|bú}{是|shì}: {不|bù} changes to *bú* before a fourth tone, as lesson 11 showed.

## Say it

```speak
{一|yī}、{二|èr}、{三|sān}、{四|sì}、{五|wǔ}
= one, two, three, four, five
{六|liù}、{七|qī}、{八|bā}、{九|jiǔ}、{十|shí}
= six, seven, eight, nine, ten
{十四|shí sì}，{四十|sì shí}
= fourteen, forty
{四|sì}{是|shì}{四|sì}，{十|shí}{是|shì}{十|shí}
= four is four, ten is ten
{九十九|jiǔ shí jiǔ}
= ninety-nine
{一月|yī yuè}
= January
```

## Common mistakes

- Mixing up {十四|shí sì} (14) and {四十|sì shí} (40), or {十二|shí èr} and {二十|èr shí}. A digit
  before 十 multiplies, after it adds.
- Saying "one ten" for 10 or the teens: 10 is {十|shí} and 15 is {十五|shí wǔ}.
- Saying {一|yī} with a changed tone inside numbers: {十一|shí yī}, not *shí yí*.
- Using {二|èr} to count things: "two people" is {两|liǎng}{个|gè}{人|rén}.
- Saying {四|sì} like English *see*, or {十|shí} like *she*: four buzzes at the teeth, ten is
  curled back.
- Writing the hooked stroke of 九 first. The left-falling stroke comes first.
- Writing the bottom of 四 or 日 before the inside. Close the box last.
- Closing 月 at the bottom. It's open, with two short strokes inside.

## Key points

- One to ten: *yī èr sān sì wǔ liù qī bā jiǔ shí* (tones 1-4-1-4-3-4-1-1-3-2).
- 11–19: 十 + digit; tens: digit + 十; then tens + ones: {九十九|jiǔ shí jiǔ}.
- {一|yī} keeps its first tone in numbers and dates.
- {二|èr} is the number; counting things takes {两|liǎng} (Chinese HSK 1).
- Characters 四 五 六 七 八 九 日 月 (5, 4, 4, 2, 2, 2, 4, 4 strokes); 日 sun, day and 月 moon,
  month began as pictures.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: First words and greetings: 你好, 谢谢, 再见
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can count to ninety-nine and write the numbers. This last lesson of the course gives you the
words you'll use first with any Chinese speaker: hello, thank you, sorry, goodbye, and "you're
welcome" and "that's all right" in reply. With {我|wǒ} (I), {你|nǐ} (you), {是|shì} (to be) and
{不|bù} (not) you'll make your first sentences: "I'm Li Ming", "I'm not Wang Fang". And you'll
write seven more characters, two of which, {你|nǐ} and {好|hǎo}, show you how characters are built
from components.

Thirteen words is a lot for one lesson, but you've heard most of them since lesson 01, and their
sounds are everything modules 1 and 2 taught: third-tone sandhi in {你好|nǐ hǎo}, the tone change of
{不|bù}, the neutral tone in {谢谢|xiè xie}.

## I and you: {我|wǒ}, {你|nǐ}

{我|wǒ} is "I" and "me"; {你|nǐ} is "you" when you speak to one person. Neither changes, whatever
its place in the sentence:

{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{李明|Lǐ Míng}。 — I'm Li Ming.
{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{王芳|Wáng Fāng}。 — You're Wang Fang.

{你|nǐ} is for friends, classmates, children and people your own age. To an older person, a
teacher or a customer, Chinese is more polite with {您|nín}, the respectful "you" (Chinese HSK 1
teaches it): {您好|nín hǎo} is a polite "hello".

## To be: {是|shì}, and not: {不|bù}

{是|shì} links two nouns: A {是|shì} B, "A is B". It's the same word for "am", "is" and "are", and
it never changes:

{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{中国|Zhōng guó}{人|rén}。 — I'm Chinese.
{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{李明|Lǐ Míng}{吗|ma}？ — Are you Li Ming? ({吗|ma} at the end makes a yes-or-no question.)

To say "not", put {不|bù} before the verb: {不|bú}{是|shì}, "am not, is not, aren't". The tone of
{不|bù} changes to *bú* before a fourth tone, as in lesson 11, and {是|shì} is a fourth tone:

{我|wǒ}{不|bú}{是|shì}{王芳|Wáng Fāng}。 — I'm not Wang Fang.

A short answer to a question with {是|shì} is {是|shì} or {不|bú}{是|shì}: Chinese has no single word
that does all the work of English "yes" and "no", and usually answers with the verb.

## Good, small: {好|hǎo}, {小|xiǎo}

{好|hǎo} is good, well, fine. {小|xiǎo} is small, little, young, the opposite of {大|dà} from
lesson 13. Chinese adjectives don't need {是|shì}: "I'm fine" is {我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}, with {很|hěn}
(very) as a light link that doesn't really mean "very" here (Chinese HSK 1 explains it).

{好|hǎo} on its own also means "OK, all right": {好|hǎo}！ {小|xiǎo} before a surname is a friendly
way to address a younger person or a close colleague: {小|xiǎo}{王|Wáng}, "young Wang".

## China: {中国|Zhōng guó}

{中国|Zhōng guó} is China, literally "the middle country" ({中|zhōng}, middle; {国|guó}, country).
Add {人|rén} for the people: {中国|Zhōng guó}{人|rén}, a Chinese person, Chinese people. In pinyin it's
written with a capital, *Zhōngguó*, like every name.

## Hello: {你好|nǐ hǎo}

{你好|nǐ hǎo} is "hello", literally "you good". Both syllables are third tones, so by the sandhi rule
of lesson 11 the first one rises: you say *ní hǎo*, though it's still written nǐ hǎo. The reply is
{你好|nǐ hǎo} too.

When you greet someone older or more senior, {您好|nín hǎo} is more polite. Notice that English
"how are you?" isn't the everyday greeting it seems: you'll find {你好吗|nǐ hǎo ma}？ ("are you
well?") in every textbook, but people use it far less than English speakers use "how are you", for
example with someone they haven't seen for a long time. Friends greet each other with {你好|nǐ hǎo},
with a name, or with a question about what the other person is doing.

## Thank you, sorry, goodbye

| Say | Meaning | Literally | Reply |
|---|---|---|---|
| {谢谢|xiè xie} | thank you, thanks | thank-thank | {不客气|bú kè qi} you're welcome |
| {对不起|duì bu qǐ} | sorry | "can't face (you)" | {没关系|méi guān xi} it doesn't matter, that's all right |
| {再见|zài jiàn} | goodbye | again-see | {再见|zài jiàn} |

- {谢谢|xiè xie}: the second *xie* is short and light, a neutral tone. To thank a particular person,
  add them: {谢谢|xiè xie}{你|nǐ}.
- {不客气|bú kè qi}: "don't be so polite". {不|bù} is *bú* here, before the fourth tone *kè*, and
  *qi* is neutral. You'll also hear {不|bú}{谢|xiè}, "no thanks needed".
- {对不起|duì bu qǐ}: an apology for something you did wrong, like stepping on someone's foot. The
  {不|bù} in the middle is light and toneless. For a lighter "sorry, excuse me", people often say
  {不好意思|bù hǎo yì si} (Chinese HSK 1).
- {没关系|méi guān xi}: "there's no connection", so "it doesn't matter, that's all right". *xi* is
  neutral.
- {再见|zài jiàn}: two falling tones. Many people also say *bye-bye*, borrowed from English and written
  {拜拜|bái bái} (also said *bāi bāi*).

## Dialogue: in the corridor

Two students meet on their first day. {王芳|Wáng Fāng} (王芳) drops a book; {李小明|Lǐ Xiǎo míng} (李小明)
picks it up. New words: {吗|ma} (makes a yes-or-no question), {很|hěn} (very; a light link before
adjectives), {也|yě} (also).

```dialogue
# In the corridor
李小明: {你好|nǐ hǎo}！
= Hello!
王芳: {你好|nǐ hǎo}！{谢谢|xiè xie}！
= Hello! Thank you!
李小明: {不客气|bú kè qi}。{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{中国|Zhōng guó}{人|rén}{吗|ma}？
= You're welcome. Are you Chinese?
王芳: {是|shì}。{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{王芳|Wáng Fāng}。{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{李明|Lǐ Míng}{吗|ma}？
= Yes. I'm Wang Fang. Are you Li Ming?
李小明: {不|bú}{是|shì}，{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{李小明|Lǐ Xiǎo míng}。
= No, I'm Li Xiaoming.
王芳: {对不起|duì bu qǐ}！
= Sorry!
李小明: {没关系|méi guān xi}。
= That's all right.
王芳: {再见|zài jiàn}！
= Goodbye!
李小明: {再见|zài jiàn}！
= Bye!
```

Notice how short the answers are: {是|shì} for "yes", {不|bú}{是|shì} for "no, I'm not". And the
name {李小明|Lǐ Xiǎo míng} has {小|xiǎo} in it: given names often use everyday characters.

## Characters

{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 中 ✎ | middle, centre | zhōng | 4 | {中国|Zhōng guó} |
| 小 ✎ | small | xiǎo | 3 | {小|xiǎo} |
| 口 ✎ | mouth | kǒu | 3 | ({门口|mén kǒu}, doorway, Chinese HSK 1) |
| 不 ✎ | not | bù | 4 | {不|bù}, {不客气|bú kè qi}, {对不起|duì bu qǐ} |
| 你 ✎ | you | nǐ | 7 | {你|nǐ}, {你好|nǐ hǎo} |
| 我 ✎ | I, me | wǒ | 7 | {我|wǒ} |
| 好 ✎ | good | hǎo | 6 | {好|hǎo}, {你好|nǐ hǎo} |

All seven are the same in traditional characters, and all seven are characters to know by hand.

### How they're built

- 口 was a picture of a mouth. It's one of the most common components: on the left of a character
  it's often about the mouth or speaking, as in {吗|ma} and {吃|chī} (to eat, Chinese HSK 1).
- 小 is three small strokes: an old way of writing "little" (some explain them as grains of sand).
- 中 is a box with a vertical line straight through its middle. As a memory aid: an arrow through
  the centre of a target.
- 你 is two components: 亻 on the left, the narrow form of {人|rén} (person) that it takes as a
  component, and 尔 on the right, an old word for "you" that also gives the sound. So you can
  read 你 as "the person you're talking to".
- 好 is 女 (woman) on the left and 子 (child) on the right. The usual explanation is that a woman
  with a child stood for "good", though scholars have proposed others. Both parts are
  characters of their own: {女|nǚ} (female) and {子|zǐ} (child), and you'll meet them as
  components often. 女 on the left is narrow, and its last stroke rises.
- 我 began as a picture of a weapon with a long handle and teeth, borrowed very early for its sound
  to write the word "I". Its look doesn't help you remember the meaning, so learn it by its
  strokes.

### Stroke order

- 中: 口 first (left side, top and right, bottom), then the long vertical through it, last: a stroke
  through everything comes last.
- 小: the middle vertical with its hook, then a short left-falling stroke on the left, then a dot on
  the right.
- 口: three strokes, not one loop and not four: the left side; the top and right side in one
  turning stroke; the bottom.
- 不: the horizontal, the left-falling stroke, the vertical, and last the dot on the right.
- 你: 亻 first (a left-falling stroke, then a vertical), then 尔: a left-falling stroke, a
  horizontal that ends in a hook, a vertical hook down the middle, and last two short strokes
  below it: a short left-falling stroke on the left, then a dot on the right.
- 我: seven strokes, a famous one to get wrong: a short left-falling stroke at the top, the
  horizontal, the vertical hook, the rising stroke at the bottom left, the long slanting hook, a
  left-falling stroke across it, and *last* the dot at the top right.
- 好: 女 first: a stroke that falls to the left and turns to the right, a long left-falling stroke,
  and a rising stroke. Then 子: a horizontal that turns down to the left, a vertical hook, and the
  horizontal across.

```trace
中小口不你我好
```

Write it: all seven are characters to know by hand. Write each one three times from memory. Then
write {你好|nǐ hǎo} and {我|wǒ}{不|bú}{是|shì}{中国|Zhōng guó}{人|rén} with the characters you
know (you can write every character in it except 是 and 国).

### The other characters in these words

The phrases of this lesson use twelve more characters. You don't need to write them yet: Chinese
HSK 1 teaches each one. Here they are with their traditional forms, which you'll see when the
Traditional switch is on:

| Character | Pinyin | In |
|---|---|---|
| 是 | shì | {是|shì} |
| 国 (traditional 國) | guó | {中国|Zhōng guó} |
| 谢 (traditional 謝) | xiè | {谢谢|xiè xie} |
| 客 | kè | {不客气|bú kè qi} |
| 气 (traditional 氣) | qì | {不客气|bú kè qi} |
| 对 (traditional 對) | duì | {对不起|duì bu qǐ} |
| 起 | qǐ | {对不起|duì bu qǐ} |
| 没 (traditional 沒) | méi | {没关系|méi guān xi} |
| 关 (traditional 關) | guān | {没关系|méi guān xi} |
| 系 (traditional 係 in this word) | xì | {没关系|méi guān xi} |
| 再 | zài | {再见|zài jiàn} |
| 见 (traditional 見) | jiàn | {再见|zài jiàn} |
=}

## Say it

```speak
{你好|nǐ hǎo}！
= Hello!
{谢谢|xiè xie}！
= Thank you!
{不客气|bú kè qi}。
= You're welcome.
{对不起|duì bu qǐ}！
= Sorry!
{没关系|méi guān xi}。
= That's all right.
{再见|zài jiàn}！
= Goodbye!
{我|wǒ}{不|bú}{是|shì}{中国|Zhōng guó}{人|rén}。
= I'm not Chinese.
```

## Pronunciation

- {你好|nǐ hǎo}: said *ní hǎo*. The first syllable rises, the second dips low.
- {我|wǒ}: *w* + *o*, like the *wo* of *woe* without the English glide at the end, low.
- {是|shì}: curled-back *sh* and the buzzing *-i*, falling. Not *she*.
- {谢谢|xiè xie}: *x* is like *sh* in *she* with the tongue flat; *ie* is like *ye* in *yes*. Fall on the
  first, then a short light second syllable: not two equal beats.
- {中国|Zhōng guó}: *zh* curled back, unaspirated; *ong* as in German *Jung*, not English *long*.
  High, then rising.
- {再见|zài jiàn}: *z* is like *ds* in *beds*; *j* is a flat-tongue sound before *i*. Both fall.
- {对不起|duì bu qǐ}: *ui* is *uei* ("dway"); a light *bu*, then a low *qǐ* with a puff of air.
- {没关系|méi guān xi}: rising, high, then light: *méi guān xi*.

## Common mistakes

- Writing or saying ~~{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{好|hǎo}~~ for "I'm fine". Adjectives don't take {是|shì}:
  {我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}.
- Saying {不|bù}{是|shì} with a fourth-tone *bù*: before a fourth tone it's *bú*.
- Pronouncing {你好|nǐ hǎo} with two full dips. The first third tone rises.
- Using {你好吗|nǐ hǎo ma} as an everyday "hi". Say {你好|nǐ hǎo}.
- Answering {谢谢|xiè xie} with {没关系|méi guān xi}, or {对不起|duì bu qǐ} with {不客气|bú kè qi}. Thanks
  get {不客气|bú kè qi}; apologies get {没关系|méi guān xi}.
- Saying {谢谢|xiè xie} as two equal fourth tones. The second one is light.
- Writing the dot of 我 early. It's the last stroke.
- Writing 口 as one loop or four strokes. It's three.

## Key points

- {我|wǒ} I, me; {你|nǐ} you (one person); {您|nín} is the polite "you" (Chinese HSK 1).
- A {是|shì} B: "A is B"; not: {不|bú}{是|shì} (bú before a fourth tone).
- {你好|nǐ hǎo} (said ní hǎo) hello; {谢谢|xiè xie} → {不客气|bú kè qi}; {对不起|duì bu qǐ} →
  {没关系|méi guān xi}; {再见|zài jiàn}.
- {好|hǎo} good, {小|xiǎo} small; adjectives don't take {是|shì}.
- Characters 中 小 口 不 你 我 好 (4, 3, 3, 4, 7, 7, 6 strokes); 你 = 亻 + {=尔=}, 好 = 女 + 子; the dot
  of 我 comes last.
- You now know the 21 characters and 25 words of this course. Chinese HSK 1 starts from them.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Where pinyin came from
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can now read and type pinyin. This honors lesson asks where it came from. Chinese characters
don't show how a word is said, so for four hundred years people have tried to write Mandarin
sounds with other symbols: Jesuit missionaries, British diplomats, Chinese linguists. You'll meet
the older spellings still seen in English (Peking, Tsingtao, Taipei), the phonetic symbols children
learn in Taiwan, and the story of Hanyu Pinyin itself. You'll also find out why English speakers
say *Tao* with a *t* although pinyin writes it *dào*.

Nothing here is needed for Chinese HSK 1. Read it for interest, and to make sense of the spellings
you'll meet in books, maps and names.

## Why Chinese needs a romanisation

A character tells a reader what a word means, but its shape usually doesn't say how to pronounce
it. A reader of Chinese simply knows that {人|rén} is *rén*. Anyone who doesn't know yet, a child
or a foreign learner, needs another way to write the sounds. A system for writing a language in
the Latin alphabet is a **[[romanisation]]** (US spelling: romanization). Pinyin is one. It is the
official one today, but it wasn't the first, and the older ones left their mark on English.

## The first romanisations: missionaries in the 1600s

The first people to write Mandarin in Latin letters were European Jesuit missionaries who lived in
China in the late Ming dynasty. Matteo Ricci, an Italian Jesuit, published a short work in Beijing in
1605 with Chinese texts annotated in Roman letters, so that Western readers could pronounce them.
In 1626 another Jesuit, Nicolas Trigault, published a guide to Chinese sounds for Western scholars,
the {西儒耳目资|Xī rú ěr mù zī} ("aid to the eyes and ears of Western scholars"), based largely on
the system Ricci and other Jesuits had worked out. These systems were written for Portuguese and
Italian readers, and they were never used much outside missionary circles.

## Wade–Giles: the English spellings

In the 19th century British diplomats and scholars needed a standard of their own. Thomas Wade, a
British diplomat and scholar, published a Mandarin textbook in 1867, and Herbert Giles used and
adjusted Wade's spelling in his large Chinese–English dictionary of 1892. Their system is called
**[[Wade–Giles]]**. For most of the 20th century it was how English-language books, newspapers and
maps wrote Chinese names, and it is still common in Taiwan's names and in older scholarship.

Wade–Giles looks strange to a pinyin reader because it writes **[[aspiration]]**, the puff of air you
met in lesson 03, with an apostrophe-like mark instead of a different letter. In pinyin *b* and *p*
are a pair, unaspirated and aspirated; in Wade–Giles they are *p* and *p'*. Tones are written as
small numbers after the syllable, and the syllables of a word are joined with hyphens.

| Wade–Giles | Pinyin | Example (Wade–Giles → pinyin) |
|---|---|---|
| p / p' | b / p | Pei-ching → Běijīng ({北京|Běi jīng}) |
| t / t' | d / t | tao → dào ({道|dào}, "the Way") · T'ai-pei → Táiběi ({台北|Tái běi}) |
| k / k' | g / k | Kao-hsiung → Gāoxióng ({高雄|Gāo xióng}) |
| ch / ch' | j or zh / q or ch | Ch'ing-tao → Qīngdǎo ({青岛|Qīng dǎo}) |
| ts / ts' | z / c | Mao Tse-tung → Máo Zédōng ({毛泽东|Máo Zé dōng}) |
| hs | x | Kao-hsiung → Gāoxióng |
| j | r | jen → rén ({人|rén}, person) |

The trouble came when the apostrophes were left out, as they usually were in newspapers and on
maps. Without them *t* and *t'* look the same, so English readers said every *t* with a puff of
air. That is why *Tao* (as in Taoism) and the title *Tao Te Ching* are said with an English *t* in
English, while in Mandarin the word is {道|dào}, with an unaspirated *d*. The city name Taipei
is T'ai-pei with the apostrophe dropped; in pinyin it's *Táiběi*.

### Peking and Tsingtao: the postal spellings

Some famous old spellings aren't Wade–Giles at all. Peking and Tsingtao are older conventional
spellings; strict Wade–Giles would be Pei-ching and Ch'ing-tao. When China's postal service fixed
its spellings of place names at a conference in 1906, the **[[postal romanisation]]**, it kept
spellings that were already in use, such as Peking. Some of these names live on in English: Peking University is the English name of
{北京大学|Běi jīng Dà xué}.

## Chinese systems: zhuyin

Chinese scholars also designed sound symbols of their own. In 1913 a national conference, the
Commission on the Unification of Pronunciation, drew up a set of phonetic symbols based on simple,
ancient forms of characters, and the Ministry of Education published them in 1918. They are
called {注音符号|zhù yīn fú hào} ("sound-marking symbols", renamed so in 1930), **[[zhuyin]]** for short, or
**[[bopomofo]]** after their first four symbols, ㄅ ㄆ ㄇ ㄈ (*b p m f*), the way "alphabet" comes from
alpha and beta.

Zhuyin isn't a romanisation: it doesn't use Latin letters. It has 37 symbols, one for each initial
and for each final or part of a final, plus tone marks:

| Word | Pinyin | Zhuyin |
|---|---|---|
| {妈|mā} | mā | ㄇㄚ |
| {你好|nǐ hǎo} | nǐ hǎo | ㄋㄧˇ ㄏㄠˇ |
| {中国|Zhōng guó} | Zhōngguó | ㄓㄨㄥ ㄍㄨㄛˊ |
| {学|xué} | xué | ㄒㄩㄝˊ |
| {是|shì} | shì | ㄕˋ |
| {妈妈|mā ma} | māma | ㄇㄚ ˙ㄇㄚ |

A few things to notice:

- The 2nd, 3rd and 4th tone marks (ˊ ˇ ˋ) are the same as in pinyin. The 1st tone is usually left
  unmarked, and the neutral tone is a dot written before the syllable (˙ㄇㄚ).
- Zhuyin writes *zhi, chi, shi, ri, zi, ci, si* with the initial alone: {是|shì} is just ㄕ plus
  its tone. That fits what lesson 06 taught: the "i" after these initials isn't the vowel of *xī*.
- ü has its own symbol, ㄩ, so there's no question of dropping dots after *j q x*.

Today zhuyin is the main way children in Taiwan learn to read: it is taught in primary school,
and children's books and textbooks print it beside each character, the way this course prints
pinyin over it. It is also used in dictionaries and is the most popular way of typing Chinese in
Taiwan (lesson 92). In mainland China it has been replaced by pinyin in schools; mainland
dictionaries such as the {现代汉语词典|Xiàn dài Hàn yǔ Cí diǎn} have long printed it only in second place, after the pinyin.

### Two romanisations of the 1920s and 30s

Chinese linguists also designed romanisations. **[[Gwoyeu Romatzyh]]** ("national language
romanisation"), adopted by the government of the Republic of China in 1928, had no tone marks or
numbers: it spelled each tone with different letters, so *tan, tarn, taan, tann* were the four
tones of one syllable. Another system, Latinxua Sin Wenz, followed in 1931. Neither replaced
characters or Wade–Giles, but pinyin later took ideas from both, and its tone marks from zhuyin.

## Hanyu Pinyin

After 1949 the government of the People's Republic of China set up a committee to design a new
romanisation. Among its members was Zhou Youguang (1906–2017), a linguist and economist often
called "the father of pinyin". After several years of work, **[[Hanyu Pinyin]]**
({汉语拼音|Hàn yǔ pīn yīn}, "spelled sounds of the Chinese language") was approved on 11 February
1958 by the National People's Congress.

Its designers made choices you've been living with all course:

- Only the 26 Latin letters, plus ü. No apostrophes for aspiration: *b/p, d/t, g/k* use the
  letters that most European languages use for similar pairs.
- Some letters were given values they don't have in English: *q* and *x* for the sounds
  Wade–Giles wrote *ch'* and *hs*, *c* for *ts'*.
- Tone marks over a vowel, the same marks as zhuyin's (ˉ ˊ ˇ ˋ), instead of numbers after the
  syllable.

Pinyin then spread beyond China. In 1979 the United States government and the American press changed
to pinyin spellings: Peking became Beijing and Mao Tse-tung became Mao Zedong.
In 1982 the International Organization for Standardization adopted pinyin as the international
standard for romanising Chinese, ISO 7098 (revised in 1991 and 2015). In 2009 Taiwan also made Hanyu
Pinyin its official romanisation, although many names there keep older spellings, such as Taipei
and Kaohsiung.

## What pinyin is used for today

Pinyin is everywhere in modern Chinese life, but always next to characters, never instead of them:

- Teaching. Children in mainland China learn pinyin early in primary school, alongside their first
  characters, and children's books print it over the characters. Learners abroad, like you, start
  with it.
- Dictionaries. Mainland dictionaries give each character's pinyin, and many order their entries
  alphabetically by it.
- Typing. Most people in mainland China type Chinese by typing pinyin (lesson 92).
- Signs and maps. Street signs, station names and maps often give the pinyin with the characters.
- Names. Mainland passports spell names in pinyin capitals, without tone marks. Since ü can't be
  typed on many systems, passports write it as YU: the surname {吕|Lǚ} is LYU, so it doesn't look
  like {陆|Lù}, LU.

```speak
{拼音|pīn yīn}
= pinyin: "spelled sounds"
{汉语拼音|Hàn yǔ pīn yīn}
= Hanyu Pinyin
{注音|zhù yīn}
= zhuyin: "marking the sound"
{北京|Běi jīng}
= Beijing (once written Peking)
{台北|Tái běi}
= Taipei (Wade–Giles T'ai-pei)
```

## Common mistakes

- Thinking Peking is "wrong". It's an older spelling, still used in some names. In Chinese the
  city is always {北京|Běi jīng}; only the way English writes it changed.
- Reading Wade–Giles spellings as pinyin. *Tao* in a Wade–Giles book is pinyin *dào*; *chi* in
  *tai chi* is *jí*; *hs* is *x*.
- Taking zhuyin for an old system nobody uses. It's how children in Taiwan learn to read, and how
  many people there type every day.
- Thinking pinyin replaced characters. It was designed to help with pronunciation, literacy and
  names; Chinese texts are written in characters.

## Key points

- A **[[romanisation]]** writes a language in Latin letters. Pinyin is the official one for Mandarin,
  but not the first: Jesuit missionaries romanised Chinese in the 1600s (Ricci 1605, Trigault 1626).
- **[[Wade–Giles]]** (Wade 1867, Giles 1892) was the usual English spelling for about a century. It
  writes aspiration with an apostrophe (*t'* = pinyin *t*, *t* = pinyin *d*) and tones with numbers,
  usually left out in names: Mao Tse-tung, T'ai-pei. Peking and Tsingtao are **[[postal romanisation]]** (1906).
- **[[Zhuyin]]** (**[[bopomofo]]**), drawn up in 1913 and published in 1918, uses 37 symbols of its own (ㄅ ㄆ ㄇ ㄈ…)
  and the same tone marks as pinyin. Children in Taiwan learn to read with it, and many people in
  Taiwan type with it.
- **[[Hanyu Pinyin]]** was approved on 11 February 1958, became ISO 7098 in 1982, and replaced Wade–Giles
  in most English writing from 1979. It is used for teaching, dictionaries, typing, signs and names
  in passports.

This lesson has no words to learn.

lessons.title: Typing Chinese
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In this app you type pinyin with tone numbers, and the app writes the tone marks: `ma3` becomes
*mǎ*. That is a learner's tool. People who write Chinese every day type characters, and most of
them do it by typing pinyin on an ordinary keyboard, without any tones at all. This lesson shows
how that works on a computer and on a phone, the other ways of typing Chinese (handwriting,
strokes, shapes and the zhuyin keyboards used in Taiwan), and how to add a Chinese keyboard to
your own devices.

Nothing new about pinyin is taught here, and you can read the lesson without changing any
settings. If you'd like to try along, add a Chinese keyboard first ("Setting it up" below).

## How a pinyin input method works

A keyboard has letters, not characters, so typing Chinese needs software between the keys and the
screen: an **[[input method]]** (or **[[IME]]**, input method editor). Windows, macOS, iOS and Android each
come with a pinyin input method. It works in three steps:

1. You type the pinyin of what you want, without tones: `mai`.
2. The input method shows the letters underlined and opens a list of characters with that
   spelling, the **[[candidates]]**, numbered 1, 2, 3…
3. You pick one. The space bar takes the first (or highlighted) candidate, and a number key takes
   that numbered one. In most input methods Enter types the letters as they are, which is how
   you type an English word without switching keyboards.

Here is what typing `mai` might show. The order depends on the input method and on what you have
typed before:

| You type | Candidates | Meanings |
|---|---|---|
| mai | 1 {买|mǎi} 2 {卖|mài} 3 {麦|mài} … | to buy, to sell, wheat |
| shi | 1 {是|shì} 2 {十|shí} 3 {事|shì} 4 {时|shí} … | to be, ten, matter, time |

Notice what is missing: the tones. A pinyin input method never asks for them, so {买|mǎi} (to buy)
and {卖|mài} (to sell) sit side by side in the same list, and you tell them apart by meaning. The
input method doesn't check your pronunciation; you check its characters. That is one reason to
learn characters as well as pinyin: you have to recognise the right one in the list.

## Words and sentences, not single characters

Typing one character at a time is slow, and it gives the input method nothing to go on. Type a
whole word, and the choice becomes easy: `xuesheng` gives {学生|xué sheng} (student) as the first
candidate, because no other common word is spelled that way. Type a short sentence,
`woshixuesheng`, and a good input method offers the whole of
{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng} at once. It splits the letters into syllables itself, picks the
likeliest words, and lets you fix any word it got wrong before you accept the sentence.

Input methods also learn. The words you choose move up the list, and **[[word prediction]]** suggests
the next word before you type it: after {你好|nǐ hǎo} you may be offered a common next word to tap.

Many input methods accept short cuts too. For common words you can often type only the first letter
of each syllable: `nh` for {你好|nǐ hǎo}, `py` for {拼音|pīn yīn}. Short cuts make the list longer,
so they work best for words you use a lot.

## ü, the apostrophe and the other spelling rules

Typing pinyin in an input method follows the spelling rules you learned in this course, with one
change for ü, which isn't on most keyboards:

- v for ü. Most pinyin input methods put ü on the v key, since pinyin has no v. Type `nv` for
  {女|nǚ} (woman) and `lv` for {绿|lǜ} (green). The app accepts v for ü too, so the habit works in
  both places.
- u after j, q, x and y. Type the u that pinyin writes: `qu` for {去|qù} (to go), `yu` for
  {鱼|yú} (fish). Only after n and l do you need v, because nu and lu are syllables of their own.
- The apostrophe. When a syllable could be split two ways, type an apostrophe where the break
  is, just as pinyin writes it. `xian` gives one-syllable words such as {先|xiān} (first) and
  {现|xiàn} (now); `xi'an` gives {西安|Xī'ān}, the city.
- Spelling counts, tones don't. A missing letter (`xuesheg`) gives the wrong candidates or
  none. Look at the underlined letters before you pick.

While Chinese input is on, the punctuation keys usually type Chinese punctuation too: the full
stop key gives 。 and the comma key gives ，.

## On a phone

Phones offer several ways to type Chinese, and many people switch between them:

- Pinyin on a full keyboard (QWERTY), as on a computer. Candidates appear in a bar above the keys.
- Pinyin on a phone keypad (often called 9-key): the letters share keys as on an old phone
  keypad (abc on one key, def on the next), and the input method works out which syllables you
  meant. The keys are bigger and easier to hit.
- Handwriting. You write a character with your finger on the screen, and the phone offers the
  characters it recognises. It's the way to type a character you can read but can't pronounce.
- Strokes. Five keys stand for the kinds of stroke: {横|héng}, {竖|shù}, {撇|piě}, {点|diǎn}
  (which also covers {捺|nà}) and one for the rest, mostly turning strokes. You tap a character's
  strokes in writing order, and the phone offers the characters that begin that way. Here stroke
  order (lesson 13) really matters: the wrong order gives the wrong candidates.
- Voice input. Speak, and the phone types the characters. The tones you learned matter here:
  clear tones give the right words.

## Shape-based input methods

Some input methods ignore pronunciation and build characters from their parts. **[[Wubi]]**
({五笔|wǔ bǐ}, "five strokes"), offered with simplified characters, types a character by its
components. **[[Cangjie]]**, offered with traditional characters, describes each character by its
shapes: in Microsoft's version, {夏|xià} (summer) is the keys M U H E. Shape-based methods take
time to learn, and they don't depend on how you pronounce a character. Most learners never need
them; it's enough to know they exist.

## Zhuyin keyboards in Taiwan

In Taiwan the most popular way to type Chinese is with zhuyin (lesson 91). A zhuyin input method
gives each key of the keyboard a zhuyin symbol as well as its letter, and it works like a pinyin one:
type the symbols for the sounds, then pick the character. One difference: zhuyin typing usually includes the tone,
because the tone marks ˊ ˇ ˋ have keys of their own. {夏天|xià tiān} (summer) is typed as the
symbols ㄒㄧㄚˋ ㄊㄧㄢ, the 4th-tone mark included. Phones in Taiwan offer zhuyin keyboards too.

## Typing in this app and typing with an input method

| | In this app (pinyin answers) | In a pinyin input method |
|---|---|---|
| You type | letters and tone numbers: `ni3hao3` | letters only: `nihao` |
| You get | pinyin with tone marks: *nǐhǎo* | characters: {你好|nǐ hǎo} |
| Tones | required and graded | never typed |
| ü | `v` or `u:` (`nv3`, `nu:3`) | v (`nv`) |
| What it checks | your pinyin and your tones | nothing: you choose the character |

The app can take both. When a question or a review card asks for pinyin, type plain letters and
digits. Switch back to your usual keyboard first, or put the input method in English mode (Shift
does it in Microsoft Pinyin). While Chinese input is on, the input method usually catches the
letters and offers characters, and a digit may pick a candidate instead of reaching the app. When an answer can be characters, as on English → Chinese review cards, you may type
the characters with your input method instead. Typing pinyin with tones trains your ear and memory
for tones; typing characters trains your eye. Both are worth doing.

## Setting it up

Menus change between versions, so if a name below doesn't match your screen, look for "Chinese"
in your language or keyboard settings.

- Windows 11. Settings › Time & language › Language & region › Add a language (next to
  Preferred languages), then choose Chinese (Simplified, China). Microsoft Pinyin comes with it.
  Switch keyboards with the Windows logo key + Space, or with the input language button on the
  taskbar. In Microsoft Pinyin, Shift switches between Chinese and English mode (英 means English).
- macOS. Apple menu › System Settings › Keyboard › Text Input › Edit, then the add button (+),
  Chinese, Simplified, and Pinyin – Simplified. Switch with the Input menu in the menu bar or
  Control-Space; the Globe (fn) key can be set to change input source too.
- iPhone and iPad. Settings › General › Keyboard › Keyboards › Add New Keyboard › Chinese,
  Simplified, then choose a layout: a pinyin keyboard (a full QWERTY one, or a phone keypad) and,
  if you like, Handwriting. Switch by touching and holding the Emoji or Switch Keyboard key.
- Android (Gboard). Settings › System › Keyboard › On-screen keyboard › Gboard › Languages, pick
  Chinese (Simplified), turn on a layout such as Pinyin or Handwriting, and tap Done. Phones from
  other makers may come with their own keyboard, with similar settings.

```speak
{键盘|jiàn pán}
= keyboard
{打字|dǎ zì}
= to type
{输入法|shū rù fǎ}
= input method
{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}。
= I'm a student. (type woshixuesheng)
```

## Common mistakes

- Expecting an input method to take tones. In most input methods a number picks a candidate, so
  `mai3` takes the third one in the list, which may not be {买|mǎi}. Type `mai` and pick the
  character.
- Taking the first candidate without looking. {买|mǎi} and {卖|mài} are spelled the same without
  tones and mean opposite things.
- Typing u for ü after n or l: `nu` gives characters read *nu* (such as {努|nǔ}), not {女|nǚ}.
  Use `nv`.
- Forgetting the apostrophe: `xian` is usually read as one syllable, so {西安|Xī'ān} may not be
  offered.
- Leaving Chinese input on when the app asks for pinyin. Switch to your usual keyboard (or English
  mode), then type `ni3hao3`.

## Key points

- An **[[input method]]** (**[[IME]]**) turns what you type into characters. With pinyin you type the
  syllables without tones and choose from numbered **[[candidates]]**: Space for the first, a number
  key for the others, Enter for the letters themselves.
- Type whole words and sentences: `xuesheng` → {学生|xué sheng}. Input methods learn your choices
  and offer **[[word prediction]]**; initials alone (`nh`) often work for common words.
- v for ü (`nv`, `lv`), u after j q x y, and an apostrophe to split syllables (`xi'an`).
- Phones add a phone-keypad pinyin layout, handwriting, stroke input (stroke order matters) and voice
  input. Shape-based methods (**[[Wubi]]**, **[[Cangjie]]**) build characters from their parts.
