- In Taiwan most people type with zhuyin, tones included.
- In this app, pinyin answers take tone numbers (`ni3hao3`): switch to your usual keyboard or the
  input method's English mode first. Answers in characters can be typed with your input method.

This lesson has no words to learn.

lessons.title: Simplified and traditional characters
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This course is written in **[[simplified characters]]**, and the Simplified/Traditional switch shows
it in **[[traditional characters]]**. This honors lesson explains the difference: when and how the
characters were simplified, why one simplified character can stand for two traditional ones, where
each script is used today, and what the switch in this app does. It describes the two scripts; it
doesn't rank them. Both write the same language, and both are read by many millions of people.

Most of this lesson compares the two scripts side by side, so its tables show both forms whichever
script you've chosen. Nothing here is needed for Chinese HSK 1.

## One language, two scripts

Simplified and traditional characters write the same Mandarin: the same words, the same grammar,
the same pronunciation and the same pinyin. What differs is the shape of some characters. Many
characters are the same in both scripts, including every character you learned to write in this
course: {=人 大 中 小 你 我 好=} look exactly the same in Taiwan or Hong Kong. Others look quite
different:

{=

| Simplified | Traditional | Pinyin | Meaning | Strokes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 学 | 學 | xué | to study | 8 / 16 |
| 书 | 書 | shū | book | 4 / 10 |
| 马 | 馬 | mǎ | horse | 3 / 10 |
| 门 | 門 | mén | door | 3 / 8 |
| 车 | 車 | chē | vehicle | 4 / 7 |
| 国 | 國 | guó | country | 8 / 11 |
| 说 | 說 | shuō | to speak | 9 / 14 |

=}

Someone who reads one script well can usually work out much of the other, because the changes
follow patterns (see "Components" below). Reading the other script fluently still takes practice.

## When: the simplification lists

Simplified forms weren't all invented in the 20th century: some had been used in handwriting, as
quick cursive or informal forms, for centuries. What was new was making them the standard for
print and school. That happened in mainland China in a series of official lists:

- 1956. The State Council approved the {汉字简化方案|Hàn zì Jiǎn huà Fāng àn} (Chinese
  Character Simplification Scheme) on 28 January 1956, and it was published on 31 January. It
  simplified 515 characters and 54 components.
- 1964. The General List of Simplified Characters gathered the simplified forms, more than 2,200
  characters, including those made by using a simplified component wherever it occurs.
- 1977–1986. A second round of simplifications was published in December 1977. It was
  poorly received and was officially withdrawn in 1986.
- 1986. The General List was published again, with a few small changes. It remained the
  standard for almost thirty years.
- 2013. The {通用规范汉字表|Tōng yòng Guī fàn Hàn zì Biǎo} (Table of General Standard Chinese
  Characters), issued by the State Council on 5 June 2013, replaced the earlier lists. It has 8,105 characters in
  three levels: 3,500 common characters, 3,000 less common ones and 1,605 for names and specialist
  terms.

Elsewhere, Singapore published its first list of simplified characters in 1969 and later took over
the mainland forms, and Malaysia adopted the same forms in 1981.

## How: the ways characters were simplified

{=

The new forms followed a handful of methods. Each row shows traditional → simplified.

| Method | Examples |
|---|---|
| A cursive (handwritten) shape made standard | 書 → 书 (book) |
| A simpler component, used everywhere it occurs | 言 → 讠: 說 → 说 (to speak), 語 → 语 (language); 金 → 钅: 錢 → 钱 (money); 食 → 饣: 飯 → 饭 (meal) |
| Only part of the character kept | 習 → 习 (to practise), 聲 → 声 (sound), 開 → 开 (to open) |
| A complicated part replaced by a simple sign | 又 in 漢 → 汉 (Chinese), 對 → 对 (right), 難 → 难 (hard), 雞 → 鸡 (chicken) |
| An old or simpler form brought back | 從 → 从 (from), 雲 → 云 (cloud), 眾 → 众 (crowd) |
| One character for several that sound alike | 發 and 髮 → 发; 乾 and 幹 → 干; 後 → 后 (and 后 itself); 麵 → 面 (and 面 itself) |

Simplified forms usually have fewer strokes, but not always: the mainland form 强 (strong) has 12, the
traditional 強 11.

=}

## Components: read one script through the other

Because a simplified component replaced the traditional one wherever it occurs, one pattern
unlocks many characters. Learn the pairs, and the other script becomes much easier to read:

{=

| Simplified component | Traditional | In |
|---|---|---|
| 讠 (speech) | 言 | 说 說 (to speak), 语 語 (language), 谢 謝 (to thank) |
| 钅 (metal) | 金 | 钱 錢 (money) |
| 饣 (food) | 食 | 饭 飯 (meal) |
| 门 (door) | 門 | 问 問 (to ask), 们 們 (plural ending) |
| 马 (horse) | 馬 | 妈 媽 (mum), 吗 嗎 (question word) |
| 贝 (shell; money) | 貝 | 贵 貴 (expensive) |

=}

You've seen some of these already: {={妈妈|mā ma}=} (mum) in lesson 01 and {={谢谢|xiè xie}=} (thank
you) in lesson 15. With the switch on Traditional, they show as 媽媽 and 謝謝: the same component
change each time.

## One simplified character, several traditional ones

The last method in the table, one character for several, matters most for anyone converting between
the scripts. Going from traditional to simplified is mostly mechanical: 發 and 髮 both become {=发=}.
Going the other way needs the word, because the right traditional character depends on the meaning:

{=

| Simplified word | Pinyin | Meaning | Traditional |
|---|---|---|---|
| 头发 | tóufa | hair | 頭髮 |
| 出发 | chūfā | to set off | 出發 |
| 干净 | gānjìng | clean | 乾淨 |
| 干活 | gànhuó | to work | 幹活 |
| 以后 | yǐhòu | after, later | 以後 |
| 皇后 | huánghòu | empress | 皇后 |
| 这里 | zhèlǐ | here | 這裡 |
| 公里 | gōnglǐ | kilometre | 公里 |

=}

This is why the app converts whole words, not single characters: it reads {={头发|tóu fa}=} as one
word and shows 頭髮, and {={出发|chū fā}=} as another and shows 出發. A lone character with several
traditional forms is checked by hand in this course, so the switch shows the right one.

## Where each script is used

- Simplified characters are the standard in mainland China, and are also used in Singapore and
  Malaysia.
- Traditional characters are used in Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau, and in many Chinese
  communities around the world.

In Chinese the two scripts are called {简体字|jiǎn tǐ zì} ("simplified-form characters") and
{繁体字|fán tǐ zì} ("complex-form characters"). In Taiwan the official name for the traditional
characters is {正体字|zhèng tǐ zì} ("standard-form characters").

### Taiwan and Hong Kong

Taiwan and Hong Kong each have their own standard for the shapes of characters: Taiwan's Ministry
of Education publishes the Standard Form of National Characters, and Hong Kong's Education Bureau a
List of Graphemes of Commonly-Used Chinese Characters. The two agree on most characters, but some
differ: "inside" is usually {=裡=} in Taiwan and {=裏=} in Hong Kong.

The places differ in some everyday words, too, not only in characters. A taxi is
{出租车|chū zū chē} in the mainland and usually {+{计程车|jì chéng chē}+} in Taiwan; a bicycle is
{自行车|zì xíng chē} in the mainland and often {+{脚踏车|jiǎo tà chē}+} in Taiwan. This course, like
the HSK exams, teaches mainland words.

## How the switch in this app works

The Simplified/Traditional switch changes the characters, and only the characters:

- It uses Taiwan character forms ({=这里=} becomes 這裡, with 裡) and keeps the mainland words: a
  taxi is still {={出租车|chū zū chē}=}, shown as 出租車.
- Both {=台=} and {=臺=} are written in Taiwan ({=台北=} and {=臺北=} are both seen); the app writes 台.
- Pinyin, meanings and the sound of every word stay the same.
- Words with a one-to-many character are converted as whole words (頭髮, 出發), as above.
- Tables like the ones in this lesson, which are about the forms themselves, stay as written.
- On review cards and typed answers, characters in either script count.
- Tracing pads show the script you've chosen. Try it: trace these three characters, then switch to
  Traditional and come back. The pads show 學, 書 and 門 instead, in the same mainland stroke order.

```trace
学书门
```

## Which script should you learn?

That depends on where you'll read and write Chinese. This course and the HSK courses after it are
written in simplified characters, the standard in mainland China and the script of the HSK exams.
If you'll mostly read Chinese from Taiwan or Hong Kong, the Traditional switch lets you study the
same lessons in traditional characters. Many learners start with one script and later learn to
read the other; the component pairs above make that much easier.

```speak
{汉字|hàn zì}
= Chinese characters
{简体字|jiǎn tǐ zì}
= simplified characters
{繁体字|fán tǐ zì}
= traditional characters
{头发|tóu fa}
= hair
{出发|chū fā}
= to set off
```

## Common mistakes

- Thinking simplified and traditional are two languages. They are two ways of writing the same
  language, with the same words and pronunciation. (Taiwan and the mainland differ in some words,
  but that isn't a matter of script.)
- Thinking every character changed. Many, including all 21 characters you can write, are the same.
- Converting character by character. {=发=} is 髮 in "hair" and 發 in "to set off"; only the word
  tells you which.
- Treating "traditional" as one fixed set. Taiwan and Hong Kong have their own standards, which
  differ in some characters ({=裡=} / {=裏=}).
- Thinking simplified forms were all invented in the 1950s. Many came from older handwriting.

## Key points

- **[[Simplified characters]]** became the standard in mainland China through official lists: 1956
  (515 characters and 54 components), 1964 (the General List), revised 1986; a second round of 1977
  was withdrawn in 1986. Since 2013 the Table of General Standard Chinese Characters (8,105
  characters) is the standard.
- Methods: cursive shapes, simpler components used everywhere ({=讠 for 言=}), part of a character
  kept, simple signs, older forms, and one character for several ({=发 for 發 and 髮=}).
- **[[Traditional characters]]** are used in Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau; simplified in mainland China,
  Singapore and Malaysia. Taiwan and Hong Kong differ in some forms ({=裡 / 裏=}).
- Converting simplified to traditional needs the word: {={头发|tóu fa}=} → 頭髮, {={出发|chū fā}=} → 出發.
- The app's switch shows Taiwan character forms with mainland words; pinyin and meanings don't
  change, and answers in either script count.

This lesson has no words to learn.

sections.name: Honors: Pinyin and characters in depth

questions.stem: What is a romanisation of Chinese?
choices: a list of characters in dictionary order
a system for writing Chinese sounds in Latin letters
a way of reading Chinese texts aloud in English
questions.explanation: A romanisation writes the sounds of a language in the Latin (Roman) alphabet. Hanyu Pinyin is one, and Wade–Giles is an older one. Simplified characters are still characters, not letters.

questions.stem: In the Wade–Giles spelling T'ai-pei (Taipei), what does the apostrophe after the T show?
choices: a break between two syllables, as in Xī'ān
that the t is aspirated, said with a puff of air
that the syllable has the 4th tone
that a letter has been left out
questions.explanation: Wade–Giles marks aspiration with an apostrophe: t' is pinyin t, and plain t is pinyin d. So T'ai-pei is Táiběi in pinyin. In pinyin the apostrophe means something else: it separates syllables, as in Xī'ān. Wade–Giles writes tones with small numbers, not apostrophes.

questions.stem: The city in Taiwan written Kaohsiung in English is Kao-hsiung in Wade–Giles. Which is its pinyin?
questions.explanation: {高雄|Gāo xióng}: Wade–Giles k without an apostrophe is unaspirated, pinyin g, and Wade–Giles hs is pinyin x. Kāo- and Kǎo- read the k as English does; Gāoshióng mixes up hs and sh.

questions.stem: Match each Wade–Giles spelling to the pinyin letter it stands for.
questions.explanation: With an apostrophe, a Wade–Giles consonant is aspirated (p' = pinyin p); without one it is unaspirated (t = d, ts = z). hs is pinyin x, and j is pinyin r: Wade–Giles jen is pinyin rén ({人|rén}).

questions.stem: The Chinese word for "the Way", {道|dào}, is spelled Tao in English (Taoism, Tao Te Ching). Why does English write it with a t?
choices: Wade–Giles writes unaspirated d as t, and English readers then said it as an English t
Mandarin speakers in the 1800s said it with a t
Pinyin changed the word from t to d in 1958
questions.explanation: In Wade–Giles, t without an apostrophe is the unaspirated sound pinyin writes d, so tao is dào. Readers who didn't know the system said it like English t. The word itself never changed; only the spelling did.

questions.stem: Peking and Tsingtao are older English spellings of {北京|Běi jīng} and {青岛|Qīng dǎo}. What are they?
choices: older conventional spellings, which the postal service also kept
questions.explanation: Strict Wade–Giles would be Pei-ching and Ch'ing-tao. Peking and Tsingtao are older conventional spellings; when China's postal service fixed its place-name spellings in 1906, it kept forms like Peking that were already in use. Pinyin gives Beijing and Qingdao, and zhuyin uses no Latin letters at all.

questions.stem: Zhuyin is also called bopomofo. Where does that name come from?
choices: from its first four symbols, ㄅ ㄆ ㄇ ㄈ (b p m f)
from the name of the man who designed it
from the four tones, said in order
from the first four words of a poem
questions.explanation: The first four zhuyin symbols are ㄅ ㄆ ㄇ ㄈ, said b, p, m, f, so the set is named after them, the way "alphabet" comes from alpha and beta. The symbols were drawn up in 1913 and published in 1918.

questions.stem: How is {是|shì} written in zhuyin?
questions.explanation: Zhuyin writes zhi, chi, shi, ri, zi, ci and si with the initial alone, so shì is ㄕ plus the 4th-tone mark. ㄕㄧˋ would add the i of xī, which isn't the sound after sh; ㄒㄧˋ is xì and ㄙˋ is sì.

questions.stem: Put these events in time order, oldest first.
choices: Matteo Ricci publishes Chinese texts with Roman letters
Thomas Wade publishes his Mandarin textbook
The Ministry of Education publishes zhuyin
questions.explanation: Ricci 1605, Wade 1867 (Giles's dictionary followed in 1892), zhuyin 1918 (drawn up in 1913), Hanyu Pinyin 11 February 1958, ISO 7098 in 1982.

questions.stem: Children in Taiwan learn to read Chinese characters with the help of which system?
questions.explanation: In Taiwan, zhuyin is taught in primary school, and children's books and textbooks print it beside each character. Children in mainland China learn pinyin instead. Wade–Giles survives in many Taiwan names, but it isn't used to teach reading, and Gwoyeu Romatzyh never became widely used.

questions.stem: Mainland passports spell names in pinyin capitals without tone marks. How is the surname {吕|Lǚ} written in a passport today?
questions.explanation: Since 2012 passports write ü as YU, so {吕|Lǚ} is LYU. LU would look like a different surname, {陆|Lù}. LV (and LU) were used in some older passports, before the spelling was made uniform; LÜ isn't used because ü can't be typed on many systems.

questions.stem: English once wrote it Peking. Type the pinyin of 北京 with its tones, using tone numbers (as in ma3): ___
questions.explanation: Běijīng: a 3rd tone, then a 1st. Typed bei3jing1, the app writes the marks. In English the name is written Beijing, without tone marks.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {拼音|pīn yīn}, pinyin ("spelled sounds"): two 1st tones, high and level.

questions.stem: What does a pinyin input method (IME) do?
choices: It reads the characters on the screen aloud
It turns pinyin typed without tones into characters you choose from a list
It adds tone marks to the pinyin you type
It translates English words into Chinese
questions.explanation: You type the syllables without tones, and the input method offers numbered candidates: characters and words with that spelling. You pick one. Adding tone marks to typed pinyin is what this app does for pinyin answers; an input method gives characters.

questions.stem: You type "mai" in a pinyin input method, and both {买|mǎi} (to buy) and {卖|mài} (to sell) appear in the list. Why?
choices: The input method has made a mistake
They are two forms of the same character
You typed the third tone by accident
A pinyin input method doesn't use tones, so every character spelled mai is offered
questions.explanation: Pinyin input methods ignore tones: mai stands for mai in any tone. You choose by meaning, so you need to recognise the character you want. 买 and 卖 are different characters with opposite meanings.

questions.stem: Which two letters do you type in a pinyin input method to get 女 (nǚ, woman)? ___
questions.explanation: Most pinyin input methods put ü on the v key, since pinyin has no v: nv gives 女. Typing nu gives characters read nu, such as {努|nǔ}. This app accepts v for ü as well (nv3 → nǚ).

questions.stem: What do you type in a pinyin input method to get {西安|Xī'ān}, the city?
questions.explanation: The apostrophe marks the break between syllables, as pinyin writes it: xi'an. Without it, xian is usually read as one syllable and gives words such as {先|xiān} and {现|xiàn}. Tone numbers aren't typed in an input method.

questions.stem: Match each way of typing Chinese to how it works.
choices: type the sounds in letters, without tones
write the character with your finger
tap the kinds of stroke in writing order
describe the character by its shapes
questions.explanation: Pinyin and zhuyin input are by sound (zhuyin with the tone marks); handwriting and stroke input are by writing; Cangjie and Wubi are by shapes. No common input method takes an English meaning.

questions.stem: A question in this app asks for the pinyin of 你好. What do you type?
choices: ni3hao3, with your Chinese keyboard switched to English mode
nihao, then pick 你好 from the candidates
questions.explanation: Pinyin answers in this app need the tones, typed as numbers: ni3hao3 becomes nǐhǎo. Switch to English mode first (Shift in Microsoft Pinyin) or to your usual keyboard, or the input method will usually catch the letters. Picking 你好 from the candidates types characters, not pinyin; nh and ni hao leave out the tones.

questions.stem: On a phone's stroke keyboard you tap a character's strokes. Why does stroke order matter there?
choices: It doesn't: the phone recognises the shape
The phone counts only the number of strokes
The candidates are the characters that begin with those strokes in that order
Each stroke key types one whole character
questions.explanation: Stroke input looks up characters by their strokes in writing order, so 十 is {横|héng} then {竖|shù}. Tap them the other way round and you get characters that begin with a {竖|shù}. Recognising the shape is what handwriting input does.

questions.stem: Many input methods accept just the first letter of each syllable of a common word. Which word might "py" give?
questions.explanation: p + y: {拼音|pīn yīn}. Other words with p + y, such as {朋友|péng you}, may be offered too; that's why short cuts give longer lists. {漂亮|piào liang} would be pl, {你好|nǐ hǎo} nh, and {苹果|píng guǒ} pg.

questions.stem: In Taiwan most people type with zhuyin. How is zhuyin typing different from typing with a pinyin input method?
choices: Zhuyin typing gives only simplified characters
Zhuyin is typed with tone numbers 1 to 4
The tone is typed too, with its own key
questions.explanation: A zhuyin input method gives each key a zhuyin symbol, and the tone marks ˊ ˇ ˋ have keys too, so {夏天|xià tiān} is typed ㄒㄧㄚˋ ㄊㄧㄢ. You still pick the character from candidates, and the characters are traditional, as used in Taiwan.

questions.stem: What is a "9-key" pinyin keyboard on a phone?
choices: Pinyin letters shared out over a phone keypad, several letters to a key
A keyboard with one key for each tone
A keyboard that types only the nine most common characters
A handwriting pad divided into nine squares
questions.explanation: Like an old phone keypad, each key carries several letters (abc, def…), and the input method works out which syllables you meant. The bigger keys are easier to hit. Pinyin input methods don't have tone keys.

questions.stem: Which character might you get by typing "lv" in a pinyin input method?
questions.explanation: v stands for ü, so lv is lü: {绿|lǜ}. {路|lù} needs lu: after l, u and ü are different syllables, which is why ü keeps its dots (and its v) there.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {键盘|jiàn pán}, keyboard: a 4th tone, then a 2nd.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {打字|dǎ zì}, to type: a 3rd tone, then a 4th. Before the 4th tone the 3rd is a low half-third, without the rise at the end.

questions.stem: What do simplified and traditional characters have in common?
choices: Nothing: they write two different languages
Every character has the same shape in both
The same words, grammar and pronunciation; only some character shapes differ
The same character shapes, but different pinyin
questions.explanation: Both scripts write the same Mandarin, with the same pinyin. Many characters are identical ({=人 大 你 好=}), and others differ in shape ({=学=} / 學). Some everyday words differ between the mainland and Taiwan, but that is a matter of vocabulary, not of script.

questions.stem: Put these steps of character simplification in mainland China in time order, oldest first.
choices: The Chinese Character Simplification Scheme (515 characters, 54 components)
The General List of Simplified Characters
A second round of simplifications is published
The second round is withdrawn and the General List is reissued
The Table of General Standard Chinese Characters (8,105 characters)
questions.explanation: The scheme was approved in January 1956, the General List followed in 1964, the second round was published in December 1977 and withdrawn in 1986 (the same year the General List was reissued), and the Table of General Standard Chinese Characters was issued in June 2013.

questions.stem: Where are traditional characters the standard script?
choices: nowhere: they appear only in old books
questions.explanation: Traditional characters are used in Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau, and in many Chinese communities abroad. Mainland China, Singapore and Malaysia use simplified characters.

questions.stem: How many characters does the 2013 Table of General Standard Chinese Characters list?
questions.explanation: The 2013 table has 8,105 characters: 3,500 common ones, 3,000 less common ones and 1,605 for names and specialist terms. 3,500 is only its first level, and 515 is the number of characters in the 1956 scheme.

questions.stem: Which is the traditional form of {=学=} (xué, to study)?
questions.explanation: {=学 (8 strokes) is 學 (16 strokes)=} in traditional characters: the complicated part above the cover became three short strokes. 覺 (jué, to feel), 舉 (jǔ, to raise) and 譽 (yù, fame) have similar tops, which were simplified in similar ways.

questions.stem: In simplified characters, the component {=讠 (in 说, 语, 谢)=} stands for which traditional component?
questions.explanation: {=讠 is the simplified form of 言 (speech): 说 說, 语 語, 谢 謝. 钅 stands for 金, 饣 for 食, and 门 for 門=}. A simplified component replaces the traditional one wherever it occurs, so one pattern unlocks many characters.

questions.stem: Why does converting simplified text to traditional need whole words, not single characters?
choices: Because traditional characters have more strokes
Because the two scripts use different grammar
Because pinyin is different in the two scripts
Because one simplified character can stand for several traditional ones
questions.explanation: {=发 stands for 發 (in 出發, to set off) and for 髮 (in 頭髮, hair); 干 for 乾 (dry, in 乾淨) and 幹 (in 幹活, to work)=}. Only the word shows which one is meant. Going the other way is mostly mechanical: 發 and 髮 both become {=发=}.

questions.stem: Which is the traditional form of {={头发|tóu fa}=} (hair)?
questions.explanation: Hair is 頭髮, with 髮. 頭發 uses 發, the {=发=} of {={出发|chū fā}=} (to set off): the mistake you get by converting character by character. 法 and 投 are different characters altogether.

questions.stem: What does this app's Simplified/Traditional switch change?
choices: The words too: a taxi becomes the word used in Taiwan
The character forms only: the words, pinyin and meanings stay the same
questions.explanation: The switch shows Taiwan character forms and keeps the mainland words: {={出租车|chū zū chē}=} (taxi) is shown as 出租車, not replaced by the Taiwan word. Pinyin and meanings don't change, and lessons, questions and vocabulary all switch.

questions.stem: Taiwan and Hong Kong both use traditional characters. Which is true?
choices: Their character forms are identical in every character
Each has its own standard, and they differ in some characters
Hong Kong uses simplified forms for common characters
Taiwan has no official standard for character shapes
questions.explanation: Taiwan's Ministry of Education and Hong Kong's Education Bureau each publish a standard for character shapes. They agree on most characters, but some differ: "inside" is usually {=裡 in Taiwan and 裏 in Hong Kong=}.

questions.stem: Which of these uses simplified characters as its standard?
questions.explanation: Singapore published its own first list of simplified characters in 1969 and later adopted the mainland forms; Malaysia adopted them in 1981. Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau use traditional characters.

questions.stem: {=汉=} (Chinese) is the simplified form of 漢. How was it simplified?
choices: A simple sign, 又, replaced a complicated part
An old form was brought back
Two characters were merged into one
A cursive shape was made standard
questions.explanation: {=The right side of 漢 was replaced by 又, as in 對 → 对, 難 → 难 and 雞 → 鸡. The water component on the left (氵) is the same in both scripts=}.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {汉字|hàn zì}, Chinese characters: two 4th tones, both falling.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the three syllables?
questions.explanation: {繁体字|fán tǐ zì}, traditional characters: 2nd, 3rd, 4th. The 3rd tone before a 4th is a low half-third.

questions.stem: How many syllables do you say in {图书馆|tú shū guǎn} (library)?
questions.explanation: Each character is one syllable, so three characters make three syllables: tú, shū, guǎn. Counting the pinyin letters or the vowels gives a wrong number; count the characters.

questions.stem: What is pinyin used for in mainland China?
choices: Showing pronunciation, typing, and writing names and signs
Writing newspapers and books instead of characters
Writing words borrowed from English only
Writing the tones of a song
questions.explanation: Pinyin shows how characters are said (in dictionaries and books for learners), it is how most people type Chinese, and it writes names on signs, maps and passports. Ordinary texts, newspapers included, are written in characters.

questions.stem: In the syllable zhōng (中, middle), what is the initial?
questions.explanation: The initial is the consonant at the start, and zh is one initial written with two letters. The final is ong, and the mark over the o shows the tone (1st). z alone would be a different initial.

questions.stem: In the syllable xué (学, to study), what is the final?
questions.explanation: x is the initial and ue is the final, the vowel part after it (it is üe, written without dots after x: lesson 05). The mark on the e is the tone (2nd), which belongs to the whole syllable.

questions.stem: Match each syllable to the pitch of its tone.
questions.explanation: The mark draws the pitch: ā is level (1st tone), á rises (2nd), ǎ dips low (3rd), à falls (4th). {妈|mā} mother, {麻|má} hemp, {马|mǎ} horse, {骂|mà} to scold.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {马|mǎ}, horse: the 3rd tone, low and dipping. Said on its own it dips and comes up a little at the end.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {妈|mā}, mother: the 1st tone, high and level, held steady from start to end.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {麻|má}, hemp: the 2nd tone, rising from the middle of your voice to the top, like a surprised "huh?".

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {骂|mà}, to scold: the 4th tone, falling sharply from high to low, like a firm "No!".

questions.stem: Which syllable means "horse"?
questions.explanation: {马|mǎ} (horse) has the 3rd tone. mā is mother, má is hemp, mà is to scold: same sounds, different tones, different words.

questions.stem: Which pinyin letter sounds roughly like the "sh" in English "she"?
questions.explanation: x is roughly the "sh" of "she", with the tongue flat: {西|xī} (west). q is roughly the "ch" of "cheese", c is "ts", and zh is a "j"-like sound with the tongue curled back.

questions.stem: How is the c in cài (菜, dish) said?
questions.explanation: Pinyin c is always a "ts" sound, with a puff of air: {菜|cài}. It is never a "k" or an "s" as in English, and "ch" is spelled ch or q in pinyin.

questions.stem: Type mǎ (马, horse) with a tone number (ma3): ___
questions.explanation: Type ma3 and the app writes mǎ: the number after a syllable is its tone. The characters 马 typed with a Chinese keyboard count too.

questions.stem: Type māma (妈妈, mum) with tone numbers (ma1 ma5): ___
questions.explanation: ma1 gives mā, and 5 (or 0) is the neutral tone, which has no mark: māma. Spaces don't matter.

questions.stem: What does "{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}。" mean?
questions.explanation: {我|wǒ} is I, {是|shì} is to be, {学生|xué sheng} is student. Chinese needs no word for "a", and {是|shì} doesn't change for person or time, so this is simply "I am a student". You would be {你|nǐ}.

questions.stem: {买|mǎi} means "to buy". What does {卖|mài}, with a 4th tone, mean?
questions.explanation: mǎi (3rd tone) is to buy and mài (4th tone) is to sell. Only the tone is different, and the meaning is the opposite: that's why tones can't be skipped.

questions.stem: Which statement about Chinese characters is true?
choices: Each character stands for one letter.
Every word is one character long.
A character's shape always shows how to say it.
Each character is said as one syllable.
questions.explanation: One character, one syllable, and usually one meaning. Words have one to four characters (most have two), and the shape of a character usually doesn't tell you its sound, which is why learners use pinyin.

questions.stem: {你好|nǐ hǎo} (hello) is written with two 3rd tones. How is it said?
choices: nǐ hǎo, both low and dipping
questions.explanation: When two 3rd tones meet, the first one rises like a 2nd tone: said ní hǎo. Pinyin still writes nǐ hǎo, the tones of each character. Lesson 11 covers this change.

questions.stem: When the app says a Chinese word aloud, what does the device's voice read?
questions.explanation: The voice always reads the characters. Computer voices often misread pinyin, so the app never gives them pinyin. Add a Chinese (Mandarin) voice in your device's speech settings if you don't have one.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {妈妈|mā ma}, mum: a 1st tone, then a short, light neutral tone with no mark.

questions.stem: On the five-level pitch scale (1 low, 5 high), which numbers describe the 4th tone?
questions.explanation: The 4th tone falls from the top of the voice to the bottom: 51. 55 is the high, level 1st tone, 35 the rising 2nd tone and 214 the dipping 3rd tone.

questions.stem: How is a 3rd tone usually said before a 1st, 2nd or 4th tone, as in {北京|Běi jīng}?
choices: with a full, slow dip and rise
questions.explanation: Before other tones a 3rd tone keeps only its low part, 21: the half-third tone. The full dip (214) comes only before a pause. It changes to a rising tone only before another 3rd tone, as in {你好|nǐ hǎo}.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {八|bā}, eight: the 1st tone, high and level.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {拔|bá}, to pull out: the 2nd tone, rising from the middle to the top.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {靶|bǎ}, target: the 3rd tone, low. On its own it dips to the bottom and comes up a little.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {爸|bà}, dad: the 4th tone, falling sharply from the top.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {姨|yí}, aunt: the 2nd tone. It starts in the middle and rises at once; a 3rd tone would stay low first.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {椅|yǐ}, chair (as in {椅子|yǐ zi}): the 3rd tone, low and dipping.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {亿|yì}, a hundred million: the 4th tone, falling from the top.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {屋|wū}, room (as in {屋子|wū zi}): the 1st tone, high and held. A 4th tone also starts high, but drops at once.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {吴|wú}, Wu (a family name): the 2nd tone, rising.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {雾|wù}, fog: the 4th tone, a short, firm fall.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {姐姐|jiě jie}, older sister: a 3rd tone (said low), then a light neutral syllable, a little higher than the low jiě.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {爸爸|bà ba}, dad: a 4th tone, then a short, low neutral syllable at the bottom of the fall.

questions.stem: How does the pitch of a neutral-tone syllable depend on the syllable before it?
choices: It copies the tone before it.
It is low after tones 1, 2 and 4, and a little higher after tone 3.
questions.explanation: A neutral syllable has no shape of its own: it is short and light, low after a 1st, 2nd or 4th tone ({妈妈|mā ma}, {爸爸|bà ba}) and a little higher after a 3rd tone ({姐姐|jiě jie}), whose half-third tone is at the bottom of the voice.

questions.stem: Match each syllable to its tone.
questions.explanation: ˉ is the 1st tone, ˊ the 2nd, ˇ the 3rd, ˋ the 4th, and no mark is the neutral tone. On i the mark takes the place of the dot.

questions.stem: Type wǔ (五, five) with a tone number (wu3): ___
questions.explanation: wu3 becomes wǔ: the 3rd tone. Typing wu with no number, or another number, gives a different syllable: wū (room), wú (Wu), wù (fog).

questions.stem: Listen. Which word did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard {米饭|mǐ fàn}, cooked rice: a low half-third tone, then a falling 4th tone. mí would rise and mì would fall from the top; fān would stay high.

questions.stem: Which syllable has the 2nd tone?
questions.explanation: The 2nd tone mark ˊ rises from left to right, like the voice: bá. bà falls (4th), bǎ dips (3rd) and bā is level (1st).

questions.stem: Which word ends in a neutral tone?
questions.explanation: {爷爷|yé ye}: the second syllable has no tone mark, so it is neutral, short and light. Běijīng, mǐfàn and lǎoshī have a full tone on both syllables.

questions.stem: What is the difference between Mandarin b and p?
choices: b is voiced (buzzing) and p is not, as in English
b is made with the teeth and p with the lips
p is said with a strong puff of air; b has none
questions.explanation: Both are made with the lips and neither buzzes. p is aspirated (a puff of air bursts out) and b is unaspirated (no puff). English speakers think of b and p as voiced and voiceless, which is why this contrast has to be learned.

questions.stem: Which English sound is closest to Mandarin b, as in {八|bā} (eight)?
questions.explanation: Mandarin b is a p with no puff, like the p after s in "spin". The b in "rubber" buzzes (it is voiced), and the p of "pin" has the puff that belongs to Mandarin p.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a Mandarin syllable?
questions.explanation: f never goes with the final i, so there is no "fee" syllable (fei, as in {飞|fēi}, to fly, does exist). bi ({笔|bǐ}, pen), pa ({怕|pà}, to fear) and fu ({福|fú}, good fortune) are all real.

questions.stem: How is the pinyin e in {饿|è} (hungry) said?
choices: like a back "uh", close to the u in "duh"
questions.explanation: Pinyin e on its own is a back, unrounded vowel: lips spread, tongue pulled back, close to "uh". It is not the e of "bed" (that sound is written e only in ie and üe), and not "ee" or "ay".

questions.stem: How do you make the vowel ü?
choices: Say oo with the lips spread
Say u and then ee quickly
Say ee and round your lips without moving your tongue
Say a short e through the nose
questions.explanation: ü has the tongue of i (high and forward) and the lips of u (tightly rounded). If the tongue moves back, it becomes u; if the lips unround, it becomes i. It is one steady sound, not a glide.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {鹅|é}, goose: the 2nd tone, rising, on the back vowel e.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {饿|è}, hungry: the 4th tone, falling. Compare {鹅|é} (goose), which rises.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {坡|pō}, slope: the 1st tone, high and level. Notice the puff on p and the slight w before the o.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {婆|pó} (as in {婆婆|pó po}, a husband's mother): the 2nd tone, rising.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {墨|mò}, ink: the 4th tone, falling from the top.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {福|fú}, good fortune: the 2nd tone, rising. You often see this character on doors at the Spring Festival.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {笔|bǐ}, pen or writing brush: the 3rd tone, low. Say the b with no puff.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {皮包|pí bāo}, handbag: a rising 2nd tone, then a high, level 1st tone (2+1).

questions.stem: Listen. Which syllable did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard {怕|pà}, to fear: aspirated p (with a puff) and a falling 4th tone. {爸|bà} (dad) has the same tone with no puff; pā and bā would be high and level.

questions.stem: Listen. Which syllable did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard {鼻|bí}, nose (as in {鼻子|bí zi}): no puff, and a rising tone. {皮|pí} (skin) has the puff; bì would fall and pǐ would be low.

questions.stem: Listen. Which syllable did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard {步|bù}, step: unaspirated b and a falling 4th tone. With a puff it would be pù; pǔ and bǔ would be low 3rd tones.

questions.stem: Listen. Which syllable did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard {鱼|yú}, fish: the vowel ü (written u after y) with a rising tone. wú has the back u with rounded lips, yí has spread lips, and yù falls.

questions.stem: Match each initial to how it is made.
choices: lips together, no puff of air
lips together, strong puff of air
lips together, air through the nose
top teeth on the lower lip
questions.explanation: All four are made at the lips. b and p differ only by aspiration (p has the puff), m goes through the nose, and f is made with the top teeth on the lower lip, as in English.

questions.stem: Type bǐ (笔, pen) with a tone number (bi3): ___
questions.explanation: bi3 becomes bǐ: the mark replaces the dot of the i. pǐ, with a puff, would be a different syllable.

questions.stem: How does the syllable bō ({波|bō}, wave) sound?
choices: like English "bow" (as in a bow and arrow)
close to "bwo", with a slight w before the o
questions.explanation: After b, p, m and f the final o is said with a short w-like glide: bō is close to "bwo". It is a pure, steady vowel, not the glide of English "bow", and not u ("boo") or e ("buh").

questions.stem: Which pair of initials differs only by aspiration (a puff of air)?
questions.explanation: g and k are made in the same place, the back of the tongue, and only k has the puff, just as with b/p and d/t. n and l are both made with the tongue tip but differ in where the air goes; d/n and g/h differ in more than the puff.

questions.stem: How is Mandarin h different from English h?
choices: It is made with the back of the tongue raised, so you hear a soft rasp.
It is said with the lips rounded.
It is the same as English h.
questions.explanation: English h is plain breath from the throat. Mandarin h is made with the back of the tongue close to the soft palate, giving light friction, like a gentle "ch" of Scottish "loch": {河|hé}, {湖|hú}.

questions.stem: Why is {女儿|nǚ ér} (daughter) written with the dots on ü?
choices: Because every ü keeps its dots
Because nu without dots is a different syllable
questions.explanation: After n and l both u and ü are possible: nǔ ({努力|nǔ lì}) and nǚ, lù ({路|lù}) and lǜ ({律|lǜ}). The dots tell them apart. After j, q, x and y the dots are dropped, because no plain u can follow those letters.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a Mandarin syllable?
questions.explanation: g, k and h never go with i (or ü). ge ({哥|gē}), ku ({哭|kū}) and he ({河|hé}) are all real. The syllables that sound a little like "gee" are spelled with j, q or x (lesson 05).

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {低|dī}, low: the 1st tone, high and level, which is a nice paradox to remember it by.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {敌|dí}, enemy: the 2nd tone, rising. No puff on the d.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {塔|tǎ}, tower or pagoda: the 3rd tone, low and dipping, with a puff on the t.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {课|kè}, class or lesson: the 4th tone, falling, with a puff on the k and the back vowel e.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {湖|hú}, lake: the 2nd tone, rising, with the rough back-of-the-mouth h.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {渴|kě}, thirsty: the 3rd tone, low and dipping.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {驴|lǘ}, donkey: the 2nd tone, on ü. Compare {炉|lú} (stove), with plain u.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {努力|nǔ lì}, to make an effort: a 3rd tone, said low (half-third), then a falling 4th tone (3+4).

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {旅游|lǚ yóu}, to travel: a low 3rd tone on lü, then a rising 2nd tone (3+2).

questions.stem: Listen. Which syllable did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard {踢|tī}, to kick: aspirated t (a puff) and a high, level 1st tone. {低|dī} (low) has the same tone without the puff; tí would rise and dì would fall.

questions.stem: Listen. Which syllable did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard {哭|kū}, to cry: aspirated k and a high 1st tone. {姑|gū} (aunt) has no puff; {苦|kǔ} (bitter) and {古|gǔ} (ancient) are low 3rd tones.

questions.stem: Listen. Which syllable did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard {律|lǜ}, law (as in {法律|fǎ lǜ}): l, the rounded front vowel ü, and a falling 4th tone. {路|lù} (road) has plain u; lǚ would be low.

questions.stem: Listen. Which syllable did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard {你|nǐ}, you: n (air through the nose) and a low 3rd tone. {李|lǐ} (the family name Li) has l; ní would rise and lì would fall.

questions.stem: Type nǚ (女, female) with a tone number. Use v for ü (nv3): ___
questions.explanation: nv3 (or nu:3) becomes nǚ. nu3 would give nǔ, a different syllable with the back vowel u.

questions.stem: Match each initial to how it is made.
choices: back of the tongue, no puff
back of the tongue, strong puff
back of the tongue, air rubbing through
questions.explanation: d/t are made with the tongue tip behind the top teeth and g/k with the back of the tongue; in each pair only the second has the puff. h is a rough sound made at the back of the mouth.

questions.stem: Which is the correct pinyin for 旅游 (to travel)?
questions.explanation: 旅 is lǚ: ü keeps its dots after l, and the tone mark sits on top of them. lǔ (with plain u) is a different syllable, and lü with no mark has lost its 3rd tone.

questions.stem: How is the q in {七|qī} (seven) said?
choices: like the ch in "cheese", tongue flat, with a puff
questions.explanation: Pinyin q is a ch-like sound with the front of the tongue flat against the roof of the mouth and a strong puff of air. It is never "k" or "kw". j is its unaspirated partner, with no puff.

questions.stem: How is the x in {西|xī} (west) said?
choices: like the sh in "she", lips spread, tongue tip down
questions.explanation: x is a "smiling sh": the tongue tip rests behind the lower teeth and the front of the tongue is close to the roof of the mouth. The English values of x ("ks", "z") don't apply, and s is a different initial (lesson 06).

questions.topic: ü after j q x y
questions.stem: In {去|qù} (to go), how is the vowel written u said?
choices: as u in "food", lips rounded and tongue back
as the back "uh" of pinyin e
as ü, tongue forward and lips rounded
questions.explanation: After j, q, x and y, u always means ü: qù is "qü". The dots are dropped because no plain u can follow q. Saying it with the back u gives a syllable that doesn't exist.

questions.topic: ü after j q x y
questions.stem: Which is the correct pinyin spelling of 鱼 (fish)?
questions.explanation: ü with no initial is written yu, and after y the dots are left off: yú. ǘ alone isn't how pinyin writes it, and wú is a different syllable with the back u ({吴|wú}).

questions.topic: ü after j q x y
questions.stem: Which is the correct pinyin spelling of 学 (to study)?
questions.explanation: The final is üe, written ue after x: xué. The dots are dropped after x, sh is a different initial, and the tone mark goes on the e, not the u.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a Mandarin syllable?
questions.explanation: j, q and x only come before i or ü (and finals that start with them). xa doesn't exist; the syllable is xia ({下|xià}, below). xi, xu (= xü) and qu (= qü) are all real.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {鸡|jī}, chicken: the 1st tone, high and level, with an unaspirated j.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {急|jí}, urgent: the 2nd tone, rising.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {起|qǐ}, to rise: the 3rd tone, low. Notice the puff on the q.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {气|qì}, air or gas: the 4th tone, falling.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {习|xí}, to practise (as in {学习|xué xí}): the 2nd tone, rising.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {戏|xì}, play or opera: the 4th tone, falling from the top.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {剧|jù}, play or drama: the 4th tone, on ü (written u after j).

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {玉|yù}, jade: the 4th tone. yu is ü with no initial.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {学习|xué xí}, to study: two rising 2nd tones (2+2).

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {许多|xǔ duō}, many: a low half-third tone, then a high 1st tone (3+1).

questions.stem: Listen. Which syllable did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard {七|qī}, seven: tongue flat, a puff of air, and a real "ee" vowel. jī has no puff, xī is a smiling "sh", and chī has the tongue curled back and a buzzed vowel (lesson 06).

questions.stem: Listen. Which syllable did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard {西|xī}, west: the smiling sh with a real "ee", high and level. shī ({诗|shī}, poem) is darker, with the tongue curled back; sī has the tongue at the teeth; xí would rise.

questions.stem: Listen. Which syllable did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard {去|qù}, to go: q with the tongue flat, then ü (written u), falling. kù would have the back-of-the-tongue k and a back u; chù a curled tongue; qǔ a low 3rd tone.

questions.stem: Type qù (去, to go) with a tone number (qu4): ___
questions.explanation: Type qu4: after q the u is ü anyway, so no v is needed, and the app writes qù, as correct pinyin does.

questions.stem: How is the i in {是|shì} (to be) said?
choices: as a buzzed vowel with the tongue tip still curled up
questions.explanation: After zh, ch, sh and r the letter i is a buzzed vowel that carries on the curled-tongue sound, roughly "shrr". It is never ee. A real ee comes after j, q, x: {戏|xì} (play) is the "shee"-like syllable.

questions.stem: How is the c in {次|cì} (time, occurrence) said?
choices: like "ts" in "cats", with a puff of air
questions.explanation: Pinyin c is always "ts" with a puff; z is its partner without the puff ("ds"). English readers often say k or s, which are different initials, and ch is the curled-tongue sound of {吃|chī}.

questions.stem: Where is the tip of the tongue for zh, ch and sh?
choices: down behind the lower front teeth
at the back of the upper front teeth
raised and curled slightly back toward the roof of the mouth
questions.explanation: zh, ch, sh and r are retroflex: the tongue tip is raised and bent back toward the hard palate. For j, q, x it rests behind the lower teeth; for z, c, s it is at the upper teeth.

questions.stem: Match each initial to where the tip of the tongue is.
choices: down behind the lower teeth, tongue flat
curled up toward the roof of the mouth
questions.explanation: Three sets: j q x with the tongue flat and the tip down, zh ch sh r with the tip curled up, and z c s with the tip at the upper teeth. In each set the first two differ only by aspiration: q, ch and c have the puff.

questions.stem: Listen. Which syllable did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard {是|shì}, to be: tongue curled up, a buzzed vowel and a falling 4th tone. xì has a bright ee, sì has the tongue at the teeth, and shí would rise.

questions.stem: Listen. Which syllable did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard {四|sì}, four: a hiss at the teeth, a short buzz and a falling tone. shì is darker (curled tongue), xì has ee, and sī would be high and level.

questions.stem: Listen. Which syllable did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard {知|zhī}, to know: tongue curled up, no puff, buzzed vowel, high and level. jī ({鸡|jī}) has the flat tongue and ee, zī the tongue at the teeth, and chī the puff.

questions.stem: Listen. Which syllable did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard {词|cí}, word: "ts" with a puff at the teeth, a short buzz, rising. qí ({旗|qí}) has ee, chí ({迟|chí}) the curled tongue, and cì falls.

questions.stem: Listen. Which syllable did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard {十|shí}, ten: curled tongue, buzzed vowel, rising 2nd tone. xí ({习|xí}) has ee, shì ({是|shì}) falls, and chí has a puff.

questions.stem: Listen. Which syllable did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard {吃|chī}, to eat: tongue curled, a strong puff, high and level. qī ({七|qī}) has the flat tongue and ee, zhī has no puff, and shī ({诗|shī}) is a hiss with no stop at the start.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {热|rè}, hot: the 4th tone, falling, with the retroflex r and the back vowel e.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {直|zhí}, straight: the 2nd tone, rising, on the buzzed vowel.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {纸|zhǐ}, paper: the 3rd tone, low and dipping.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {迟|chí}, late: the 2nd tone, rising, with the aspirated ch.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {齿|chǐ}, tooth: the 3rd tone, low.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {紫|zǐ}, purple: the 3rd tone, low, with z at the teeth and the short buzzed vowel.

questions.stem: Listen and type the syllable you hear, with a tone number (for example ma1): ___
questions.explanation: You heard {书|shū}, book: sh with the tongue curled, the back vowel u, and a high, level 1st tone: type shu1.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {汉字|hàn zì}, Chinese characters: two falling 4th tones (4+4). The first falls a little less far, so the second can fall again.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {生日|shēng rì}, birthday: a high 1st tone, then a falling 4th tone (1+4).

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {老师|lǎo shī}, teacher: a low half-third tone, then a high 1st tone (3+1), with the buzzed vowel after sh.

questions.stem: Which is the correct pinyin for 贵 (expensive)?
questions.explanation: After an initial, uei is written ui, and in ui the tone mark goes on the last letter: guì (4th tone). guèi is the long form, which pinyin doesn't write after an initial; gùi puts the mark on the wrong letter; guí has the wrong tone.

questions.stem: The final iou with no initial and a 3rd tone, as in 有 (to have), is written:
questions.explanation: With no initial, the i- at the start of a final becomes y: iou → you, and the mark goes on the o of ou: yǒu. The short form iu is used only after an initial (liù, jiǔ).

questions.stem: How is the final ei in {北|běi} (north) said?
questions.explanation: ei is close to "ay" in "day": {北|běi} sounds like "bay" said low. Saying "bee" is a common English reading of the spelling; "eye" is the final ai ({爱|ài}).

questions.stem: How is the final ou in {狗|gǒu} (dog) said?
questions.explanation: ou is close to "oh" in "go", with rounded lips: {狗|gǒu} is "go", not "goo". The "ow" of "how" is spelled ao in pinyin ({高|gāo}).

questions.stem: In {鞋|xié} (shoe) and {学|xué} (to study), how is the e said?
questions.explanation: After i and ü, in ie and üe, e is the e of "yes". The back "uh" is the sound of e on its own ({饿|è}, {喝|hē}).

questions.stem: How is each final written when the syllable has no initial?
questions.explanation: A single vowel gets y or w added (yi, wu, yu); in a longer final the first letter becomes y or w (ya, wo); ü becomes yu and loses its dots (yu, yue).

questions.stem: Which spelling is wrong?
questions.explanation: In ui and iu the tone mark goes on the second letter, the last vowel: shuǐ (water). liù (six), guì (expensive) and jiǔ (nine) are all correct.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {来|lái}, to come: the 2nd tone, rising, on the final ai.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {黑|hēi}, black: the 1st tone, high and level, on ei ("hay").

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {狗|gǒu}, dog: the 3rd tone, low, on ou.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {鞋|xié}, shoe: the 2nd tone, rising, with the e of "yes".

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {叫|jiào}, to be called: the 4th tone, falling, on iao.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {牛|niú}, cow or ox: the 2nd tone. In the 1st and 2nd tones the hidden o of iu is short.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {雪|xuě}, snow: the 3rd tone, low, on üe (written ue after x).

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {外|wài}, outside: the 4th tone. wai is uai with no initial.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {九月|jiǔ yuè}, September: a low half-third tone, then a falling 4th tone (3+4).

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {谢谢|xiè xie}, thank you: a falling 4th tone, then a light, low neutral syllable (4 + neutral).

questions.stem: Listen. Which syllable did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard {九|jiǔ}, nine: j, then iu with its hidden o ("jyoh"), low. jǔ has the vowel ü, zhǒu the curled tongue, and qiǔ a puff.

questions.stem: Listen. Which syllable did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard {对|duì}, right or correct: no puff on d, then ui ("dway"), falling. tuì has a puff, dèi lacks the w-glide, and duò ends in o.

questions.stem: Type liù (六, six) with a tone number (liu4): ___
questions.explanation: liu4 becomes liù: the mark goes on the u, the last letter of iu. The hidden o (liou) isn't written after an initial.

questions.stem: Which syllable ends with the tip of the tongue pressed behind the upper front teeth?
questions.explanation: fàn ends in -n, made with the tongue tip up behind the upper teeth. fàng, xīng and péng end in -ng, made with the back of the tongue against the soft palate while the tip stays down.

questions.stem: How does the final ian in {天|tiān} (sky, day) sound?
choices: roughly like "tyen": the a is raised toward e
like "teen", with no vowel between i and n
questions.explanation: In ian the a is pulled up almost to an e, so {天|tiān} sounds close to "tyen" and {钱|qián} close to "chyen". A deep a belongs to iang ({墙|qiáng}); "teen" would be in, the final of {今|jīn}.

questions.stem: Which is the correct spelling of 选 (to choose), x + üan with the third tone?
questions.explanation: After j, q, x and y the dots on ü are dropped, so x + üan is written xuǎn (and still said with rounded lips). xüǎn keeps dots the rule removes, xuǎng adds an ending that isn't there, and shuǎn has a different initial.

questions.stem: What is the final in jūn (军, army)?
questions.explanation: j, q, x and y are never followed by a plain u, so un after them is always ün: jūn, qún, xùn, yún. After any other initial un stands for uen: chūn, dùn, lùn.

questions.stem: Which of these syllables does not exist in Mandarin?
questions.explanation: b, p, m and f combine with eng ({风|fēng}, wind) but never with ong, so there is no fong. fēng, fāng and fàn are all real syllables.

questions.stem: The final uen after the initial ch, first tone (春, spring). How is it written?
questions.explanation: After an initial, uen is shortened to un: chūn, as uei becomes ui. The e is still heard faintly ("chwun"). Only without an initial does it keep every letter: wen. chǖn is impossible (ü never follows ch), and chōng is a different final.

questions.stem: Which syllable has the same final as tiān?
questions.explanation: tiān and nián both have ian (said "yen"). tīng has ing, qiáng has iang (a deep a and -ng), and xīn has in.

questions.stem: How is the final ing written with no initial? Type it with the first tone (as in 英, English), using 1 for the tone: ___
questions.explanation: Alone, i-finals are written with y. For in and ing the y is simply added: yīn, yīng (not yiing). Typed ying1, it becomes yīng.

questions.stem: Type {今天|jīn tiān} (today) in pinyin with tone numbers (jin1 tian1): ___
questions.explanation: 今天 is jīntiān: in (ee + n) then ian ("tyen"), both first tones. Both syllables end in -n, with the tongue tip up.

questions.stem: Type the syllable of 元 (yuan, the unit of money), y + üan with the second tone, using a tone number: ___
questions.explanation: üan without an initial is written yuan, and the second tone goes on the a: yuán (type yuan2). The u stands for ü, so round your lips.

questions.stem: Match each final to the way it is written with no initial.
questions.explanation: Alone, i-finals take y (yan, yin), u-finals take w (wen, weng) and ü-finals take yu (yuan, yun). There is no wong: ong always follows an initial.

questions.stem: Listen. Which syllable did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard {新|xīn} (new): the tongue tip closes the syllable with -n. {星|xīng} (star) ends with the back of the tongue, -ng; qīn starts with q; xūn has the rounded ü.

questions.stem: Listen. Which syllable did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard {墙|qiáng} (wall): a deep, open a and -ng. {钱|qián} (money) would have the raised "yen" vowel and -n; qióng has the o of ong; jiáng starts with the unaspirated j.

questions.stem: Listen. Which syllable did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard {放|fàng} (to put): a deep a and -ng. {饭|fàn} (meal) has a brighter a and ends with the tongue tip; fèng has the central e vowel; huàng starts with h and a u glide.

questions.stem: Listen. Which syllable did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard {朋|péng}, the first syllable of {朋友|péng you} (friend): the central e and -ng. {盆|pén} (basin) ends in -n, píng has i, and pán has a.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {钱|qián}, money: the second tone, rising. Listen for the "yen" sound of ian as well.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: {冷|lěng}, cold: the third tone. Said alone it dips low and rises again at the end.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {房间|fáng jiān}, room: a rising second tone, then a high, level first tone. Both syllables end in nasals: -ang, then -ian.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {电影|diàn yǐng}, film: a falling fourth tone, then a third tone, which stays low at the end of the word.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {医院|yī yuàn}, hospital: a high first tone, then a falling fourth. yuàn is ü + an, said with rounded lips and a raised a ("ywen").

questions.stem: Which is the correct spelling of 贵 (expensive), fourth tone?
questions.explanation: In ui the last vowel takes the mark: guì. ui is short for uei, whose main vowel e isn't written, so the mark moves to the last letter. gùi marks the wrong vowel, güì adds dots that don't belong, and gūi has the wrong tone and vowel.

questions.stem: Which is the correct spelling of 六 (six), fourth tone?
questions.explanation: In iu, as in ui, the last vowel takes the mark: liù. lìu and líu put it on the i; lioù writes out the hidden o, which pinyin leaves out after an initial.

questions.stem: In 小 (small), x + iao with the third tone, which letter carries the tone mark?
questions.explanation: If a syllable has an a, the a always takes the mark: xiǎo. The "last vowel" rule is only for syllables with no a, e or ou, such as liù and guì.

questions.stem: Which is the correct spelling of 学 (to learn)?
questions.explanation: After x the dots of ü are dropped (x is never followed by a plain u), and in üe the e takes the mark: xué. xúe marks the wrong vowel, and shué starts with a different initial.

questions.stem: What does the 5 mean in the tone-number spelling "xie4 xie5" (谢谢, thanks)?
choices: the neutral tone: written with no mark
a fifth tone that falls very low
questions.explanation: In tone numbers 5 (or 0, or no number) is the neutral tone, which has no mark: xièxie. Mandarin has four full tones and the neutral tone, not a fifth full tone.

questions.stem: How is the city of 西安 (Xi'an) written in pinyin?
questions.explanation: It has two syllables, Xī and ān, so an apostrophe goes before the syllable that starts with a: Xī'ān. Xiān would be one syllable (like {先|xiān}, first), and the hyphen isn't used here.

questions.stem: Written without spaces, which of these words needs an apostrophe?
questions.explanation: The second syllable of 平安 starts with a, so it is written píng'ān; without the apostrophe it could be read pín + gān. Syllables starting with y or w (yī, wén) and with a consonant (tiān) already show where they begin.

questions.stem: How is {女儿|nǚ ér} (daughter) written as one word?
questions.explanation: The apostrophe goes between the syllables, before the one that starts with e: nǚ'ér. Dictionaries write it before every syllable inside a word that starts with a, o or e.

questions.stem: How is {朋友|péng you} (friend) written when pinyin stands on its own?
questions.explanation: Pinyin is written in words, so the two syllables of one word are joined: péngyou. The app shows the pinyin one syllable per character only to place it over each character.

questions.stem: How is the name 王芳 (surname 王 Wáng, given name 芳 Fāng) written in pinyin?
questions.explanation: Surname first, then the given name, each with a capital and a space between them: Wáng Fāng. Putting the given name first follows English order, and the other two join the names or leave out the capitals.

questions.stem: Which is the correct way to write {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}。 (I'm a student.) in pinyin?
questions.explanation: Words are separated by spaces, the syllables of a word are joined, and the sentence starts with a capital: Wǒ shì xuésheng. The others miss the capital, split xuésheng or run the words together.

questions.stem: Type "nǚ" (female) using v for ü and a tone number (nv3): ___
questions.explanation: nv3 becomes nǚ: v stands for ü, and 3 puts the third-tone mark over it. After n and l the dots matter: nu3 would be nǔ, a different syllable.

questions.stem: Type the pinyin of 绿 (green), l + ü with the fourth tone, using v (or u:) for ü and a tone number: ___
questions.explanation: lv4 (or lu:4) becomes lǜ. Without the dots it would be lù, as in {路|lù} (road), so after l the ü must be typed and written.

questions.stem: Type {西安|Xī ān} (the city of Xi'an) in pinyin with tone numbers: ___
questions.explanation: Xi1an1 (or Xi1'an1) becomes Xī'ān: two first tones. When it's written, the apostrophe shows that it is two syllables, not xiān. When you type, the apostrophe and the capital don't matter.

questions.stem: Match each syllable in tone numbers to its spelling with a tone mark.
questions.explanation: a, else e, else the o of ou, else the last vowel: hǎo (a), xué (e), duō (o is the last vowel), liù and guì (the last vowel). lìu puts the mark on the wrong vowel.

questions.stem: Listen. Which spelling matches what you heard?
questions.explanation: You heard {牛|niú} (cow), the second tone. iu takes the mark on its last vowel, so níu is misspelled; liú starts with l, and nóu has a different final.

questions.stem: Listen. Which spelling matches what you heard?
questions.explanation: You heard {鱼|yú} (fish): ü with the second tone. Without an initial, ü is written yu and the dots are dropped, so yǘ is wrong. wú has a plain u and yóu a different final.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {女儿|nǚ ér}, daughter: a third tone, said low (a half-third) before the rising second tone of ér. Written as one word it is nǚ'ér.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {可爱|kě ài}, cute: a low third tone, then a falling fourth. As one word it is written kě'ài, with an apostrophe before the a.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {西安|Xī ān}, the city of Xi'an: two high, level first tones. {先|xiān} (first) would be a single syllable.

questions.stem: In {老师|lǎo shī} (teacher), how is the first syllable said?
choices: low, without rising again (a half-third tone)
dipping low and rising back up
questions.explanation: Before any tone except another third, a third tone stays low and doesn't rise: the half-third tone. The full dip and rise comes only alone or at the end of a phrase. It changes to a second tone only before another third tone (nǐ hǎo said ní hǎo).

questions.stem: Which word has the tone pattern 2+3?
questions.explanation: píngguǒ rises on píng, then drops low on guǒ: 2+3. xiǎoshí is the reverse, 3+2; míngtiān is 2+1 and mǐfàn 3+4.

questions.stem: Which word has a neutral-tone second syllable?
questions.explanation: The second syllable of māma has no mark: it's neutral, as in every repeated family word (bàba, gēge, jiějie). The other three have two full tones.

questions.stem: After which tone is a neutral-tone syllable said higher than after the others?
questions.explanation: The low third tone leaves room to go up, so the neutral syllable after it is higher: {姐姐|jiě jie}, {我们|wǒ men}. After the 1st, 2nd and 4th tones it's low: {妈妈|mā ma}, {朋友|péng you}, {爸爸|bà ba}.

questions.stem: dōngxi, with a neutral second syllable, means "thing, stuff". What does dōngxī, with two first tones, mean?
questions.explanation: dōngxī (东 east + 西 west) means "east and west". The neutral tone is what makes {东西|dōng xi} "thing": a neutral syllable can tell two words apart.

questions.stem: You're saying a word with two full tones, such as gōngzuò (work). What's the best advice?
choices: stress the first syllable and shorten the second, as in English
give both syllables their full tone and their full length
make the second syllable short and neutral
say the second syllable twice as loud
questions.explanation: Descriptions of Mandarin stress differ, but every syllable with a full tone keeps its vowel and its tone. Shortening one syllable, as English speakers tend to, makes gōngzuò hard to understand. Only neutral-tone syllables are short and light.

questions.stem: 你好 (hello) is written nǐ hǎo. Which tones do you hear when it's said?
questions.explanation: Two third tones in a row: the first is said as a second tone, so you hear 2+3 (ní hǎo). It is still written nǐ hǎo. Lesson 11 practises this change.

questions.stem: Which two words have the same tone pattern?
questions.explanation: míngtiān (tomorrow) and shíjiān (time) are both 2+1. píngguǒ is 2+3 but xiǎoshí 3+2; lǎoshī is 3+1 but xuéxí 2+2; gōngzuò is 1+4 but wèntí 4+2.

questions.stem: Type 谢谢 (thank you) in pinyin with tone numbers, using 5 for the neutral tone: ___
questions.explanation: xie4 xie5 becomes xièxie: a fourth tone, then a neutral syllable with no mark. Two full falls (xiè xiè) would sound stilted.

questions.stem: Type 老师 (teacher) in pinyin with tone numbers: ___
questions.explanation: lao3 shi1 becomes lǎoshī: 3+1. The third tone is said low, with no rise, before the high shī.

questions.stem: Match each word (written without tone marks) to its tone pattern.
questions.explanation: jīntiān 1+1, xuéxiào 2+4, mǐfàn 3+4, diànnǎo 4+3 and péngyou 2 + neutral: all models from the table of 20 patterns.

questions.stem: Wang Fang meets her teacher and greets him. What does she say?
questions.explanation: {老师|lǎo shī}{好|hǎo}, "teacher + good", is how students greet a teacher: 3+1, then 3. {好|hǎo}{老师|lǎo shī} would mean "a good teacher", {你|nǐ}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī} "you are a teacher", and {再见|zài jiàn} is goodbye.

questions.stem: Listen. Which word did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard {小时|xiǎo shí} (hour): a low half-third tone, then a rise, 3+2. Don't confuse it with 2+3, which rises first.

questions.stem: Listen. Which word did you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard {再见|zài jiàn} (goodbye): two falling tones in a zigzag, the first falling only halfway, the second all the way down. 4+4.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {中国|Zhōng guó}, China: 1+2. Keep zhōng high and flat, then rise on guó.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {苹果|píng guǒ}, apple: 2+3. The voice rises, then drops low.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {老师|lǎo shī}, teacher: 3+1. The third tone is a low half-third before the high, level shī.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {电脑|diàn nǎo}, computer: 4+3. A fall, then the voice stays low.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {朋友|péng you}, friend: 2 + neutral. The second syllable is short, light and low.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {姐姐|jiě jie}, older sister: 3 + neutral. After the low third tone, the neutral syllable sits higher.

questions.stem: How is 你好 (hello), written nǐ hǎo, said?
choices: with two full dips, nǐ hǎo
questions.explanation: Before another third tone, a third tone is said as a second: ní hǎo. The last syllable keeps its third tone. Two full dips would be slow and unnatural, and the change never affects the second syllable.

questions.stem: Why does pinyin keep writing nǐ hǎo, not ní hǎo?
choices: because the change is optional and most speakers don't make it
because ní hǎo would mean something else
because pinyin shows each syllable's own tone, and the change follows automatically from the next syllable
because only the second syllable changes
questions.explanation: Pinyin writes the dictionary tone of each syllable. The 3+3 change depends on the syllable that follows, and it's completely regular, so readers apply it themselves. Every speaker makes it, and it's the first syllable that changes.

questions.stem: In which phrase is 不 said bú?
questions.explanation: 不 becomes bú only before a fourth tone, and shì is a fourth tone: bú shì. Before lái (2nd), hǎo (3rd) and chī (1st) it stays bù.

questions.stem: In which phrase is 一 said yí?
questions.explanation: Before a fourth tone 一 is yí: yí gè ({个|gè} is a fourth tone, even when said lightly). Before the first, second and third tones of tiān, nián and qǐ it is yì.

questions.stem: In which of these is 一 said yī, its original tone?
questions.explanation: As an ordinal (第一 dì yī), in counting, in numbers and dates and at the end of a word, 一 keeps yī. In front of a following syllable it changes: yíxià, yìqǐ, yìdiǎnr.

questions.stem: How does this course write 看一看 (have a look)?
questions.explanation: Between a repeated verb, 一 is light and toneless: kàn yi kàn. It would be yí before a 4th tone elsewhere, but in this V-一-V pattern it loses its tone.

questions.stem: How does this course write 好不好 (is that OK?)?
questions.explanation: In an "A not A" question, 不 is light: hǎo bu hǎo. bú appears only before a fourth tone, and 好 keeps its written third tone: háo is never written.

questions.stem: 展览馆 (exhibition hall) is 展览 zhǎnlǎn (exhibition) + 馆 guǎn (hall), three third tones. How is it usually said?
choices: zhǎn lǎn guǎn, with no change
questions.explanation: A two-syllable word plus one: both syllables of 展览 rise, and the last keeps its third tone: zhán lán guǎn (2+2+3). Compare 小老虎 xiǎo + lǎohǔ, said xiǎo láo hǔ.

questions.stem: 一定 (certainly) is written yídìng in this course. How do most dictionaries write it?
questions.explanation: Dictionaries write 一 and 不 with their original tones everywhere: yīdìng, bùshì. The national standard allows the changed tones in teaching, which is what this course does. Both spellings are the same word, said yídìng.

questions.stem: Type 不是 (isn't) as this course writes it, with tone numbers: ___
questions.explanation: bu2 shi4: before the fourth tone of shì, 不 is bú. Dictionaries write bùshì, but you say bú shì either way.

questions.stem: Type 一起 (together) as this course writes it, with tone numbers: ___
questions.explanation: yi4 qi3: before the third tone of qǐ, 一 is yì. Before a fourth tone it would be yí (yíxià).

questions.stem: How is 一 said in each phrase?
questions.explanation: yí before a fourth tone (gè), yì before tones 1 to 3 (tiān, diǎnr), yī as a number or ordinal (第一), and light between a repeated verb (看一看).

questions.stem: Reading out a phone number, how do many people say the digit 1?
questions.explanation: In phone and room numbers 1 is often said yāo, so it can't be mistaken for {七|qī} (seven). In other counting it is yī.

questions.stem: Listen. How is 不 said in what you hear?
questions.explanation: You heard {不要|bú yào} (don't): yào is a fourth tone, so 不 rises: bú.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables? (Give the written tones or the ones you hear.)
questions.explanation: {你好|nǐ hǎo}: written 3+3, said 2+3. Either answer counts.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables? (Give the written tones or the ones you hear.)
questions.explanation: {水果|shuǐ guǒ}, fruit: written 3+3, said shuí guǒ, 2+3.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {不是|bú shì}, isn't: 2+4. Before the fourth tone of shì, 不 rises.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {一定|yí dìng}, certainly: 2+4. 一 rises before a fourth tone.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the two syllables?
questions.explanation: {一天|yì tiān}, one day: 4+1. Before the first tone of tiān, 一 falls.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the three syllables? (Give the written tones or the ones you hear.)
questions.explanation: {展览馆|zhǎn lǎn guǎn}, exhibition hall: written 3+3+3. It is {展览|zhǎn lǎn} + {馆|guǎn}, so both syllables of 展览 rise and you usually hear zhán lán guǎn, 2+2+3. The written tones count too.

questions.stem: Listen. Which tones are the three syllables? (Give the written tones or the ones you hear.)
questions.explanation: {小老虎|xiǎo lǎo hǔ}, little tiger: written 3+3+3. It is {小|xiǎo} + {老虎|lǎo hǔ}: {老|lǎo} rises before {虎|hǔ}, and {小|xiǎo} usually stays low, so you hear 3+2+3 (xiǎo láo hǔ). Fast speakers may say 2+2+3, and that counts too, as do the written tones.

questions.stem: How many syllables is 哪儿 (where?)?
questions.explanation: In erhua words 儿 isn't a syllable of its own: it melts into the one before as an r sound. {哪儿|nǎr} is one syllable written with two characters. 儿 is a syllable (ér) only in words like {女儿|nǚ ér}.

questions.stem: How is 一点儿 (a little), written yìdiǎnr, pronounced?
choices: yìdiǎn ér, with 儿 as its own syllable
with a clear n, then r
yìdiǎr: the n is dropped before the r
questions.explanation: Before the erhua r, a final -n or -i disappears: diǎnr sounds diǎr, wánr sounds wár. The spelling keeps the n so the word can still be looked up.

questions.stem: How is 一点儿 (a little) written in pinyin?
questions.explanation: Add -r to the syllable and keep its spelling: yìdiǎnr. yìdiǎr writes the sound, not the spelling; yìdiǎn'ér would make 儿 a syllable of its own.

questions.stem: Where is erhua most common?
choices: Beijing and much of northern China
the far south, such as Guangdong
questions.explanation: Erhua is typical of Beijing and the north. It's very rare in Taiwan and Singapore, and many southern speakers use it much less. The plain forms ({哪里|nǎ lǐ}, {这里|zhè lǐ}) are standard everywhere.

questions.stem: Which word means the same as {哪儿|nǎr} (where?) but has no erhua?
questions.explanation: {哪里|nǎ lǐ} is "where?" without erhua, usual in the south and in Taiwan. {那里|nà lǐ} and {那儿|nàr} mean "there" (fourth tone), and {这儿|zhèr} means "here".

questions.stem: In {空儿|kòngr} (free time), what happens to the -ng before the erhua r?
choices: it is dropped, and the vowel is said through the nose
it stays, and the r follows it
it stays, and the r is silent
questions.explanation: Before the erhua r, -ng disappears but leaves the vowel nasal. A final -n or -i simply disappears.

questions.stem: Which of these is not a correct pinyin spelling?
questions.explanation: After j, q, x and y the dots of ü are dropped, so the syllable is written ju (jù, jú…), never jü. After n and l the dots stay (nǚ), and yú is the correct spelling of ü alone.

questions.stem: Which of these syllables does not exist in Mandarin?
questions.explanation: g, k and h never go with i-finals, so there is no gi. ji and xi have the i of "ee"; zhi has the buzzed vowel that follows zh ch sh r z c s.

questions.stem: Which of these syllables does not exist in Mandarin?
questions.explanation: ü goes only after n, l, j, q, x and y, so there is no bü. bu (as in {不|bù}), lü ({绿|lǜ}) and nü ({女|nǚ}) are all real.

questions.stem: Not counting tones, about how many different syllables does Mandarin have?
